The words have reached him, but his mind has not yet arrived; their essence has not yet merged, and his emotions have not yet been forgotten.

Unable to avoid it, he forcibly writes down a few words in a song titled "Jiepeiling" (The Unfastening of the Girdle). To those with clear eyes, if one looks upon this, thirty blows of the staff will not be spared.
Why is this so? It is because adding frost to snow is improper. The "Jiepeiling" says: Before heaven and before earth, what name and what form can there be?

Amanta is beyond all comparison; enlightenment is encountered at every turn. It is simply that people are unwilling to accept this, remaining instead mired in saṃsāra through their attachment to names and forms.
Within the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm, there is neither thought nor conception; the rice of Luling requires no deliberation.
As soon as the blood-vessels are unobstructed, one knows it at once. Striking wood produces no sound; striking empty space turns all into golden resonance.
Standing in the snow in the cypress courtyard was a total failure. To realize non-action is to find rest in the present moment. A hundred times, a thousand times—it is simply this.
The solitary, perfect moon of the mind requires no polishing; it is eternally bright and pure, without excess and without deficiency, beyond hearing and beyond speaking.
The old man of Shaoyang obtained but a single fragment; when the Ten Sages and Three Worthies heard it mentioned, their souls dissolved and their courage shattered.
Only Puan remained utterly tranquil and extinguished. Suddenly, a monk named Daochen arrived from Sichuan through the snow. Upon meeting the Master, he said:
"This is not a friend I have invited," he said, and so they proceeded to cross-examine one another. As blows and shouts flew back and forth, their minds reached a secret accord.
The monk said, "The Master is a man of the Second Coming; you shall greatly propagate our Way—who else but you could do so? Thereupon, he pointed to the snow, wrote a verse, and departed.

From then on, he extensively established ferries and bridges, venerated stupas and temples, and provided protection against calamities and misfortunes. Though his movements affected both heaven and the world, even ghosts and spirits could not fathom his transformations.
His talismans, hymns, and medicinal waters were verified in the world more than once. He once praised himself, saying: "Heaven! Heaven!

Having awakened to the Dharma of non-arising, I speak of that which cannot be spoken as Chan. Opening these two flaps of skin, I encompass the earth and include the heavens. What is the Buddha? Ten [times ten]."
18,000 [characters]. On the twenty-first day of the seventh month in the fifth year of the Qiandao era (the Jichou year), he bathed and wrote this verse on the western wall of his quarters:
"Rain and sun alternate as the precious elephant shines; East, west, south, and north, the chaotic clouds deepen."
Countless people have lost their pearls and suffered through calamities; may this illusory response to your provisional capacity purify them. The "Rescue of the Withered Tree" is hereby completed.
Having finished writing, he sat in the full lotus position and passed away. On the first day of the eleventh month of winter, his entire body was enshrined in a stupa.
In the first month of the sixth year of the Chunxi era (the Jihai year), his disciple Ying Shi wrote this and requested that Linjiang Ganzhai Xie E compose an inscription.

Regarding this stupa, I, Ciyu, being of dull wit, have received the entrustment of the twenty-third generation of transmission; I have therefore compiled these brief accounts to inform those who study hereafter.
As for the various miraculous responses, they are detailed in the Inner Biography. Thus it is said.
The Way of the Buddha, as inscribed upon this stupa epitaph, takes compassion as its essence and skillful means as its function.

Beyond these, all empty talk and hollow rhetoric—whether it be the arduous exertion of mind and heart to the point of wasting days and years, or dwelling in mountain caves while frequenting marketplaces—are none of them the Buddha’s fundamental intent. Therefore:
As for those who serve as his disciples—those with square robes and shaven heads who depart—they too must rely on this to attain correctness.
Twenty years ago, while I was in my hometown, I frequently heard that there was a monk in Yuanzhou named Puan;

what he had attained was beyond my knowledge, yet his deeds were deeply capable of moving the ears and eyes of people. Consequently, throughout the rivers and lakes, they rushed about, bowing in devotion.
He moved [the people], regretting that they could not see [the Buddha]. Yet his earnest exhortations did no more than encourage them to do good and warn them against doing evil;
he verified for them what constitutes auspiciousness and blessing, and moved them by what constitutes misfortune and calamity.
Those who listened were all sufficiently inspired to arouse their virtuous hearts and eliminate their evil thoughts. Instances such as these numbered in the tens of millions.

As for those worldly undertakings that rely on material causes—such as building bridges and repairing roads to aid people—at all places where waves and tides pose dangers, they have frequently accomplished great works.
Their engineering prowess is magnificent, and their architectural design and atmosphere illuminate the mountains and rivers.
Thus, when discussing meritorious acts of construction, one must invariably cite Puan as the exemplar. Others...
As for those who have undertaken construction projects, many have followed the legacy of Puan; I too lament that I have not yet been able to see him even once to fulfill my long-cherished wish.
Whenever I pass over his bridge, I always gaze intently at the inscriptions and verses he left behind, filled with admiration and envy.
For the most part, this arises from the skillful means (*upāya*) of compassion. Is not the Way of the Buddha found herein?

In the first month of the sixth year of the Chunxi era, his disciple, the monk Yingshi, generously dispatched a monk bearing a letter, along with a record of his life’s achievements (*xing-shi*) composed by Ouyang Shimei, the Assistant Secretary of the Regional Inspectorate of Jingnan.
Both arrived together, entrusting him with the task of writing an inscription for his stupa. His words were as follows:

It is said: "More than ten years have passed since our former master entered nirvana. Whenever I reflect upon the gift of the Dharma-milk that brought me great peace and joy, I feel a sense of deficiency and regret at the lack of proper rites.
Alas! I truly cannot help but voice my previous sentiments; therefore, it is fitting to compose this inscription.
The Master’s name was Yinsu; he was the son of the Yu family from Yichun County. At the age of six, he had a dream (as described). [The dream involved] a *śarīra*-bead. His parents..."

For this reason, he was permitted to leave the household life under the Venerable Master Hyon of Soryongwon. At the age of twenty-seven, he shaved his head; the following year, he received full ordination.
The Master’s appearance was imposing and his intellectual nature was skillful and wise. Master Hyon recognized his potential and encouraged him to recite the scriptures.

The Master said, "I have heard that the fundamental principle of all Buddhas must consist in attaining realization within the mind. Counting characters and following the lines of the text provides no benefit."
Having thus taken his leave of his teacher, he traveled through the regions of Lake Xiang and called upon Master Zhong of Mugaan at Daopei.

He then inquired about the myriad dharmas [and so forth]. Later, he returned to his home monastery. In the year of Guiyou, a master named Cihua from a neighboring temple was invited by the assembly to serve as abbot.

As the temple had no permanent endowment, the Master lived with a coarse cotton quilt and robes of paper; he ate only morning gruel and evening meals. Aside from his meditative concentration, he devoted himself solely to reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and its commentaries. One—
One day he attained great enlightenment; sweat flowed from his entire body, and with joy he said, "I have now personally realized the realm of the *Avataṃsaka*.
He then composed a verse, beginning with "Squeezing... (and so forth). From this point on, whenever he uttered words, they awakened both the profound and the manifest;

it was as if it happened spontaneously, without being sought. One day, a monk named Daochen suddenly arrived, braving the snow. Upon seeing him, the Master looked at him and said with delight, "This..."
"I have not sought out friends for this," he said. Thereupon, they sat together in silence, engaging in a dialogue of questions and answers, sometimes laughing and sometimes shouting.
The monk said, "The Master is one who has returned; before long, you shall greatly propagate our Teaching. He then pointed at the snow, wrote a verse, and departed.
The Master then withdrew to a hermitage on the Southern Ridge, adopting the name Puan (Universal Hermitage).

He forgot his concerns for the world until Ding Junji, the Circuit Inspector of the four counties, together with the elder Liu Ruming, jointly requested him to leave the mountains, pledging to provide funds for expenses so that he might once again extend his compassionate transformation by rebuilding the Buddha Hall.
The Master declined, but could not prevail; he ultimately acceded to their request. Consequently, those who admired the Way and were drawn toward his influence became numerous.
The Master then taught them according to their needs, or wrote verses for them. For those suffering from illness, he would break off grass to serve as medicine, and they were healed immediately.
When there was a pestilence such that people could not even travel to one another's doors, the Master gave them verses, and all were completely cured.
As for praying for rain or fine weather, felling monstrous trees, or destroying licentious shrines, his spiritual responses were manifold. Thus it was.

Public works were extensively undertaken. The wealthy contributed their wealth; the poor contributed their labor; and the skilled contributed their arts. Because of this, the temple was completely renovated.
For thousands of li in every direction, roads were cleared and bridges were built; that people delighted in performing such virtuous deeds was entirely due to the Master’s transformational influence.
Someone asked the Master, "What practice did you cultivate to attain this? The Master then drew in the air and said, "Do you understand?
The man replied, "I do not. The Master said, "Cease, cease; there is no need to speak. His sharp wit and profound eloquence were often like this.

Furthermore, his songs, hymns, and praises circulated widely among the people; for instance, the *Song of Realizing the Way* and the *Record of Judging the Source* have already become prevalent in the world. Suddenly—
One day, he requested a brush and wrote a verse in the abbot’s quarters (as follows): “Withered wood saves and delivers. Having finished the verse, he addressed the assembly, saying:
“The Buddhas do not appear in the world, nor is there any nirvana. Those who enter my room will surely be able to achieve profound resonance.”
He skillfully guarded and maintained himself, ensuring that he did not fall away from his practice. He requested a bath, changed his robes, and sat in the full lotus posture in meditative stillness.
This was on the twenty-first day of the seventh month in the fifth year of the Qiandao era. He was fifty-five years of age, with twenty-eight years of monastic seniority (*bhikṣu-varṣa*).
On the first day of the eleventh month, his entire body was enshrined in a stupa. At that time, the fourfold assembly gathered like clouds; the sound of their lamentation shook the mountains.
This is, in brief, the general outline of Master Gu’s life from beginning to end. From what I have heard, his wondrous deeds and extraordinary traces have certainly been recorded repeatedly;
they cannot be fully recounted in a single account. For now, I shall provide a preface and compose an inscription based on the circumstances of his time in Jingnan.
The Inscription reads: The Buddha thinks of sentient beings and extensively provides for their salvation; yet because he follows the ordinary Way, some may not easily attain awakening.

At times he manifests extraordinary and magnificent deeds, startling the ears and eyes, to stir their virtuous hearts. Like piling up earth to form a mountain, Master Puan’s fame resounds throughout his native land.
Those who hear of him or behold him find silent realization. He has also constructed halls and buildings, and established bridges and causeways. Thus he acts...
The skillful means of this proclamation have deep roots and a long current. Even so, it is but a playful manifestation. Its movement is not movement;
its stillness is not stillness. The Master is without mind; the clouds part and the moon shines bright. The Way of the Master endures forever—what need is there for an inscription?
The Imperial Preface to *Puan* (etcetera):

"To awaken to the Way through the mind; to realize the mind through the Way. Vast and boundless, it has no limit or shore. The Master, having attained awakening upon reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, said:
(etcetera). Suddenly he was enlightened. After a long while, he bowed his head again and said with a smile: 'Fortunately, I have encountered [the Buddha]...'"
It may be said (and so forth). The two men looked at each other and laughed (and so forth). Quiescence. He ascended the hall to address the assembly:
"The manifestations of response are not the ultimate reality; the Buddha arises from conditions. For kalpas as numerous as dust motes they have remained unawakened, yet today there is a cause.

Puan points the wayward back to the correct path: first, maintain the precepts and meditative concentration to settle the household; next, assist in the cultivation of the Dharma to repay the state. After three years have passed, the Buddhist temple is about to..."
Pervading everywhere throughout the ten directions, his spiritual resources were inexhaustible. The monks and practitioners all forgot their hunger and lost track of their sleep;
they exerted themselves with steadfast resolve, each enduring hardship and bitterness without ever turning back. Though beset by demons and slandered, they maintained their own resolute commitment.

Neither do they harm life or injure the spirit, nor do they abandon their homes or lose their livelihoods. They contemplate the great matter of birth and death and reflect on the difficulty of escaping the cycles of karma.

If you do not awaken yourself to awaken others, who will deliver you? Now observe that those who have attained enlightenment and become Buddhas or Bodhisattvas all did so by cultivating their minds over many kalpas;
once they fully comprehend a single thought-moment, they immediately understand how to transform the great earth, mountains, and rivers. And...

He fashioned them of gold, yet cast aside the jade and gold of the world so that they were all equal to mere rubble. Within the wondrous gate of formlessness, he manifested hundreds of thousands of samādhis;
he transformed the myriad classes of beings to preach the One Mind, subduing a hundred heresies to rely upon the True Path.

In his discourse on Chan, even a blink of an eye was nothing other than the true mark (dharmatā). To point the way for those lost in delusion, there must be no passing over until full awakening. Furthermore, he enlightened kings, dukes, and ministers.
Regarding these marks: that you, O virtuous and noble Prince, are thus endowed—if you had not cultivated the causes through the ten wholesome paths of action, how could you be as you are today?
That you possess these ten marks in their entirety is entirely due to the power of past causes; it is now that you receive their fruit. Thus one must lament for the various classes of beings.
Poor and lowly, their clothing does not cover their bodies and their food does not fill their mouths.

They are driven by others and find no moment of rest. When the kalpa ends, they are born again, wearing fur and bearing horns; even after ten thousand kalpas, it is difficult to convert them, and through a thousand lifetimes, how can they escape the wheel of suffering?

The cause of affliction lies in the greed and anger of life after life; the source of suffering arises from the karmic bonds formed birth after birth. By whom were these causes of suffering and affliction created? Fundamentally...
Coming here is but one's own mind; from where could wealth and honor be obtained? The losing of the game is fundamentally equal [to winning].

Therefore, the Buddha, relying on great compassion, regards all sentient beings as his only child. He extensively proclaims vast vows and firmly erects the banner of the Dharma; he provisionally teaches the Three Vehicles to point the way back to the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
If there were no Buddhas to preach the Dharma, who would establish the ten stages of sages and the three levels of worthies? If one does not pay homage to the Buddha...
Master: How can one strive to transcend the mundane and enter the sacred? The Dharma does not arise in isolation; its conditions lie within the minds of the assembly.

To achieve it together through mutual praise, one must rely upon a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). A spiritual friend distinguishes between good and evil, delusion and awakening, unlike ordinary sentiments that merely pursue appearances and follow sounds.
How can one distinguish the true from the false within this? If it is true, the Dharma-body is pure; there is a creator who expediently transforms sentient beings.

Only by attaining a point of entry does one awaken for oneself and become able to distinguish the black from the white. Mind and object are as one. If it is false, form and emptiness are muddled, and speech and silence are deceptive.
One may discourse on the sutras without understanding the Buddha’s intent, and speak of Chan while failing to enter the penetration of the school. From oneself—
One's own karmic consciousness is vast and empty, with no fundamental basis to rely upon. How much more so when one attempts to untie the bonds of a prisoner or carry a person while intoxicated?
A thousand-year dark room meets no lamp; to further grind ink thickly and splash it about is like a blind man leading the way, causing all the sightless to fall into a perilous pit.
Using heterodox arts to treat delusion results in the entire family perishing from an epidemic. Those of the True Dharma understand this.

When the mind reaches its source, its essence is like empty space; without moving a step, the Dharma pervades the ten directions, and in a single kṣaṇa, one perfectly accomplishes the state beyond outflows.
Nature and characteristics are equal; phenomena and principle are both as they are. One has never seen a single sentient being who does not have immeasurable radiance as their retinue.
Within the mirror of the myriad phenomena, there are no shadows or traces; in a single room with a thousand lamps, the flames overlap in layers. If one can...
It is thus that one truly manifests the state of renunciation; if this is not yet the case, one must simply engage in self-reflection. Therefore, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states:

"Even the realization of the Way involves no attainment, for the fundamental nature is already complete. It further says: "When awakening pervades the ten directions, one immediately attains the Buddha-way.
And it also says: "The teachings of the *sūtras* are like a finger pointing at the moon; if one sees the moon, one understands what the finger was pointing to."
Ultimately, it is not the moon. To rely on an incorrect teacher is what is called a "false teacher. The errors and faults of a false teacher are not the fault of sentient beings.

Good son, the sutras are the Buddha’s words; dhyāna is the Buddha’s mind. Mind and speech are not mere texts; the Buddha-dharma is beyond verbal expression. Therefore, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
"There is no dharma that can be preached; this is called preaching the Dharma. Taking formlessness as form—this is called reality.
No phenomena can be apprehended; this is called true attainment. No mind can be apprehended; this is called the true mind.
The true mind pervades all places, yet it has no dual nature. Upon the ground of non-abiding, it establishes all dharmas.
Therefore, the Elder Puan, having received the Buddha’s wisdom and my samādhi in its entirety—neither deficient nor superfluous—dwells eternally in the world without desire for anything.
This matter is supramundane; how could one speak of its own merit? For twelve years, I kept it deeply hidden and secret, leisurely searching through the treasury of the teachings.

Without relying on words and letters, I beheld the Dharmakāya. I perused the *Lamp of the Transmission* with diligence, discerning and shattering its mechanical devices to transcend the patriarchal intent.
The Dharma-body pervades the entire person; the Dharma is majestic and sublime. The ten thousand dharmas are but mind; True Suchness is uniquely revealed.
For this reason, when he saw people questioning what was not seen, he responded to the Master with difficult words; realizing that the Way is wordless, he entered a solitary peak to hide his traces.
Yet, seeing those with faith rushing to pay their respects, never leaving him morning or night, he again exercised his wisdom and compassion—the virtue of the Buddha’s grace.

If one contemplates this present life, it can be resolved once and for all, and one will no longer be deluded. Yet, by observing the succession of kalpas, one realizes that only through diligent cultivation can one achieve true accord with reality.
Although I have attained liberation myself, I take pity on the masses who remain lost. If I do not respond to beings according to their capacities, there will ultimately be no benefit for them here.

The Sūtra says: "It is solely by means of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision that sentient beings are shown and awakened. Thus, the World-Honored One appeared in the world. If there were no sentient beings, the Buddha would have neither coming nor going;
it would be like placing one's head upon one's own head. Responding to sounds and responding to forms, those who know me do not require even half a person;
those who do not know me may manifest as hundreds or thousands. I am like a wild crane or a solitary cloud; my Dharmakāya is perfectly complete.
You are like the moon reflected in water or flowers in the sky; you have no fundamental basis to rely upon. If I point my finger-tip to indicate the true mark (*dharmatā*), you call me mad.
If I take up my staff to investigate the mind, you become terrified. If I instruct you to read sutras or recite mantras, you are like a blind child who has lost its mother’s milk.
If I instruct you to prostrate to the Buddha or practice seated meditation, it only results in being bound by the Dharma. If I instruct you to always remain by my side...
There is nothing to be chewed upon. Contemplating deeply through shallow metaphors, one examines their underlying nature and finds it difficult to entrust them to the profound pivot.

Thus, one cannot avoid provisionally establishing a "transformed city" (nirvāṇa) as a temporary resting place for weary toil, while pointing toward the ultimate destination: the Treasure Place. This Treasure Place is near; it is your original home.
The Great Treasure is boundless, yet you have not been able to utilize it. Your parents think of you; seeing no means to reach you, they desire your return and thus entrust [this teaching] to you.

I entrust this to you as a precious treasure. If you do not decline the long journey nor shrink from the hardships of the road, taking tranquility as your heart and the solitary cloud as your companion, then day after day and year after year, without seeking satiety in food, the principle of reality will manifest before you; and without seeking comfort in dwelling, concentration and wisdom will remain ever-perfected.
Suddenly, hearing the warbling of orioles on the willow paths and the calls of those selling flowers under the sky, you shall witness it with your own eyes.
The father’s body is boundless; when the son arrives, the seven treasures are spread upon the ground. What more need be said of the realm of the *Avataṃsaka*?

Cease for a moment your boasting of the Western Paradise of Ultimate Bliss. Had it not been for the fisherman guiding him into the deep stream, how could he have passed through the Dragon Gate and attained the highest degree?
Upon first hearing the Buddha’s teaching, I thought I would remain forever a sentient being; today, through this wondrous hearing, I have attained sudden enlightenment, and the Buddha—
There is no separate essence. Therefore, I have established this ancient monastery, the Cihua (Compassionate Transformation) Doctrinal Center. First, I pray for the Emperor’s life to be boundless;
next, I repay the grace of the ministers and the Chancellor, as well as the four debts of gratitude and the three realms of existence—all of which are my own mind.

If my mind is pure, the Dharma-realm is at peace; if my mind turns away from it, I commit the karma of the Avīci Hell. May Heaven endure long and Earth last forever, and may the rain of Dharma and the breeze of compassion prevail. May we all assemble here.
All things share a single source; they are equal to heaven and earth as one. Cherish this.
Ascending the hall to instruct the assembly, he said:
"The three realms are mind alone—only a Buddha understands this. The myriad dharmas are consciousness alone—who else knows it? Delusion and enlightenment are fundamentally..."

There is no authority to establish transformation; it is just like using yellow leaves to stop a child’s crying. Nirvana and birth-and-death are both like dreams. Who are the Ten Sages and the Three Worthies?
There is a thing prior to heaven that has no form or appearance; words cannot reach its essence—Amitābha. This very Amitābha is your own mind;
do not trouble yourself to seek it outside of appearances. The three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas are established according to the occasion.
Mind, mind, mind is just this very moment. If a person does not understand that the mind has no characteristics, they will cling to objects and be deluded regarding the truth;

they will be attached to form while perceiving form and sound as having no dual essence. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth preach the True Sutra. I dare ask you all: how is the True Sutra preached?
(After a long silence, he said: Now the wondrous sound is without interruption; it is only because Kāśyapa does not hear what can be heard. Furthermore:
He said: "Do you understand? If you can understand it right here, then I grant that you share the same single radiance as the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and enjoy it together with me, Puan.
If this is not yet so, then I shall now, without sparing my verbal karma, speak for you."
I shall now explain this further for you all to break through [delusion]. Good son, do you understand?
The entire world of heaven and earth is your single eye; the body born of your parents is but a single film.
All ordinary people do not know this one adamantine, wondrously luminous, perfectly reflecting, and unfailing eye, yet they stubbornly cling to a father...
Born of the mother-condition, obscured by the dust of the minute; thus one mistakes the flowers of the sky for the true reality and grasps at the moon in the water as a real form.
When will birth and death ever cease? On what day will one emerge from drowning in the cycle of saṃsāra? Killing and devouring one another sows the seeds of bitter retribution;
loving and lustful attachment is the root of birth and death. Changing heads and faces, the familiar becomes the stranger; wearing horns and shrouded in fur.
Regarding extinction and non-extinction: for the time being, you do not know that within a single mote of dust, the Buddhas of the ten directions are ceaselessly preaching the Dharma;

nor do you know that within a single mote of dust, there are eighty-four thousand Avīci hells. You merely insist on taking existence as non-existence and the unreal as real. As the ancient masters said:
"When a single film obscures the eye, the flowers in the sky are perceived as real forms. It is like grasping at the moon reflected in water.
Pervading the entire realm, one suddenly awakens to the original mind; there is no dharma that is not understood.

If one can, in a single thought-moment, behold a true teacher (kalyāṇamitra) and, upon hearing the Dharma, receive it with faith, one will spontaneously attain the opening of the mind. Instantly, one realizes one's nature, which fills the Dharma-realm.

Nothing fails to harmonize; no particle remains unpenetrated; no dharma remains uncomprehended. Free from both self and what belongs to self—who is it that attains this? It is ineffable, yet it is the truth.
It is constantly said: it cannot be obtained, yet it is obtained in this very way. Taking the Dharma as one’s body, that body contains the infinite space of the ten directions;
not even a single mote of dust has ever existed in opposition to me, nor do I perceive a single dharma as something I have attained.
If one reaches this state, one is like a single wheel of the precious moon, solitary, luminous, and serenely illuminating; or like a single *maṇi* jewel.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "It manifests according to form, yet is without name or mark; it is without limit or manifestation, absolute and beyond dependence; it is neither large nor small, and it is neither born nor extinguished.
It illuminates the myriad phenomena with light that never ceases. Only in this way is one truly able to break open the subtle dust;

if one does not accord with suchness, one will never reach the ultimate. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "There was a wise man who broke open a particle of dust and brought forth from it this sūtra scroll, its measure being as vast as the cosmos."

Equal to the great trichiliocosm. The Buddha’s words are not false, yet few believe and understand them. Good sons and good daughters, if you do not now give rise to even a single wholesome thought, you are but beings of evil karma.
When the Buddha pronounces a single word of goodness and bestows a name upon you, and when a person makes a wholesome vow, the heavens will surely grant it.
All merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges arise from this single wholesome act.
It shall never change or decay. For eons in hell you will suffer pain; because of this single evil deed, you will incur retribution and find it difficult to escape the wheel of suffering.
Good and evil depend solely on your own mind; suffering and joy are experienced by you alone. If, even now, greed, anger, and delusion do not cease—
The three evil realms are fixed and difficult to escape; now, with compassion and firm wisdom, one is certain to see one's nature and attain the Buddha-way.
Nowadays, fools see the fruit but do not know its cause; in every thought they give rise to ignorance, which is just like failing to sow the seed.

Empty-handed, one reaps the harvest of autumn; morning and evening, one engages in killing. Facing death, one calls upon Avalokiteśvara, yet it is difficult for even a Buddha’s appearance to save one.
All efforts are spent in vain; once lost is this human body, one falls among the fur-bearing creatures for ten thousand kalpas.
The wise man, verifying the fruit, thereby knows the cause; he realizes that reality is neither form nor name. When words fill the world, there is no fault of the mouth; when conduct fills the world—
The assembly all held him in reverence. If you wish to broadly deliver beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it is better that you first realize your own true mind.

Only when you have attained the realization that the mindless state is originally the Buddha can you employ skillful means to guide the multitude of living beings. It is impossible for one who does not maintain the precepts themselves to cause others to maintain them;
it is impossible for one who is not pure themselves to cause others to be pure; it is impossible for one who has not seen their own nature themselves to cause others to see it...
To see the nature of another is impossible. To untie the bonds of another while one’s own bonds remain unloosed is impossible.
Therefore, the ancient masters said: "To urge the blind and deaf when the deluded have not yet understood is to add a layer of mud upon the earth.
"The intent of the awakened person is like the intent of the deluded; they constantly dwell within delusion and do not encounter it. O virtuous ones, do you now fear evil?

Delight in goodness. Observe the fasts and uphold the precepts. You must by no means rely upon external paths or demonic influences, gathering at night and dispersing at dawn, coveting beauty and wealth, propagating heretical teachings, or giving rise to false rumors.
These are merely laypeople falsely claiming to be of the Southern School or Northern Patriarchate, practicing the stages of the four fruits of arhatship, and corrupting the people’s lineages;
they bring no lasting benefit. If government officials do not investigate them thoroughly to their roots, [the harm will continue]. Do not...
It causes one to be seized by others; if alive, one enters a prison that is no light matter, and if dead, one falls into the Avīci Hell that is no shallow depth.

O virtuous ones! Erroneous teachings are like frost and ice, while the Right Path is like the sun. When the brilliant sun shines in the heavens, there is nowhere it does not illuminate; frost and ice melt away when the sun is warm.

The Buddha’s preaching of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the scriptures, when brought together, converge upon this single remedy for the cataract of ignorance. It is as if one has suffered from chronic illness for many years.
Seeking no medicine, over five thousand scrolls are needlessly spread out. The retinues of the Demon King gather in throngs; morning and evening they chant folk songs as their place of practice.
Only the *Puan* (Universal Hut) contains the true essentials. With one voice and different mouths, they praise our Emperor.
When the great assembly praises our Emperor with a single phrase, how would you speak of it? (After a long silence, he said: "With this profound mind, I offer myself to all lands."
This is precisely what is called repaying the debt of gratitude to the nation. Be careful.
Regarding the formal discourse on bathing the Buddha:
it is fundamentally nameless. Those ancient sages who silently realized this numinous awareness provisionally designated it as the "Dharma-body without marks," O Gautama.

With a wife’s earnest concern, he provisionally says that there is birth; yet birth is fundamentally non-birth, and cessation is fundamentally non-cessation. Birth and cessation are fundamentally non-existent.

For one who possesses the complete Valley-Spirit (*guśen*), skillful means manifest and conceal themselves. Our Buddha Śākyamuni, during his causal stage (*yindi*) over kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, gave away his body, life, and wealth in alms;
he forgot his own person for the sake of the Dharma, yet all of this did not transcend the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Therefore, his true mind had not yet been realized. Directly...

Upon meeting Dīpaṃkara, because he attained non-attainment regarding all phenomena, he first gave rise to the bodhicitta and was then granted the prediction that he would become a Buddha in a future age under the provisional name Śākyamuni.
Because this karmic case remained unresolved, he could not avoid the temporary manifestation of illusion;
he emerged by blending with the myriad things, yet remained profoundly still as a single dharmakāya. This occurred on the eighth day of the fourth month.

On that day, Māyā’s side opened and Siddhārtha was born by transformation. Earth deities supported and cradled him; nine dragons spat forth water to sprinkle his boundless body within the pure *dharmadhātu*.
Taking seven steps, lotuses sprang up beneath his feet. Pointing to heaven and pointing to earth, who would dare respond? At such a moment as this—
The two do not see each other. Had they encountered Yunmen’s single blow of the staff, who would have been willing to step forward and ask questions?
It is truly like a dog that forgets a thousand hunger pangs after one full meal; the living beings of the great earth do not even realize the poison in their own hearts and mouths.
Old Yunmen should have been finished long ago before he had even seen Muni. Today is the Buddha-Bathing Festival, yet Puan was not like this; in the past, he had not yet seen it as such.
Lamp. My Way is clearly manifest and revealed; yet when one sees it and knows it, it is as if it were never there.
How much more so before leaving Tuṣita Heaven, descending into the royal palace, emerging from the mother’s womb, and finishing the work of saving sentient beings?

Furthermore, after preaching the Dharma for forty-nine years, manifesting all manner of transformations and supernatural powers, and finally entering Nirvana at the Twin Trees—it is increasingly without end.
Now I ask the great assembly: Is there anyone here who possesses even a single eye? Come forth! I shall bear witness with you as we all bathe the Buddha.
If this is not yet so, then contemplate this verse of mine: I bow my head to Māyā, the one of great belly, Who, beneath the tree of sorrowlessness, grasped a branch with her hand.
Mother and child have remained unfindable to this day; The falling petals and the singing birds reveal it.
The entire mechanism [of the mind]. A Dharma talk on the *Nirvāṇa-maṇḍala*:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas subject to arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss. Thus the Tathāgata realized *nirvāṇa*.
Nirvāṇa: eternally severing birth and death. If one can listen with a mind of forgetfulness, one shall attain immeasurable bliss.

Master Puan used the diagram of Nirvāṇa to manifest the form of the lunar disc, provisionally establishing a gate of transformation and instruction to gather those who have first resolved their minds toward enlightenment, so that they might see their nature and become Buddhas.
A Dharma Talk for the Assembly:

The Great Awakened One who shatters a single mote of dust manifests both essence and function in their entirety. He expounds the five thousand and forty-eight scrolls as the exegesis of the teachings;
every word is substantial in its essence. He points toward the eighty-four thousand wondrous gates, all of which return to the ocean of nature. In the place of function, there is no...

Emptiness. Its phenomena and principles are vast and all-encompassing; its unfolding and withdrawal are sovereign and free. Have you not seen that before Heaven there was only the One Qi (Vital Energy), which provisionally adopts names by way of the Dao?

It contains and accommodates the myriad things, persisting through eternity from antiquity to the present. It is detached from all characteristics and natures, yet it is the solitary luminosity of the Perfect School’s numinous awareness.
From the empty kalpa until this very day, it neither perishes nor arises; it neither increases nor decreases. Originally, there are no four modes of birth.

The six realms of existence all arise from deluded thoughts. Out of compassion, the ancient sages left behind scriptures and established canons, desiring to lead sentient beings to turn back toward themselves.
They provisionally designated the names of Confucianism, Buddhism, and Taoism; they established images to point toward the mind and used provisional words to enter the essential.

Thus, the Confucian tradition investigates Kong and Meng, the Way is perfected in Lao and Zhuang, and Buddhism explores the true void. These three origins are one body. As for that body, it is neither empty nor...
Form is neither existent nor non-existent; it encompasses heaven and earth without leaving out a single thing. It benefits sentient beings while its constant radiance shines alone.

Regarding such a wondrous foundation, it is rare to encounter one who grasps its essential principle. The sages are distant and the heterodoxies are deep; the demons are strong and the Dharma is weak.

Since Bodhidharma came from the West, he has not established reliance on words and letters, but has pointed directly at the human mind, so that by seeing one’s nature, one becomes a Buddha. We rely upon this single flower opening into five petals.
Only when the leaves fall and the fruit ripens is it truly complete. Thereafter, the Sixth Patriarch, Zen Master Dajian, transmitted this universally throughout the world;
mind-to-mind, they were sealed in realization, and it was called the "Transmission of the Lamp. This clear and lucid spiritual awareness is revealed according to the capacity of each individual.

Yet, some remain mired in emptiness or stagnate in stillness, while others cling to forms and run hither and thither in pursuit. They carry their heavy burdens across a thousand mountains and ten thousand waters, remaining unaware that their very bodies are the site of enlightenment.
Moment by moment, dwelling amidst sensory objects, they turn their backs on awakening; they fall away from the Middle Way and forget it, sinking forever into the realm of Māra.

There may be laypeople and secular scholars who observe the eight-precept fasts of the four stages of fruition, yet all are entangled in the pursuit of trivial gain, destroying the very lineage of the people.

Each dies like a living turtle shedding its shell; every person ends up like a live fox being skinned alive. They will swiftly enter Avīci and sink forever into the Uninterrupted Hell. Thus spoke the Ancient Masters.
It is said: "One blind man leads a multitude of blind men; pulling one another, they fall into a pit of fire. The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states:

"This is not the fault of sentient beings, but the error of false teachers. Have you not seen how when Bodhidharma first arrived at Shaolin, he sat facing the wall for nine years, so that not even a drop of water could pass?

The Second Patriarch stood in the snow and cut off his arm; even so, it remains doubtful whether Bodhidharma truly existed. The Second Patriarch said, "I pray that the Master will grant me peace of mind.
Bodhidharma replied, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall grant you peace. The Second Patriarch said, "When I search for my mind, it is utterly unobtainable.
Bodhidharma said, "I have granted you peace of mind. Thereupon, the Second Patriarch attained sudden and great enlightenment, realizing that his original mind pervades all things.
Only by dwelling in this state can one truly comprehend the intent of Bodhidharma’s coming from the West. This lineage was transmitted in succession down to the Sixth Patriarch;

even his current preaching cannot compare with that of the former sages, being merely name without substance. Among those of us in the later schools, who knows how we have turned our backs on awakening and joined with the dust of the mundane, making it difficult to seek right view?
Puan first investigated the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* with precision, and subsequently mastered the "Ocean Store" (the Tripitaka). Suddenly, he beheld the tower of Maitreya.

[The Master] opened [the case]: "Only after personally witnessing the places where Sudhana practiced could one realize that within the chamber of Vimalakīrti, light and non-duality are interpenetrating.
Thus, upon seeing the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*’s sevenfold investigation of the mind, one knows that Ānanda had not yet clarified this matter;

his mind opened instantaneously, and he attained a vast and penetrating realization of the true mark (*dharmatā*). With the mind and what is outside the mind becoming harmoniously integrated, samādhi manifested before him—this was like placing a head atop a head."

Thus, he uplifts those who come after him. For this reason, he sports in the Prajñāpāramitā and establishes Nirvāṇa, reviving the regulations of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and revealing them so that ordinary minds may enter with faith.
He universally proclaims to the good sons of the ten directions: At the assembly of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the Buddha...
He spoke to Ānanda: "From the very beginning, there have been no worlds and no sentient beings. It is because of delusion that birth exists;
because of birth, extinction exists. Birth and extinction are called 'delusion. To extinguish delusion is called 'the Real. This is termed the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa.
Now, Nirvāṇa is the fundamental nature of sentient beings; therefore, it is called 'Nirvāṇa. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
Whether born from a womb, born from an egg, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether possessing form or formless;
whether with perception or without perception—I shall cause them all to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and bring them to final liberation. The *Heart Sūtra* says:
"Far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, one reaches ultimate *nirvāṇa*. Prime Minister Pei said: "It is quiescent, eternal, and blissful; therefore it is called *nie*."
“P’an. Good son, the three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. Consciousness is like a dream or an illusion; the mind is fundamentally nirvāṇa.

This single path is suchness (tathatā), penetrating the profound and the subtle. Therefore, a sutra says: ‘If one wishes to thoroughly know all Buddhas of the three periods of time, one should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm:
everything is created by mind alone. If a person can practice the ten wholesome deeds, they will receive a rebirth as a reward.”

Receiving heavenly blessings, they steadfastly uphold the five precepts and again obtain a human body. Upon observing the dharma-realm, one sees that— with the exception of those who attain Buddhahood by perceiving their nature in a single thought—
all other births among kings, high ministers, prominent officials, and the wealthy and noble, whose physical forms are dignified and handsome, and who possess intelligence and wisdom,
are due to their cultivation of merit and blessings, their practice of kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, and their non-retrogression from the roots of goodness.

Rebirth occurs in such ways. If one understands the cause and recognizes the fruit, one may advance in cultivation, realize the fundamental mind, see one's nature and attain Buddhahood, remaining forever unchanging and indestructible.
Observe those who are poor and lowly, those who wear fur and bear horns, those that tread upon the earth, and those that fly through the air.

Of the thousands of kinds and myriad species, all have been humans for successive lifetimes who committed the ten unwholesome karmas—practicing killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—and thus invited this retribution.
As the Sūtra says: "The pleasures of the world are all causes of suffering. Therefore, once one loses the human body, it will not be regained for ten thousand kalpas;
only the Buddha knows this, while ordinary sentiments cannot fathom it. If one does not clarify these principles, how can one lead and encourage the deluded masses?

To repay the Buddha’s kindness—how could this not be called "knowing one's teacher"? I prostrate and pray that all you sons of the Buddha will fully resolve upon Bodhicitta, return to the source, and restore the origin, thereby avoiding sinking into the evil realms.
If you reach this point, it is truly like cutting through nails and severing iron; you will turn the wheel of non-retrogression.
If you simply possess the heart of resolve, you will certainly not be deceived. Even if an iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of your head, your concentration and wisdom would remain perfect.
May it be clearly understood that nothing shall be lost. We offer prayers for the Emperor’s ten-thousand-year holy life and for the long endurance of the state.

May the *dharmadhātu* of all Buddhas remain ever active, with the Wheel of Dharma constantly turning. May civil rule flourish and military conflict subside; may rain and wind be harmonious, bringing peace throughout the world and joy to the people.

Universally worship the Buddhas of the Three Bodies and Four Wisdoms. Within a single thought-moment spanning *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, may body and mind become one, pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*. The Dharma...

The body does not perish, and its lifespan is infinite. One month consists of sixty days as a provisional standard; one year has four seasonal meetings to symbolize the *Santong*. When deluded thoughts do not arise, there is neither loss nor gain.

Five thousand [verses] are linked together and bestowed throughout the world. What has been attained has never been intended for separate use; together they form an offering that continues the ancestral tradition.
At first, the Dharma was difficult to transmit, for I feared people would not believe; at Huangmei, only five hundred [monks] remained.

Master Lu, now everyone is worthy of being entrusted with the Dharma. To serve the nation and support the family, the principle is inexhaustible. Do not say that the Patriarch appeared in the Western Land;
in a single kṣaṇa, if you are willing to accept it, your own mind will be penetrated.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction is bliss.
The Tathāgata has realized nirvāṇa and forever severed birth and death. If you can listen with a sincere heart, you shall attain immeasurable bliss."

Puan said: "Those whose faith is pure and clear shall together enter the diagram of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. Regarding the two characters "Yuan" (Complete) and "Pu" (Universal), he addressed the assembly on the occasion of the novice Pu’s formal lecture, saying:
"This treasure-place herein does not arise from deluded thoughts; it is the luminosity of the mind-ground, manifesting through transformation in myriad ways."
It is due to conditions. Thus, the human mind and the Buddha’s practice, and the Buddha’s practice and the human mind—when encountering the final kalpa, hell appears before one;
when meeting those with clear vision, it is the realm of Maitreya. Why is this so? Because that which is performed is without deliberate intent, and thus it naturally accords with reality.
For two or three years, I have not used even a drop of wine or animal furs. What matter has remained unfulfilled? Day after day I have kept my door shut.

Regarding the material wealth offered by those who trust in me, I have never lacked for anything. The Way does not consist in haughtiness toward things; it manifests the Buddha of True Nature—how could it turn its back on people? The Dharma-body responds universally;
if it did not manifest spiritual resonance within things, how would it differ from a sun painted on paper? If it does indeed respond to the hearts of the multitude, it is radiant.

The brilliant, blazing light shines everywhere; it is difficult for the holy and the ordinary to distinguish one another. Dragons and snakes are intermingled, dwelling together; delusion and awakening share the same radiance.
The Buddha is of one essence with sentient beings, yet this is realized only through awakening. Through the movement and stillness of its message, the Dharma benefits all hearts.

When lost in delusion, everything belongs to the dream-wandering of birth and death; with ignorance and perversion, one tells dreams within a dream, unable to distinguish between delusion and awakening, intoxicated.

Do not let intoxicants cloud your senses; those who look on and mock you should be rebuked. Good son, if you seek liberation, it can only be accomplished by relying upon a teacher and the trainings of morality, concentration, and wisdom.
As days pass and months deepen, when *prajñā* becomes fully matured, the mind-dharma will manifest before you. This depends on your own exertion; do not hesitate.
Though you may be at peace today, tomorrow’s safety cannot be guaranteed. Man is like a rootless plant or grass on a riverbank; when the current is swift, it is difficult to retain. Furthermore—

There is no one who cannot be saved. Who is the master of the waves? Only the Buddha of the vast true mind, which is fundamentally neither extinguished nor born, like empty space that encompasses heaven and earth.
When manifesting provisional names, it is inexhaustible; when establishing the banner of Dharma, it is immeasurable and boundless.
The followers of the Two Vehicles and external paths do not penetrate this mystery; within the dharmas of sense-bases and objects, they merely grasp at empty fabrications.
How strange! They recklessly claim that the Buddhas have some dharma to be taught; they speculate about the Dharmakāya and falsely identify the conscious spirit as the self.

They do not seek further the great awakening or the realization of the mind, but instead single-mindedly cherish the words of others. Consequently, though they study extensively and acquire much knowledge, they end up slandering the teachings.
If this old monk had not realized the mind, I would be as ignorant as you. Fortunately, I am now fully endowed with the primordial and eternal, and the light of my intent is inexhaustible;
therefore, I shut my door all day long, fearing the encounter with drunken men. At times I speak with bitter words, yet you do not act upon them.

To indulge in such behavior morning and evening is merely to deceive oneself. Out of laziness, one fears meeting the Master; refusing to quiet the mind and repent, one busies oneself with worldly affairs.

Thus, the devas and nāgas rebuke them, and the protectors of the Dharma refuse to shield them. Suddenly, karmic retribution manifests before their eyes, impossible to hide from the gaze of the assembly.

If one were a person who truly believes in the Buddha and relies on the Dharma to practice—sacrificing even their own body for the sake of the Dharma, like cold ashes and extinguished embers—[they would not act thus].
The Moon deeply reflected upon the ancient worthies: that one cannot encounter the Tathāgata through meager roots of goodness. He further contemplated his own person:

it lacks even a single virtue to support or augment the manifold good deeds. Even if he were to hang a stone from his waist throughout the twelve periods of the day, he would still harbor deluded thoughts and a coarse mind;

and even if he were to grind his bones to powder and shatter his body, it would be difficult to find a skilled craftsman within this state. Now, therefore, he abandons the secular world and severs all attachments. Suddenly—
Having encountered such a person, why not swiftly discern the subtle mechanism? With a ground of sincere faith, step by step rely upon the Suchness;

moment after moment, do not regress, so that you may ultimately reach *nirvāṇa* and certainly return to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). You will be no different from the Buddha; devas and nāgas will protect you, ghosts and spirits will look up to you in reliance, and malevolent demons will be crushed and fallen.
Thus, the profound wind shall not fall for a thousand ages, and throughout long kalpas, the fundamental light shall remain unmoving. So it is.
These words of the final testament have been transmitted and upheld by the Dharma-protectors; the fundamental tenets thus established cannot be destroyed even by the fires at the end of an eon.
Such profound and subtle matters arise from the single mind. To abandon the short for the long—how could this be realized through another?

Buddhist teachings are like a finger pointing at the moon; the Patriarchs' words are like pouring water to reveal the ice. Only after seeing the moon can one know its light, and only after melting the ice can it become water. Thereafter, [the truth] becomes vast.

I am moved by the grace of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; even at the cost of my life, it would be difficult to repay it. For ages I was deluded regarding the mind-dharma and did not emerge from the dust and toil of the world.
Now, having realized the cause of Buddhahood and perceived my true nature, I am forever liberated from birth and death. To have this earnestly held in mind—how joyful this is!
How could one compare this to the Ten Sages and Three Worthies, or the Two Vehicles’ perfect enlightenment? Their five aggregates are not yet empty and their saṃsāra does not cease. Let [them] be...

Your intelligence transcends the world; yet you have not escaped the cycle of the triple realm. Even if you were to move mountains and fill the seas, you would still fall within the non-form realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Nevertheless, though thunder and lightning may rush about, they do not go beyond the boundaries of the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

Even if one were to charge straight through them, one would still not transcend the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas. You have not yet realized that your own self is fundamentally non-existent, and that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are like illusions.

One must simply exhaust illusion so that awakening becomes perfect, thereby possessing the true mark (*dharmatā*). Taking the great earth, mountains, and rivers as one’s own self, one reveals *tathatā* through form and emptiness, light and darkness.
Pointing to the cypress by the south gate to indicate the mind, and looking at the pine to the west to manifest the intent, the square inch of the heart is utterly transcendent of subject and object.
Within the great trichiliocosm there is nothing false; even a single atom is a field of enjoyment, and body and mind do not fall into existence or non-existence.
This is knowledge and vision. To bring it forth for others is not a matter of sounds or forms; to point directly to the human mind in this way is what constitutes a true renunciant.
Only then will you not mislead beginners of later generations. Observe the present time: having gathered here as renunciants, what do you seek?

I teach you to uphold the precepts, yet you do not maintain even a single one. I instruct you to clarify the mind, yet your jealousy increases all the more. I teach you to strike the bell and offer praise...
This incantation does not have a single clear character; it merely follows the crowd and stirs up clamor at will, seeking only to pass through.

It intends to make you come and go with reverence and extensively cultivate conditions for joyful association. Yet you further desire to seek solitude for yourself, thereby deluding your consciousness and sinking your spirit.
When the vital energies (*prāṇa*) are disharmonious, they naturally form the basis of illness; all undertakings become difficult, and ultimately, one undergoes decay.

Furthermore, you have entered the ranks of Māra’s followers, where for hundreds of thousands of millions of *kalpas* you will not encounter a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Now that you have encountered me and left the household life, I know your place of origin and I also know your destination.
You are just like flowers in the sky: arising from the void and returning to the void. I cannot grant you full meditative absorption (*samādhi*). You...
"You are a demon-king! I shall cast you into the realm of Māra; let us both return to the path of Māra.

"If my Dharma-body is such as this—wherein the Dharma-body is like a fierce flame and evil demons are like frost and ice, and you are but that which is melted away—the Dharma-body is eternally abiding, spanning from antiquity to the present, forever without change or decay.
Therefore, the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas transmit only this mind. Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, this..."
The fundamental principle remains unimpaired. Although you have heard this, your karmic consciousness does not believe it; yet tomorrow morning, you shall naturally meet with failure and ruin.
Do not say that there are still sick men beneath the gate of a skilled physician, nor that dull iron still remains within a fully functioning forge.

This is simply because you remain under a covered basin and refuse to open your eyes. While your dark, rotten, and decayed roots perish, this light is ever-present; yet you do not follow its direct instruction.
Do not trouble yourself with many words. If this is the true root of goodness, why should it require such effort? Each of you must exert yourselves; simply cultivate a heart of resolve.
At all times, the ultimate reality is just so. Take care.

The two characters "Yuan" (Perfect) and "Pu" (Universal), shown to disciples as a discourse on the life-blood of the lineage, are still merely provisional names. Although they are provisional names, they are used to discuss the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). If one relies upon the orthodox tradition:
For you, there is not even a speck of dust that serves as a condition or a counterpart for this old monk.

You are simply one born from the Buddha’s own mouth, transformed by birth according to the Dharma, who has realized true suchness (bhūtatathatā) and is merely designated by the name "Son of the Śākya. You have thoroughly understood that names and forms arise from nowhere at all.

Because illusory dust is extinguished, that which is not illusory does not undergo extinction. Although all illusions are exhausted, one does not enter into annihilation. To understand such a Dharma is to have neither attainment nor realization.
If there were attainment or realization, one would inevitably fall into the extremes of nihilism or eternalism. To state the essential point: it is true and not false.
The real and the unreal are transparently clear from both surface and core, verifiable by those with clear vision. Why is this? The exterior is the provisional form and color;
the interior is the actual mind-nature. If the mind-nature is real, then the form and color are radiant; if the form and color are inferior and weak, then the mind-nature is empty and false.
"You follow your karmic consciousness and forcibly comply with your teacher’s countenance; you do not rely on your own fundamental nature, but instead follow delusion.

This is why you increase ignorance and give rise to all manner of opposition and compliance, thereby manifesting these fruits. Do you understand this? A song says: 'If one realizes it, karmic obstacles are originally empty;
if one does not realize it, one must repay past debts. Your past debts—how could they be fully recounted? Ten thousand deaths!"
Throughout a thousand lifetimes, habitual tendencies have been formed everywhere. Your fundamental nature has not transcended its parents. Why is this?

Through the union of paternal essence and maternal blood, conditioned by craving, your consciousness encounters these conditions like a bamboo shoot emerging from the stalk; whether bitter or sweet, hard or soft, it is ultimately not different [from the parent].
Therefore, when the Buddha awakened to the perfection of the *dharmakāya*, which is like empty space, he first attained a wondrous understanding within his own body.

All sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas; therefore, the twelve links of dependent origination and the six *pāramitās* are expounded to teach and transform sentient beings so that they may return to the source and restore their original nature.
By breaking open a single mote of dust, one recognizes one’s own mind, which is equal in measure to the *dharmadhātu*.

Pointing toward the provisional to reach the real, a mere stroke of ink becomes a sutra, serving as the *tathāgatagarbha*. If even a single faculty gives rise to faith, the ground of the mind will open and be cleared.

One is then able to penetrate and transcend the habitual tendencies accumulated over successive lifetimes, realizing that these are but empty flowers and that, in reality, there is no cycle of rebirth.

The Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment while on the causal ground and is no longer deluded; sentient beings, however, fall into inversion due to their delusions, and the cycle of birth and death does not cease.

As birth and death do not cease, they are tormented by old age, sickness, and death; friends and enemies gather and disperse; and within the six realms and three miserable paths, they are born with fur and horns upon their heads.
Yet, there has been no final rest. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching most urgently highlights this great affliction. Often, before one is awakened, the mind does not yet consent;
yet once it moves, it passes through kalpas, dedicating body, life, and wealth to offer in service to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
One universally cultivates the excellent causes of the myriad practices, maintaining compassion for a hundred kalpas, with every thought-moment of diligent effort, never once regressing. I.
When the time, season, and juncture arrive, it is like suddenly waking from a dream; there is no longer birth or death, and one is liberated from karmic conditions.

Like space, unimpeded, one returns to observe the world as if it were a matter within a dream, thereby being able to act in accordance with circumstances and give rise to various illusory manifestations to extensively transform deluded followers.
Verifying the root for oneself, one recognizes the branches; approaching the manifest fruit, one knows the cause. Reaching the ultimate limit of both self and others, all— [The text ends here.]
It is all like this. Whether entering or exiting, moving or still, only I myself know it. As for birth-and-death and nirvana, who is there to make such distinctions?
Why is this so? Because the nature of empty space is such; because it is eternally unmoving; because within the Tathāgatagarbha there is neither arising nor ceasing, and neither knowing nor seeing;
and because it is like the nature of the Dharma-realm, ultimately perfect and pervasive throughout the ten directions. This is what is called the ground of the causal stage.
The Practice of the Dharma. All Tathāgatas of the ten directions and all Bodhisattvas have, without exception, attained liberation by means of this.
The true source is limpid and profound, its brilliance penetrating throughout space; the ocean of awakening is vast and expansive, universally nourishing the entire Dharma-realm.

It is a rarity in the world, unheard of even in the heavens. Transcending the sages and surpassing the ordinary, it is a priceless *maṇi* jewel. For this reason, this Dharma is difficult for father and son to transmit; it passes beyond...
Between the ears and eyes, ruler and subject meet only in vain toil. The Way is not a realm of perception;

one must simply be willing to cast oneself from a cliff to feed a tiger, cut off one's own flesh to save a hawk, relinquish the precious throne as if discarding tears or spittle, and extinguish body and mind as if they were a corpse.

Knowing that one does not depart from compassion to become a Buddha, one must surely practice and refine one's conduct. If one does not extinguish the worldly mind and refine one’s conduct, how can one be called fit to manifest the practice of cultivation?
If one does not act for the sake of the assembly to provide necessary conditions, with what could one inspire a unified heart of praise?

Blessings arise from such praise; transgressions are extinguished through compassionate forbearance. Transgression and blessing depend on the person; the worthy and the foolish each maintain their own path. Thus one realizes the Dharma.
This is the great matter of one’s own body; how could I dare speak recklessly? As soon as there is right and wrong, confusion and delusion arise in profusion.

It is merely like trying to balance a needle on its point because of a mustard seed—difficult to encounter, rarely met. It is like a blind turtle resting temporarily upon a floating log; when has this ever been seen?
The wisdom of wondrous observation does not emerge from the teacher’s mind. When the objects of perception are understood as empty, this is the true Buddha. Why is this so?

You all rely on illusion to speak of awakening, thereby deceiving your own minds. With a mind of discursive knowledge, you speculate about the Tathāgata and use worldly language to construct the Buddha’s wisdom and vision.

This is logically a deception and slander; you do not escape the barrier of Māra. Indulging your whims and exalting yourselves, you harbor secret resentment and jealousy while remaining unaware of it yourselves.
Look, look! As your merit wanes, both illness and suffering arrive together, and you further increase your burden within the fruits of karma.

Anger. Furthermore, one adds slander toward True Suchness (tathatā). Not being able to partake [of its benefits] is a lack of merit; not being able to enjoy it is a lack of conditions. To be缠繞 (bound) by chronic illness is the karmic retribution.
To harbor resentment toward oneself and others is the consciousness of karma (karmavijñāna). If one does not recognize the mind, [this state persists].

How can one escape this illness? If one lacks the Six Perfections, demons will possess one's renunciation; if one does not believe in the True Words (mantras), it would be better to cultivate the seeds of the laity.
Though the Master points out a thousand words, they are like pouring water onto the back of a duck; though a layperson speaks half a sentence, it is like an arrow piercing through a plantain tree.
Puan seems to mistake a thief for his son; fortunately, my walls are firm and strong. You all are like sheep wearing tiger skins;
wherever you go, you will constantly encounter tigers and leopards, yet you do not realize your own ugliness. No clear-eyed person can be deceived. If it were not so...
To call one's ancestors "teachers" is like stuffing pigs' trotters and sheep's intestines into a sack—it is far from sufficient. Why do you not investigate and examine this with thorough detail?

The Buddha-dharma is by no means easily attained; it requires that every step be in accordance with the scriptures, beginning with the practice of the six perfections. One must understand the profound mystery of the Buddha’s teaching without becoming attached to words and names.

Pointing east while speaking of the west, not allowing even a hair’s breadth of conceptualization to stand—though one knows the Buddha-dharma, the distinction between the holy and the ordinary remains difficult to transcend.
Understood. One must indeed employ skillful means, yet not dwell upon the conditions of transformation.

Since I have realized the mind, through the Buddha’s instruction, if I wish to repay the Buddha’s profound kindness, I shall joyfully encounter the present Buddha-sons. The three realms are my Buddha’s single mind;
the myriad dharmas are the Buddha’s single consciousness. Whether one dwells atop a solitary peak or passes through the marketplace and the streets, one remains profoundly still.
Yet it is eternally quiescent. Thus, in a single thought-moment, it is as swift as the wind; its retinue is vast, and its chamber is wide and expansive, capable of accommodating lion thrones.
It does not undergo birth and death like ordinary beings; only those who have realized the Way speak of it without distinction.
When the wind enters the pine ridges, while others possess discrimination, I am without discrimination; when I possess discrimination, others are without discrimination.
It is distinct. Thus one knows that the primary and its attendants are layered upon one another, resembling a thousand lamps within a single room;
their essence and characteristics are equal, like ten thousand images within a single mirror. Even so, you still speak in your sleep. The Buddhas are likewise thus.

Be swift to rouse yourself and reform your practice to cultivate the truth. Do not cling to ignorance, for it is of no benefit to your own affairs. Those who believe me in this way will reach the ultimate.
To become a Buddha. Those who do not rely on such [teachings] are entirely bound by their previous words. This bloodline precept and admonition discusses such matters directly.
○ Recorded by the Master:
Instructions for Novices from the Stainless Hall.
Eh! Those who have left the dust and escaped the mundane world are fit to enter the Zen gate and the Vinaya door.

Only those who can "sever the nail and cut through the iron" are worthy to behold the hammer and tongs of the one with eyes. Why is this so? Because there is not much to the Buddha-dharma; it is difficult for anyone to master it over the long run.
Have you not seen how, beneath the assembly at Huangmei, among five hundred disciples, in the end only Old Lu alone was permitted? To this day—
The entire world is the Caoxi [Dharma]. As for the rest, they recklessly claim to be the Southern School or the Northern Patriarch;

those who burn incense and boast of being "Fruits of the Fourth Stage" are all greedy for wealth and lustful for beauty, bringing ruin to good people. This has continued until the present day, such that ordinary minds cannot fathom it.

They suffer in the worldly prisons while alive and enter the Avīci Hell after death. How could they clarify the Buddha-nature of their own minds and avoid running off in the company of demons? Buddha.
I have expounded the entire Great Canon of Teachings, yet you do not seek them further; instead, you follow others to pay homage to village folk.
You deludedly claim to have fulfilled the four vows. Ha! You have not yet even resolved your karmic consciousness, so how could I possibly be liberated now?
I am being scorched by the burning house, while you are greedily attached to form and wealth. Both of us are thus frantic and distracted; where is the Buddha-dharma in this?

If demons afflict my body and my body is possessed by demons, then it will remain forever like hell. But if my mind realizes the Buddha, then...

The splendor of ten thousand ages! Thus one knows that delusion and enlightenment are distinct from one another, yet the One Mind is not two. You all should rely upon my correct instruction and quickly take it up;
do so without exhausting your mental or physical strength. If you continue to follow the braying of a donkey, you will inevitably meet with a scene of utter disorder.

The morning light shines everywhere within the solitary peaks; searching here and there, the Master is nowhere to be seen. Since ancient times, the sages of the highest caliber have rarely appeared, for they were unwilling to settle for mere superficial effort.
Five thousand scrolls of sutras and teachings were left behind, yet those who look upon them only wander further down the path of delusion.
Ordinary people, driven by greed and attachment, treat these as mere worldly affairs; few encounter this old Lu of Caoxi. From this day forward, no longer...

He attained the Way. He prostrated to his teacher, left the household life, and requested ordination. The elder teacher looked at him with a single glance and recognized all of you through and through.
If you are one who has returned as a seed of *prajñā*, the conditions will naturally harmonize even before you have spoken.
The teacher, moreover, must not harbor deluded thoughts or engage in excessive calculation. The karma beneath your very feet is vast and boundless; you do not realize it, yet you simply continue on.
"I prostrate before you, O man of clear vision, and seek to leave the household life. How should I instruct you? I tell you:
from time immemorial until now, your great nostrils have long been pierced by me with the staff of a hare’s horn. You yourself do not know this.
Son of good family, the nature and characteristics [of all things] are equal; I cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to extinction."
I deliver immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings; yet, in truth, there is not a single sentient being who attains liberation. Why is this?
If there were such a thing as a "Universal Compassionate Teacher," he would not be a Universal Compassionate Teacher. Take care.
Small Assembly:
All sentient beings, down to the most minute insect, are fully endowed with Buddha-nature. Yet, having fallen into a single mote of dust, they are unable to awaken on their own;

only a Buddha can know this. Although Buddhas manifest enlightened activities to extensively transform all living beings, they must endure the confusion caused by heterodox schools that distort the sound [of the Dharma].
They deceive and delude their followers, constructing temples and erecting statues in hundreds of varieties. Their worldly gains entangle them like hemp or millet.
Master and disciple, elder and junior, rely upon one another, treating the scriptures of the Tathāgata as mere tools for craftsmen, greedily seeking only wine and food.
They take hand-bells, gongs, bells, and chimes as their music, pursuing these desires without satiety or contentment. Therefore, in the Lotus Sutra...

The Sūtra says: "If one causes others to perform music—such as playing the lute (*vīṇā*), gongs (*ghaṇṭā*), and bronze cymbals (*tāla*)—to make offerings to the Buddha, they shall all attain the Way of Buddhahood.

This is the transformation of the seed-nature of ignorance (*avidyā*). Whether in motion or stillness, everything returns to the mind; birth and death are nothing but the Buddha, and the Buddha is one's own mind. How could the mind undergo arising and ceasing?
Wandering and pursuing external objects, it transforms from moment to moment, appearing in ten thousand forms and a thousand varieties, extending endlessly.
Sunk in the sea of suffering, when the Buddhas preach the Dharma, who recognizes the mind that is without preaching?

When they provisionally establish the "transformed city," who understands awakening after a single night's stay? Alas for these sentient beings! Their habitual tendencies are deeply entrenched; though they hear a single word of the sutra, they do not recognize its true nature.
One may behold a single image, yet how can one truly know its essential substance? If one perceives it through form or seeks it through sound, both constitute deviant paths.
Now that you, as children of the renunciant life, have arrived at this point, do not err in your interpretation; rather, examine carefully what kind of principle this is.
An ancient said: "Listen to their words and observe their conduct. If words and deeds diverge, and heart and mouth do not accord—such is the nature of greed for wealth.

Attached to form, they harbor anger and joy without restraint; their movement and stillness depart from the truth, as they unite with sensory dust and turn their backs on awakening. Seeing existence and seeing non-existence, they fear poverty and grieve over death.
