Regarding the Dharma Words on Assisting with Firewood: For those who sincerely believe in the Buddha-dharma, assisting with firewood is not difficult. Those who renounce secular life to become monastics and practice according to the teachings will certainly attain the wondrous function of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Carrying wood by exerting physical strength is a subtle transition from existence to non-existence; it is a realm beyond the ordinary, transcending both sound and form.
Beyond this, the body is revealed in its majestic presence. Within the principle of the unified whole (*ekakalpa-lakṣaṇa*), who is self and who is other?
At the limit of form (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), there is total penetration into samādhi. Do you understand? Have you realized it? Do you believe in non-duality?

If you fall into the "second moon," do not deceive yourself; you will incur the retribution of the Avīci Hell. If the Master has not yet fully penetrated these hundreds of thousands of immeasurable [realms]—
Samādhi. Not even a single ant may be used or employed recklessly. If one is not liberated oneself, yet further subjects others to servitude, what kind of principle is that?
It will swiftly bring the retribution of the three evil realms, and one’s suffering will not escape the cycle of saṃsāra. Good son!

The two characters for "leaving home" (pravrajyā) are a gateway to liberation. Diligently practicing asceticism, one benefits both oneself and others; one does not listen to right or wrong, nor seek out good or evil.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one perceives things according to reality as they truly are. One does not cling to existence or non-existence, nor does one associate with worldly dust.

Thus transcending the ranks of ordinary beings, one’s observance of the precepts becomes firm and steadfast. With tranquil mindfulness and vigor, one asks whenever doubt arises and acts immediately upon encountering opposition.

Patience. Where there is habituation, there is immediate detachment. Where there is craving or anger, where there is thought, there is no-thought. When thought is absent, one is correct; when thought is present, one is deviant.

Where there is thought, one is a worldling; no-thought is the renunciant. The renunciant leaves behind all existence. To leave behind all existence is liberation. Through liberation, one finally perceives one's nature.
Perceiving one's nature means there is no self. Being without self, one becomes as suchness.
It is so. When it is thus established, "I have heard" is realized. "I have heard" is precisely "at one time. "At one time" is immeasurable kalpas. Immeasurable kalpas are the Buddha.
The Buddha takes the Dharma as his body, encompassing the inexhaustible empty space of the ten directions.
Empty space is itself the Dharmakāya. The Dharmakāya is like empty space; it manifests forms in response to things, like the moon reflected in water. Have you understood this empty space?

Furthermore, one does not see the Dharma-body. Why is it that one does not see the Dharma-body? It is because of the presence of the view of self, the view of a person, the view of a body, and the view of extremes;
for this reason, one does not see it. This single word "view" has, from antiquity to the present, deceived thousands upon thousands of practitioners and misled countless ordinary people.
They recognize it but do not understand it. The Buddha [teaches that] the Dharma-body is all-pervasive, like...
The eyes observe universally; swallowing space and merging with form, they are yet not the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
Being absolute and beyond all relativity, they are not the self, person, sentient being, or life-span. Once one has reached such a state, only then can one enter the gate of the first bhūmi.

One who possesses such insight then transcends the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*) and speaks of the immeasurable four propositions; they sever the hundred negations (*śata-apavāda*) and resolve the faults and transgressions accumulated over kalpas.
Although this is so, one does not forget right mindfulness for even a single thought-moment; neither separated nor united, one remains earnestly and without abandonment.
The source is the profound, serene Sea-Seal (*sāgara-mudrā*); this is called the Sea-Seal. Within its dense array of wisdom, it contains the ten thousand phenomena—this is expedient means (*upāya*).
Directly pointing to the human mind, one attains the meaning without relying on words and letters;

it is simply to break the legs of Bodhidharma’s journey from the West, lest the person of original nature be led astray. To attain the mind in its own place is neither turning toward nor away; for nine years he faced the wall in silent radiance.
Standing in the courtyard amidst the snow, that foolish fellow dried his mouth with thirsting craving in the midst of the sea. Now there are many indeed...
The mind is inverted; you who study the Way are like those disputing in a dream. For now, investigate within your own mind and verify this according to reality.

You must observe that all the ancient masters were likewise so. By no means deceive yourself or give rise to self-contempt; such delusion and slander will surely bring about the karma of the Avīci Hell.
Until full awakening is attained, rely upon the scriptures. While your practice is not yet perfected, let your body follow your words—do not...

The learning of the essential framework is for those of immeasurable capacity. To apply medicine according to the illness, one must have intentionality. Pointing toward the provisional to return to the real rescues deluded sentiments;

yet who understands this intent, given that delusion and enlightenment differ? Even the Three Vehicles are not yet fully clarified; failing to accord with the One Vehicle constitutes being a non-Buddhist (tīrthika).

Having passed through lifetimes without knowing how to maintain the precepts, one merely exerts oneself in the north, south, east, and west. Though one’s mouth is full of literary compositions, they do not accord [with the truth].
Meaning. Never having drawn near to right knowledge and vision, they see form and hear sound while playing with the consciousness-spirit.
How many times have skulls been reduced to mere skin? Not a single person remains who seeks [the truth] beneath the forest trees. They recklessly take profound explanations to be worldly affairs;

the five thousand [monks] who escaped the net have turned to dust. To read the scriptures one must hire them with money; Buddhist services rely entirely upon the sound of gongs and cymbals. [They eat] leftovers, cakes, and...
Leather, gauze, silk, the flesh of pigs, sheep, dogs, and horses, and the violation of the sutras—whether monk or layperson alike, these lead one to revolve through the realms of suffering.
One betrays the heart of the ancient Buddha Muni, causing the masses to abound in the lack of virtuous conduct. Compassion is rare; the destitute and poor stand alone.

Among a thousand, not one attains honor, glory, wealth, or nobility. Bodhisattvas and celestial immortals do not descend to be born here. Human heads and faces are as numerous as hemp seeds and millet grains.

Killing, stealing, greed, and anger surpass the minds of beasts; regardless of whether it lasts for a moment or sinks into an ocean of kalpas, one merely seeks the spirit of pleasure before one's eyes.
Turning one’s back on good and evil, one approaches the place of no release. Burning incense and joining palms, one calls upon Avalokiteśvara:

"O Greatly Compassionate One, come to save us from suffering! In an instant, life is severed and the lamentation is profound; throughout one's entire life, not even a hair’s breadth of goodness was sown. Remorse and fear intersect.

Only when the master is gone does one realize that death is now imminent and regret is beyond thought. Boundless black karma has been created by myself alone. I send this message to those in the world who have not yet died:
do not squander your time; turn your minds back [to the Way] early. How much more so for those who have left the household life and attained direct realization?

With murmured words, they point directly to the truth, which is the same in antiquity as it is today. Therefore, they distinguish the mind while performing their labors, using diligence to compensate for lack of skill and assist the original spirit. Thus...

Meeting those who come and go, he does not look with a deliberate mind; the Great Matter remains unaccomplished, yet his precepts and conduct are profound. He merely desires a mind as empty as one who has passed the imperial examinations;

turning his head, he rescues and receives those who have not yet returned home. Only then does he accord with the Master’s great vow; sighing deeply, he says: "The difficult comes first, the easy follows. At the crossroads of the street, he sees no guests;
atop the solitary peak, he gazes upon the multitudes of living beings. His livelihood of gathering firewood is fundamentally...
It is so. I shall not fail this old monk of that time. For now, let it rest; say no more.
On the thirteenth day of the coming month, I shall further provide for you. If it is still not sufficient, it shall certainly be fulfilled by the end of this month.

Even if winds rage and snow falls, even if the earth turns and heaven overturns—it is none of your business. Simply continue sitting in meditation and reading the scriptures, regardless of the four heavens.
Even if the Gate-Kings come, they cannot move you; quickly seek liberation and complete your renunciation of the world.
This great matter must take awakening as its standard. Take care, Old Monk. I have established a record of firewood consumption behind the abbot’s quarters to calculate merits and demerits;
there is not even a hair’s breadth of error. Each of you should examine this for yourselves.
In conversation regarding the Dharma with the Magistrate of Pingxiang, he attained self-awakening without a teacher; his mind was greatly liberated—non-empty and non-abiding.

I, the old man Puban, amidst the stillness of this Dharma assembly, in a place long removed from names and severed from forms, offer up a single incense stick of wondrous fragrance and say: "Ten billion Ganges-sands..."

All Buddhas fully enter the Dharma-realm of fragrant light. Bodhisattvas, through their innate wisdom, simultaneously know how to make offerings; with a single mind they pervade the realm, encompassing all lands within a mote of dust.
With a single word they achieve universal penetration, responding to all without exception. Thus we know that the imperial lineage and ancestral clans have all revered the excellent cause of Prajñā.
Now, for the sake of the secular world, they provide the guiding principles, wherein the hidden and the manifest are entirely interconnected. This is a fortunate convergence.
The Magistrate of this District and County has appeared in this world; inwardly he harbors a mind of meditative joy, while outwardly he acts as the master who encourages agriculture.

There is no principle that does not penetrate him, and no matter that he does not encompass. To those far and near he is one and the same; between ancient and modern he is no different. His constant radiance has long been in harmony with the Way.
One deeply knows that it is difficult to act; in this age of the Dharma’s decline, powerful demons abound, and among them, a companion is rarely found.
Within the clear treasury of the teachings, not a single word remains unexhausted. The Buddha-body is like empty space—who can grasp its meaning and forget the words?
Who understands the formless samādhi? "Buddha" has the meaning of awakening; all that has form is empty. The nature of phenomena is serene, the ocean-seal of the one mind. This is the true Sangha.

Thoroughly understanding the Dharma, one remains unsoiled by sensory dust; whether in motion or stillness, one’s essence is in union with True Suchness (*tathatā*). Every movement and gesture manifests the Seal of the Mind (*cittamudrā*).

For deluded followers who are difficult to transform, one follows the circumstances and relies on the "yellow leaf" expedient to stop their crying. Fenggan was loquacious; yet, within the gate of the True Lineage, even ten thousand eons would be insufficient to repay his kindness.
One cannot avoid using a single mirror for both barbarian and Han; its total radiance illuminates all things, revealing that the myriad phenomena are entirely illusory.
Therefore, the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* states: "When illusion ceases, awakening is perfect; for the awakened mind is unmoving.

Thus, for over twenty years, I have been like one guarding a stump waiting for a hare, much like those who sat facing the wall at Shaolin. My hearing and seeing were as if I were a fool; in the eyes of the worldly, I was regarded as a mere shaven-headed object.
Even if I had spoken of Chan or the Way, it would have been heard like a dog barking or thunder rolling. Even if one were to part the grass and gaze [upon me]...
Wind. Deluded views turn one into a deaf and blind man. I deeply believe the words of the ancients: "The Buddhas did not appear in the world; for forty-nine years they preached.
The Patriarchs did not come from the West; at Shaolin there is a wondrous secret. Such extraordinary fellow practitioners may truly be said to share the same wind from a thousand miles away.

As for those who have realized the definitive meaning of the ancient and modern Buddhas, they speak only of the One Mind. Though delusion and enlightenment differ, the sound [of the Dharma] remains the same.

Forms appear, yet what is seen and heard differs from one to another. The wheel of the world turns with frantic haste; birth and death occur in a mere instant. To realize this for oneself is beyond mere thought.

Though all are liberated within the self, sentient beings do not yet understand it. Therefore, I have emerged from my hermitage to face external conditions with no fixed mind, taking the dharma-realm as my place of practice and performing buddha-work to transform sentient beings. Yet those with the commoner’s fleshly eyes rarely perceive this, even after passing through kalpas.

I encountered a man of the Way. Among the myriad species of sentient beings, those who are submerged in suffering do not encounter the True Transformation; thus, my manifested response is not ultimate reality.
Wealth and status do not obstruct me, for I desire only to open the two paths of humans and devas, transforming the mundane into the sacred, thereby repaying the Imperial Grace.

Furthermore, by having roads laid out and bridges constructed, may the magistrates and officials of the prefectures and counties rejoice in benefiting the people so they suffer no hardship, and may merchants and travelers travel with ease.

Earth, water, fire, and wind—the three calamities transform into auspiciousness. Thus we know that the Buddhas of antiquity likewise relied on compassion; those of the present who penetrate all quarters are also like this.
By virtue of this great aspiration, they open this vast mind, directly pointing toward purity and bliss. From the white eyebrows, fragrant seals fall from the void.

The eight classes of beings and dragon spirits harmonize their light and share in the joy. A withered tree of a thousand years suddenly blooms; one long submerged in the dark waters [is now liberated].

Today the jewel has appeared. To the County Magistrate, Great Layman of the Court Council, who causes the Buddha-dharma to flourish—a true son of the Realized One—may you be honored with billions of precious blessings.
Together with the Layman Zhenru of Liling.

Sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas. The word "Buddha" (佛) is a Sanskrit term from the Western Heavens; in the language of Tang, it means "Awakened. Although the names for Buddha differ, their realization of oneness is the same.

If people do not comprehend this fundamental nature, they chase after the superficial, wandering here and there. A gentleman should attend to the root; once the root is established, the Buddha-nature is the same.
When one penetrates this oneness, all matters are concluded, and one will ultimately never again be caged by the dust of the world. This is because the essence is not the dust itself.
Movement. The fundamental reality contains all in harmonious fusion. Before Heaven, there was only this; throughout antiquity and the present, no trace of its study remains.

It is difficult to comprehend where its intent lies; it blocks out dull emptiness and the emptiness of form. Originally, there is nothing to point toward, yet people falsely speak of "form and emptiness.

If delusion can be extinguished, how could the true essence ever be exhausted? This true essence has no shape or appearance, yet it is not separate from within shape and appearance. All illusory substance is false and deceptive. Great!
Wisdom arises from within; when illusion is exhausted, awakening is perfected. The light of the mind is vast and pervasive; this pervasion is without counterpart.

Heaven and earth are contained therein, as are the myriad phenomena of the universe—all appearing as reflections within a single mirror. Within the mirror is my true essence, serene and profound, sealing all in its simplicity.
If one can follow this path, they are fundamentally identical to the Principle. Merely maintain the purity of your nature. [The eyes...]

The ears are as if blind and deaf; feelings are forgotten and thoughts are exhausted. Suddenly one realizes that one’s own body is empty, understanding for oneself that fundamentally there is nothing.
One forcibly employs the words of the Way to communicate, yet this Dharma remains stuck among various studies. All are illusory forms mutually containing one another.

If one leaves behind all marks, the spirit penetrates beyond the physical form. On the left and right, one encounters its source; no vexation enters the breast. Even "I" cannot be found—this is not...
How could I possibly obtain them? My kin are like a dream; they are not enemies, yet I do not encounter them again. Those children of today are all ancestors from a former life.
One root comes and then departs, just as one observes the leaves of a mulberry tree: the original tree has never moved, though its leaves wither in autumn.
Once the leaves fall, they sprout again the following year; the deep roots need not fear the wind. One should simply be able to protect them with diligent effort; do not...
To cause fire and insects to destroy the very root is to fall into poverty for ten thousand kalpas; to now worry about birth and death is like weeping in vain at the void.
Not knowing that the void is fundamentally non-existent is like a cataract arising within the eye. Although one with clear vision speaks the truth, it cannot be understood by the blind or the deaf.

that the Buddhas, out of compassion and through skillful means, secretly speak and openly expound [the truth] within the very minds of these sentient beings.
The entire great treasury of the teachings has been circulated, extensively providing guidance and reception according to the capacities of those with sharp or dull faculties.

thus, a sutra says: "All sutras take the mind as their essence; non-gate is the gate of the Dharma. If one understands the mind, there is no dharma that is not complete. Alas! How can it be otherwise?

Schools are divided between north and south, and teachings are proclaimed as sudden or gradual. People discard the root to pursue the branches, competing for what is right and contending over what is wrong.

They proclaim the correct and the deviant, and delusions arise on all four sides. For this reason, the Elder Puan could not restrain himself and was compelled to show his head, revealing the light of the One Mind.

It encompasses and harmonizes all phenomena; it is neither mind nor Buddha, yet it is both mind and Buddha. Its wondrous function extends in all directions, acting with sovereign freedom according to circumstances.
Language cannot fully express it, and the intellect cannot fathom its source. It establishes neither right nor wrong, sitting firmly to cut off the distinction between sages and ordinary beings.
This is none other than Śākyamuni Buddha himself, manifesting in his sixteen-foot golden body; yet even he receives thirty blows and is driven out. Why is this so?

Within the twelve periods of the day, simply do not harbor thoughts or emotions, and do not give rise to attachment. Then, the environment is the mind, and phenomena are the principle. Let distracting conditions...

To the Senior Seat Huixian (顯首座) and the Venerable Mingchan (明禪): you have entered the profound abyss of principle. Mañjuśrī is your essence; Samantabhadra is your wondrous function. Fengshan has attained the essential meaning.

When all is clearly understood, what words can be spoken? It is eternally present and never lacking; wherever the eye touches, it is boundless. To show the practitioner of perfect responsiveness:

Ordinary people have long been habituated to the notions of self and person, delighting in and clinging to sounds and forms, pursuing sensory objects while turning their backs on the truth.

If you wish to attain swift realization, it is simply this. A thousand million times, take care.
A Dharma Talk for the Assembly:

For many years we have been companions, yet she has hurried past me. In Silla I bowed my head and searched, but could not find her.
Raising your head, you have missed it once more. Today, the ignorant know; this is not a forced proclamation.
If there were one who truly knew, they would still not escape turning it into a calamity. *Ei!* The Seven Patriarchs and the Two or Three [Ancestors] leave no form behind;

throughout kalpas and *asaṃkhyeya* aeons, it has been only this. From antiquity until now, they have never eaten a meal; their bellies are full and their breath even, yet they are never hungry. How lamentable, to grasp at the moon in the night!

I exhort you all, O Evayamati: originally you did not recognize your own head, so why must you still labor so hard in such agitation?

I tell you all: those who do good have encountered many demons since time immemorial. Buddha and demon are of one essence; it is only a matter of the empty mind. When the mind is deluded, it fails to awaken and stinginess becomes a thief.
When the mind awakens, it turns its head and immediately casts away gold. Do not blame the deluded mind for fearing the thief; the thieving mind faces you at every turn.
Difficult to seek; the three realms of suffering and the hells are obtained because of this. I report to you: you must guard against what is benevolent and what is not.

This is no place for a practitioner to leave preliminary footnotes. To avoid his coming with joy and departing in hesitation, throughout the three hundred and sixty days of the year, do not let the distortions of dreams and fantasies ever cease.

The great spirit of birth and death is startled; only realizing the fundamental mind is called supreme.

In a fleeting moment, suddenly hearing that there is fundamentally no mind, one is liberated from millions and billions of cycles of sinking and drowning. I send word to all people: do not tread upon the void. The railing is unstable; do not rely upon it.
Do not let them fall into the deep pit below; first, you must speak to them. As they come and go, let the mind remain unattached; sounds, scents, tastes, and touches may be encountered as they arise.
Standing alone on a solitary peak, who can be one's companion? While the mundane world is in a state of frantic bustle, my Way is wondrous.
This is not for the sake of beating the gong to attend assemblies; it is simply a desire that the true mind does not turn its back. Do not burn incense to offer to the gods.
Relying on the Buddha, one awakens to the discourse on the letterless samādhi through words; yet words clarify while the mind remains deluded, like a man who speaks while blind.

Eating coarse gruel from a mortar and plain rice with pickled soup, I only wish that you remain diligent and never retreat, for I know not when we shall meet again. When the Way is realized, the mind is empty and without opposition.

The *Treasure Store Treatise* states: "Detached from all marks of name and form, one truly perceives the Tathāgatagarbha. One can transform speech into scripture; the original mind is not a mere model.

To speak of existence is itself non-existence; to speak of non-existence lacks any artifice. Without realizing how to spontaneously transform the scriptures, one relies on words to produce deluded thoughts."
Pushing a wooden wheel in a dream—who can repay such a gift of faith? Not even a cow, horse, or sheep emerges; one enters another’s pen to be raised there.
A single coin and four characters are enough to bring both oneself and others to ruin. The awakened one gives rise to the true mechanism; the deluded fall into the iron net.
The Buddhist teachings of emptiness and signlessness perfectly accord with the Unsurpassed [Truth]. The Drum of Heaven explains the sutras; through repentance, immeasurable sins are purified.

Whether existence or non-existence, emptiness or non-emptiness, it is the ultimate reality, free from falsehood. With perfect faith, one attains the six supernormal powers; one need not carve images of devas or nagas.
Simply thus turning the Heart Sutra—within this, who could intend to direct themselves?
For the sake of the junior monk Yuan Tong’s entry into nirvana, he gave a small-scale discourse in the small hall, saying:
"Birth and death and nirvana are like a dream from yesterday; sentient beings and all Buddhas are just like flowers in the sky. Thus it was realized.

Only when one fundamentally understands emptiness can one act in this manner. As long as the essence and its function remain unclarified, what is heard and seen will differ; though the teachings of the Tripitaka are manifest, the doubts are difficult to penetrate.

He personally received the true cause; therefore, at this time, he attained realization spontaneously without a teacher. Had he not possessed innate wisdom from past lives, how could he have believed in these scriptures?
From birth, he has always known this matter; though dwelling amidst the dust of the world, he remains unstained. When the opportune moment arrived, he attained self-communication.

Although the donors have been distracted by a hundred disturbances and the construction projects by a thousand anxieties, my fundamental nature remains as tranquil as space; it encompasses all objects like reflections in a mirror.

Thus, his wondrous responses are both vertical and horizontal, entirely without flaw or deficiency. Here he establishes conditions for transformation and undertakes construction; there he institutes the teaching and builds bridges.
He never severs the fundamental essence while universally responding to the ten directions; he does not cling to names and forms, yet every single thing serves as a pointing seal.

I only fear that in this age of the Dharma’s decline, heterodoxy flourishes while those with true faith are rare. Yet there was a young master named Yuantong, whose family home was not far away and whose parents were both still living.
At the age of twelve, he left home to become a monk under the venerable Master Shoulong; however, he had not yet completed his first year.
When the Master passed away, his parents escorted him to the funeral; he then returned his respects to the Elder Monk and consented to follow the rules to study the Avatamsaka teachings.

Thereafter, he mingled with virtuous friends, daily engaging in mutual inquiry with the Jinshi (Metropolitan Graduate). Morning and evening he did not forget [his studies], gaining a subtle understanding of their essential message.
He has served as a monk for six years. Although young in age, his wisdom resembles that of an ancient master. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining;
speaking, remaining silent, or acting—he never violates the teachings of this old monk. For the past year or two, he could not endure the influence of demons and was nearly at fault.

Fortunately, he encountered this old monk, whose mind is able to transform all things. Suddenly, from the first month, he entered the room, burned incense with great devotion, prostrated himself, and addressed me thus:

The Master said, "Your accumulated merit from past lives is not extensive; though you have penetrated [the truth], it is not yet complete. As chronic illnesses arise, your body is often weary and exhausted.

Although there are many matters to attend to, you cannot accomplish even one. If you wish to seek liberation and stillness, you must rely entirely upon the compassion of the Master. The old monk rebuked him.
Thereupon, he ceased speaking. After a long while, the Master drew figures in the air with his finger and said, "This is what is making you ill for you;
what thing is making you ill for you? The monk then prostrated himself and returned to his quarters in silence.

Furthermore, on the night of the twenty-seventh day of the second month, taking both emptiness and illusion together, he addressed the Master again, saying, "I requested a bath on the third day of the third month; may it be granted? The Master—
He did not answer. On the evening of the third day of the third month, he requested water to bathe his body, changed his clothes, and sought out a bamboo chair.
He sat upright and composedly for a long while. Then he said to the attendant Yuanqing, "Please have the Master come to my room; I wish to write a verse before entering the eternal light of nirvana.
Would that be acceptable? The attendant followed his instructions. Once the Master had arrived, Shizi remained silent, and the assembly of disciples were all hushed.
He took paper and wrote a verse, saying: "The marks of dreams, illusions, and empty flowers—how can they be taken as real? Now I am no longer driven by them; I roam at ease, free from external dust.
He then joined his palms and requested the Master to return to the abbot's quarters. Thereafter, he entrusted his younger brother, Yuanzhi, with the lineage.

Do not allow the mother to wail and weep, nor disturb the venerable teacher’s Dharma assembly. Entrust your younger brother Yuanrong and others to inform the teacher that it would be best to simply seek one barrel for cremation;

there is no need for a coffin, as such things involve various expenses. The offerings from the donors of the ten directions should be used only to ensure the proper handling of the matter and then set aside.
All matters are like dreams and illusions; in the end, they are all entirely thus.
"Yes. He then immediately closed his eyes and spoke no more. He remained silent and unmoving, continuing in this state until the end. What could possibly be done?

This old monk, for the time being, cannot avoid complying with the wishes of the donor. I shall not trouble you further, whether you are donors from near or afar, or fellow practitioners on the path to Nirvana.

"Thirty blows of the staff! You shall leave the monastery this very moment. The old monk shook out his sleeves and entered a stone cave on the Southern Ridge to sit in meditation, never to show his face again.
If you follow what the old monk has told you, do not trouble your spirit in the least;

simply ensure that faith remains far-reaching and enduring, so that the true monk remains imperishable. It would be better to have other offerings and tributes than to return to your own mind. Thus spoke the old monk.

From antiquity to the present, those who have returned to the source through the ten thousand transformations have done so solely by taking their own mind as the fundamental principle. To seek outside the mind is to turn one’s back on awakening and align with the dust of sensory objects;
thus, one follows the path of karma. Furthermore, the reason all Buddhas preach the Dharma is for the sake of sentient beings. This is the ancestral tradition of the world.
The Master replied: "It is likewise so. If there were no sentient beings, there would be no Dharma to be taught.

Upon realizing the purity of one's own nature, one awakens to the fact that all sentient beings are fundamentally neither born nor extinguished; they are of a single essence, pure and like an illusion.

I open wide the precious treasury to bestow pearls and jewels. Within this, there is not a single hair’s breadth of partiality.

Repairing the Hepu Bridge east of the city, its self-nature is perfectly interfused and unobstructed. Like drifting clouds and withered wood, it is left to the wind. Do not marvel that the Way-man has no skillful means;
he is like a floating log encountered by a blind turtle. His responsive transformations are not real, yet they do not oppose the mind. Both existence and non-existence are cast aside—this is the Way.
It must be accomplished. Meeting [him], one immediately gains consent; there is no passing in vain. At the bridge by Hepu, verify the fruit and the cause.
[This is] the reply to Layman Xinzhai regarding the laying of the bridge.
I, [Name], respectfully submit: It must be that Xinzhai’s mind is thus without-mind. Truly, I say it is rare, rare indeed! The old donkey should respond.
Movement belongs solely to wind. Can wind be named? The Samādhi of Shutting the Door is a universal penetration, identical in all things. The Teacher with the Yellow Face said:
"In a trichiliocosm, even a single drop of rain is as if seen with one's own eyes.
Yet, even if one carefully examines every object of use, this is still not the ultimate liberation. As for the final phrase, I ask Xinzhai to speak it. If you can speak it—
One should simply eat a bowl of rice. If you cannot speak it, one should simply eat a bowl of rice. Furthermore, fearing there may be no one with whom to entrust this, Yuanqi is also acceptable;
his lineage is clear. Examine his fine writings: he is diligent and sufficient in recognizing the宗 (zong/essence), and his profound intent is vast and comprehensive.
Lord and attendant are mutually fused, manifesting both the root and the branches. Compassion and wisdom...

The same movement; mind and object are without difference. Because of being solitary and exposed, do not falsely seek to cease. Once the Great [Sun] has risen, it is difficult for the stars to be fully seen.
The mist over the river and the plum rain, however, recognize the true sound. For one who has emerged from the head, what limit is there? A lion cub possesses the power of fearlessness.
Filling the eyes, those who know each other do not recognize one another; withered trees and cold ashes, I alone know them. Vast and deep, the source is drawn from with diligence;
the wild crane perched upon the tall pine reveals my teacher. My teacher’s mind—his mind is ever tranquil. Within the light of eternal tranquility, he benefits all people.
Otherwise, tell me, by whose power does he ride? [○@、]. Obtained, obtained! Zhongneng, his mouth breathes forth light for ten thousand years—how fresh!
Exhaustively practicing the "Heart-Fasting" (*xinzhai*) and all other paths of cultivation, one discerns the great matter of one's own life and delivers all sentient beings.
As the ancients said: "Studying the Way is like drilling for fire; when smoke appears, do not stop. Only when the golden star manifests can you return home and reach the end.
Once again, donning a pair of worn-out boots, with the ropes of illusory power made firm, he turns back to depart and returns, becoming entirely like a Buddha.
Matters. If there were no one else to carry the board, why not use it? Guhyapada Vajrapāṇi, you have already shown excessive agitation by raising your eyebrows;
if you glare with bared teeth, it will instantly spread everywhere. I fear that this "good news" from a hundred li away will summon the old monk.
O Four Heavenly Kings, even if you lift it, it will not move. O Yuanqi, you should know this: do not cause me distress. On the ninth day of the first month, I shall enter the South again.
Yan: His nostrils pierce the heavens; clouds rise to bring rain, and dew congeals to form frost. The final phrase: harvest in autumn, store away in winter.
An old man’s drowsy chatter is nothing but a cause for laughter. Take care.

Appended is a verse by the Shu monk Xue, together with its preface. The Shu monk Dao Cun visited Shushan in the seventh month of the nineteenth year of the Shaoheng era and attained enlightenment. He specifically went to the place of the Chan practitioner Min to seek confirmation. (The origins, the monastery where he received his training, and the master from whom he received the Dharma—these details of his life from beginning to end are not known to later generations; this account is based solely on what was recorded by Puan. [He] traveled throughout all directions seeking a spiritual friend; such a person was rare indeed. Later, during the winter months of the *xin-si* year, he suddenly arrived at Nanquan. There, his realization accorded perfectly with that of Puan.

They spoke of the ancestral Way (*zudao*) and found no divergence in their understanding. Each, through the samādhi of formlessness (*animitta-samādhi*), interrogated the other repeatedly until their minds were sealed by one another’s hearts and all dharmas were seen as interpenetrating.

Like a needle meeting its eye or a magnet attracting its pin, they were in perfect harmony. *Note: The text provided contains a fragmentary character at the end ("毫"), suggesting the source may have been cut off. The translation reflects the available portion.*
The details were not separated by even a hair’s breadth. Suddenly, a practitioner requested further instruction. The Sichuanese monk then pointed to the snow and composed a verse;

Puan followed suit, adding three lines to each of the first, until eight verses were completed. As they played with the joy of the Dharma and the delight of Chan, the two men laughed together, unaware that they had arrived here at this point of defeat.
Verse:
Before the courtyard, snowflakes fall in profusion; wondrous touch and numinous clarity respond through the universal gate. This was not because Yaoshan had no use for it;
he merely caused Master Pang to awaken his descendants.
Always entering the gate of the Way within my own house; amidst non-speaking, one hears what is not heard.
Step by step, penetrating the barrier, the ground is secure; Mount Sumeru leaps and strikes against Mount Kunlun.
When a practitioner reaches this point, they should turn their head back; this thing has always been present everywhere.
Unless one is willing to accept it oneself, one will not believe that objective conditions have neither good nor bad.
To avoid being swept away by the waves of past karma, enter directly through the gate of the Perfect Sound and Universal Eye. Guest and host are clearly distinct—who understands this?
If one is not a person of universal penetration, do not discuss it with them.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time follow this same path. Heaven has no gate and earth has no door; the myriad phenomena of the universe are swallowed by a single light.
Through kalpas, it has never lacked so much as a pinch of salt or a drop of vinegar.

A hundred thousand expedient means are but one universe; yet those who attain it must still distinguish between black and white. Before the essence of the pearl is clarified, it appears as five colors;
before you even lift your head, the hawk has already passed through the Luo village.
If the *kappiya-kāraka* (pure man) trusts in ordinary matters, piercing through the skull from the nasal cavity to the other side— where many become one and one becomes many—
the old woman to the east of the city is difficult to avoid.
The appearance of the mountain elder naturally remains; from the ancestral lineage, not a single word has been passed down. North, south, east, and west—there is nothing else besides this;
its radiance shines everywhere, standing alone as the Honored One.

The Verse on Entering through the Three Gateways: Those who enter through the gateway of Mañjuśrī will find the great earth, mountains, and rivers assisting them to give rise to radiance. Ancient temples, incense, and flowers lie in silent solitude;

there, one burns incense and practices cultivation to repay the nation and transform the deluded masses. When a worthy sage arrives here, they must turn their heads back; they pull at the grass and gaze upon the wind.
He smiled and nodded his head.
Those who enter through the Gate of Avalokiteśvara—frogs and earthworms—assist you in manifesting your radiance. This dwelling has no boundaries and no walls;
it fills the empty space, a truly vast and open expanse. Coming and going, one simply says the Master is broad-minded. How could this compare to Yongjia?
The One-Night Awakening:
Those who enter through the gate of his universal hut arrive without moving a step. The livelihood of this man of the Way is like empty space;

responding to things without mind, how could he be the same as the world? He provisionally establishes a conjured city to mark the place of treasure, briefly pointing out the guest’s dwelling within the vast realm.
Having arrived here, one finally knows that all coming and going are entirely without difference. One releases the vast awakening-flower of the emptiness of emptiness;

reaching the state where there is no high or low, it is like plain, unadulterated tea. Harmonizing with the clouds, one stays overnight upon a bed of mist and dawn-light; tomorrow, one shall go to households everywhere, east and west.
Regarding the solicitation for alms-food:
the incense and flowers of ancient temples have no permanent source of income; yet now, the solicitation for offerings continues without interruption.

Because of this, the Dharma assemblies lack adornments, and from the hour of the Rabbit (morning) until the meal at the Dragon (noon), there is nothing to offer the four classes of beings who come. If a donor of sublime offerings would generously provide [funds],...
With a great mind, he causes others to forget a thousand hungers with a single meal; drumming his belly and singing songs, he delights in the Way.

The monk’s conduct does not concern itself with food or clothing, yet he carries out the transformation of donors. The local deities and mountain spirits do not receive incense or lamps, yet he elevates the commoners and connects with the laity.
Should there be even a single grain bestowed upon him, it shall never go to waste. How could its value ever be measured by that of Luling? It is certainly without peer.

Matter. If you are willing to believe that your own mind does not depend on another for awakening, then last year there was no turning away from the three directions, and today the Dharma has no gates or portals.
I pray you do not harbor doubts or engage in speculative calculation; let it be as it is, allowing killing and giving life according to the moment. It is said:

"If one does not read the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, one will not know the wealth and nobility of the Buddha. He transformed those three thousand and seventy disciples, fearing only that the stream of delusion might increase in jealousy.
Do not worry about scarcity, but worry about inequality. For generations to come, there shall always be honor and wealth.
My Way is mindless; it is a matter of rice and gruel. When hungry, eat; when thirsty, drink—there is nothing else to do. When one family has trouble, a hundred families grieve.
When the mind is pure, it is like the Pure Land of the Buddha. The price of rice in Luling is as usual. When even a single grain is broken, the whole body is revealed. Be careful!

Transforming the inexhaustible calendar, who knows the intent behind establishing the illusory city? A universal rain falls in harmony, moistening ten thousand functions. The great root, branches, and joints are all fully revealed;
how is this different from the time Maitreya descended to birth? The stone child claps his hands, pointing toward the clouds; the wooden maiden holds her flute in harmony.

Water blowing. Let us ask: who understands how to dance with a lantern? One who knows there is no-self joyfully grasps the hammer. *Ei!* Regarding the Dharma words for practicing the path according to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:
in the world of white silver, everything one touches does not go beyond Samantabhadra; when awakening to the reality of True Suchness (*tathatā*), whether in motion or stillness—
There is nothing that is not the Buddha’s work. At the seven locations and nine assemblies, the great essentials for examining the mind are found in the "Eight Returns.
Within this wondrous, profound, and total mastery, the vast voice remains unmoving yet universally responds. Herein, the function of wisdom and the essence of insight are impartial;

the three thousand companions have now perfected their fruition. The light of the jeweled towers and terraces appears everywhere. May we, at this very moment, celebrate this repentance and together journey afar to Amitābha, with the dragon deities.

Together we praise the Way, yet it remains without merit. Śakra, hearing this with reverence, finds no equal to the Buddha; how marvelous! Thus it is that throughout the three realms, both vertically and horizontally, the One Way encompasses all.
Its accomplishment is not a matter of days. We humbly pray: may the Imperial domain remain eternally firm, and may the Sun of the Buddha increase in brilliance.

May the officials of the prefectures and counties protect the people so they may enjoy their labors; may the local deities of this mountain constantly hear the sound of the *brahman* chants; and may all sentient beings throughout the world universally receive [this blessing].

Prajñā: throughout the successive dynasties, those whose minds had not yet realized it shall now follow wisdom and turn the wheel together with it. From the past and present, those who have abandoned their lands to establish mountain hermitages all enter the Samādhi of the Universal Hut.
The Dharma-heirs of the present attain ultimate Bodhi; the faithful of this ocean-like assembly all return to the True Mark (dharmatā).

The transmission of the lamp is inexhaustible; how could the wisdom of the Dharma ever be exhausted? Its wondrous response is like the moon reflected in water or flowers in the sky, bringing sentient beings to full maturity.
On the path of awakening, I rely on the Imperial Enlightenment for testimony and look up to the Dragon and Heaven for clear discernment.
The County Vice-Magistrate of Pingxiang requested a verse;
I have remained shut in my door all day, not receiving a single letter. When one attains the meaning, the words are forgotten—nothing is restricted. I present this to the people of the world.
Gathering together, we vainly discuss the trivial matters of birth and death. Let us burn incense with sincere faith, blending its light with the world.

Fortune and misfortune are both the mind; how could they be different? The mind is fundamentally complete and true, containing all phenomena. It is only because the six sense bases give rise to various delusions.

When the eyes, ears, tongue, nose, body, and mind are stilled, what thing within can obstruct the bright pearl? Shining upon heaven and earth, it is never destroyed. It is not the mind that is greedy.
Life is falsely measured as but a moment; the mandate of Heaven is fifty days before one shall attain awakening. Following the "sixty ears" (the age of sixty), let the mind roam freely as it pleases.

Though an old man emerges a hundred times, his radiance remains unchanging. Cease your efforts on the Gengshen day to seek Mañjuśrī; realize that the Way is contained within this very mind, which encompasses the Dharma-realm.
Since the mind responds to things without attachment, it is in harmony with Bodhi. Simply exhort all people not to fear; why labor the mind to seek anything outside?
For you, my lord, who possess the essence of the single thought of true emptiness— if you are willing to believe that the path of non-mind is not in vain—

I offer this incense from the Puan Hermitage as a dedication to you, the Great Layman Xie Dai, the Pacifier. For one whose illusions have vanished and awakening is perfected, wondrous intent is beyond concealment.
Bestow upon me two [teachings] from the tip of the brush. Samādhi is neither delusion nor enlightenment; how could the world ever recognize it? Where shall one seek its gateway?

The six characters of compassionate transformation shine forth; for a thousand ages people have revered them. The Elephant emerged with the name Puan (Universal Hut); devas and dragons constantly provide protection.
The Dharma-foundation was entrusted to the worthy Marquis; how can its benefits be measured? Alas, those who pursue superficial currents wander in confusion, losing the original path.
Though spanning thousands and tens of thousands of miles, the essence remains without interval; whether mundane or supramundane, these are not my concern.

Only the wild crane attains its own state of mindless response, and thus it is so. I thank you for your consolation. When your cloud-chariot is densely arrayed over Baling, I pray you will cast upon me your compassionate gaze.

One look. Cherish this! [○@、] Puhui said, "The Magistrate of Pingxiang County commissioned a pure and joyful monk to first seek these words: 'While staying at Xuanfeng Bridge Inn, I longed for the crowing of the cock. At dawn, my eyes were not yet open;

Danxia had already extinguished the fire and roasted the wooden Buddha until it turned to ash.'"* *Note: This is a famous verse by Master Puhui (普化) of the Tang dynasty, recorded in the *Wudeng Huiyuan*. The "fire" refers to the furnace used to burn the wooden Buddha; "roasting" implies the act of burning it away.*
The abbot’s eyebrows and beard fell out; Hanshan cried out, "Excellent! The wooden man has no self-nature; the mechanism is urged on by the pulling of the string.

In pure bliss there is nothing to do; the golden strings vibrate as the notes come forth. A solitary crane perches atop the pine peak; having attained this realization, he is too weary to keep company.
Master Lun grasps his brush and faces the cliff’s edge; parting the clouds and trailing the rain, he returns. When Vimalakīrti poses a question, he wags his finger toward Tiantai.
He marks the Dharma-words of the Arhats:
a thousand lamps within a single room, ten thousand phenomena reflected in a mirror. The Buddha manifests as one body and many bodies; the Dharma unfolds as many teachings and a single teaching.
The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possess the six supernormal powers; their beginning and end share the same root. Their fundamental tenets distinguish between delusion and awakening.

Sometimes they manifest at Tiantai or the Southern Peak (Nanyue), traveling back and forth between the heavens and the human realm. To point to their essence is to remain unawakened to the whole body;

as for their practice and understanding, they employ compassion to engage with sentient beings. The Srotāpanna is bound by shackles and manacles; the Sakṛdāgāmin hammers a stake into empty space; the Anāgāmin adds snow upon snow.
Adding frost to the snow; Arhats add salt to the ocean. Five hundred and eight hundred, like the sands of the Ganges River—lords and attendants intermingled, an illusion like a Buddha-activity.
Neither Buddhas nor Patriarchs are lacking; no Arhats remain. The wondrousness of the Hall of Universal Radiance is difficult to fathom.

The lay devotee bestows alms according to his heart’s inclination; these offerings are ever present before one’s eyes and shall never fall into emptiness. For this reason, his name is inscribed to manifest eternally and remain imperishable.
Thus, the three gates are titled.
Mysterious beyond the mysterious; the gateway to all wonders. Empty beyond the empty; the one Dharma eternally abides.
To see the original true face, one must enter directly through these three gates. It is also said: "No gate is the Dharma-gate;
no entry is the true entry. You revere the Buddha’s mind with faith; all conditioned phenomena fall short. By relinquishing wealth and detaching from signs, you accord with the unborn. Heaven.
The ear-cavity admits dust without establishing it;
this is based on the words of Peng Bao for designating the Dharma Hall.
For it is said: "A mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru; the tip of a needle gathers the ocean of lands. Thus, there are thirty-two thousand lion thrones.
Even the chamber of Vimalakīrti is still vast; within the city of one hundred and ten precious jewels, Sudhana remains unmoving yet ever-pervasive.
Thus we know that throughout hundreds of thousands of worlds, the realm of the Buddha manifests before us. The Dharma-body is majestic and grand; how could it be subject to construction or creation?

It is solely because the mind clings to objects that one turns away from awakening and undergoes the toil of worldly existence. When the wise establish provisional teachings to mark the fundamental principle, those with faith are able to attain sudden realization.
One laments the boundless longing for a father, yet finds no way to repay his kindness even with a mustard seed;

one grieves over the mother’s affliction caused by this physical body, wondering upon what merit one can rely to celebrate eternal peace. For this reason, gold and grain are offered to erect a great jeweled monastery. Wondrous...
The sound is perfectly pervasive and eternally proclaimed; heaven and earth share the same root as a single body. Mind itself is Buddha; outside of Buddha there is no mind.
All sentient beings are entirely encompassed within this light. Born through the conditions of father and mother, they are both originally quiescent.

The father is quiescent and thus constitutes bliss; the mother gives birth to phenomena through non-birth. The younger brothers—the myriad practices—are perfectly luminous; the nine clans contain the traces of the numinous.
Consciousness. At this very moment, to offer this profound mind to every dust mote and land is what is called repaying the Buddha’s grace.

*Song of the Shared Wheel* (Written by the Master in the fourth year of the Qiandao era, during the month of the Buddha’s birth, at Dongjing, so as to benefit his disciples’ understanding and prevent it from becoming obscure):
"Responding to conditions with mutual interchange, not empty but identical; turning this public matter spontaneously according to the time—what need is there for a thousand-fathom hemp rope?"
A pull. A light flick from the fingertip fills the entire world; lively and sparkling, it shines with clarity. Successive and continuous, it never ceases. Who recognizes that pivotal switch?
Shaking it idly, one is laughed at as drifting here and there. Even being able to respond, it merely aids in indolence.

There is nothing sought that cannot be attained within this wheel; even dropping a stone at this moment would be a clumsy stratagem. Though effort is great, merit is slight, and it is difficult for the multitude to provide offerings;
yet its utility is sparse while its intent is rich and profound. The eighty thousand afflictions melt into a single point; hunger and thirst are forever extinguished, and from this one is liberated.
For generations, descendants shall attain prosperity and flourish; without expending effort, there is true ease. One transcends the current of delusion and draws forth [the treasure] from the well.
In the midst, do not let the rope snap and sink to the bottom of the mud. Hands and feet bewildered, their tracks vanish into the void.

In vain you speak of the wheel turning inside and out; those who come to observe must not be heedless. Know that from the beginning there is nothing to be said; bending, stretching, bowing, and rising demonstrate the ancestral wind.
Hymn in Praise of the Thirty-Six Patriarchs, No.
1: Venerable Kāśyapa. The Lion’s Body is non-dual;
when he plucked the flower, the smile was in response. From that moment the lamp of Dīpaṃkara blazed forth; its light remains unbroken, shining brilliantly to this day.
Regarding the second, Venerable Ānanda:

for whom was it easy and for whom was it difficult? Though his learning was vast, he had not yet penetrated the barrier; suddenly he realized emptiness and non-self, and the inner ocean once again concealed its mountains.
Third is the Venerable Śāṇakavāsin;
Śāṇakavāsin was free from worldly affairs and possessed profound realization of the definitive meaning. This Dharma is inexpressible; it is transmitted through the turning of thought to Mārutta.
The fourth was the Venerable Upagupta;
by the power of samādhi, he subdued Māra, transmitted the Dharma as the seeds of incense, and his spirit remained superior to that of Cūḍapanthaka.
Regarding the Venerable Tīṣya, the fifth patriarch:
when Tīṣya was first born, his radiance surpassed that of the sun, moon, and lamps; springs gushed forth from the mountain peaks, and few people traveled this path.
The sixth was the Venerable Great Being Mīḍhaka.
He recalled the ancient Asita, for whom the heterodox and orthodox were one path, and there was no dharma that was not harmonized.
The seventh, Venerable Vasumitra, was such that a needle could not pierce him.
With right mindfulness, what need is there for great exertion? In a former kalpa, he personally made offerings to the Tathāgata.
Seat. In the kingdom of King Xiang, he met his spiritual friend, the eighth patriarch, Venerable Buddhanandi.
Light radiated from his *uṣṇīṣa*; upon meeting his teacher and discussing the meaning of the Dharma, he attained entry into *samādhi*.
The ninth, Vimalakīrti: Vimalakīrti was ever-awake.
His parents were not kinsmen of the Buddha. For fifty years he neither walked nor spoke.
Upon seeing the original person, he realized purity.
The tenth is Venerable Pārśva;
his original name was Duṣprasaha. A clay ox enters the sea to plow. Turning a thousand million times according to conditions, there is neither the unsurpassed nor any practice.
The eleventh, the Venerable Pūrṇayaśas, said: "Alas, Gautama!
O Pūrṇayaśas alone, you do not cling to the categories of existence or non-existence; you cause the lotus of the Dharma to bloom everywhere."
Twelfth is the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa.

He manifested a hundred billion emanations of himself; his treatises were profound and his expositions infinite. With the six supernormal powers and samādhi, he subdued Māra not by means of physical form, sound, or physical strength.
Thirteenth, the Venerable Kambala:
Master Kambala was originally a non-Buddhist who attained the state of perfect truth. He realized this primary principle that it is neither old nor new.
Fourteenth, the Venerable Nāgārjuna:
Nāgārjuna is not a physical form; he alone manifests the essence of the full moon. His preaching of the Dharma is like space; it is not with a tongue that he speaks the ultimate truth.
The fifteenth was the Venerable Kanadeva. Kanadeva cast a needle into his bowl;

he profoundly realized the liberation of mind through signlessness (*animitta-cetovimukti*). Discerning that he was a person who had returned due to the cause of a black ear of grain, he employed skillful illusions without failing by even a hair’s breadth.
The sixteenth, Venerable Rāhula:
in the past, he sat under a *śāla* tree. Thus, Rāhula and Siṃha sat together to eat. He entrusted [the lineage] to Prajñāmaha.
The seventeenth was Venerable Saṃghanandin, the Noble Prince of Adornment.
Saṃgha was his name, and Nandin his title. He abandoned his kingdom and shunned worldly glory, then entered into samādhi.
The Eighteenth: Venerable Gayāsīta. Gayāsīta returned from among men;
he constantly held a round mirror free from dust. The wind-bells do not ring—their resonance is my own mind.
Once returning to the constant radiance, he shall never turn back again.
The nineteenth, Venerable Kumāralata, was born in the kingdom of Yuezhi and named Kumāralata.
He was predicted by the Venerable One [Nāgārjuna] as one who would ride upon the vehicle of non-duality and Amitābha.
The twentieth is the Venerable Jayata.
Regarding the ground of Jayata’s practice: in the past, he was the deity Maheśvara. Having realized the nature of non-action for a single moment, his great attainment transcended words.
The Twenty-first: Venerable Bāṣpa.
Once, while paying homage to the Great Radiance, Venerable Bāṣpa drew upon the Buddha’s face with his staff; he repented this transgression and returned to his original state of purity.
The twenty-second is the Honored One Maṇḍala;
his kingdom is named Constant Sovereignty. Prince Maṇḍala transformed cranes into Bodhisattvas, and his every movement stirred the surging river of dhyāna.
The Twenty-third: Venerable Hulanā. Hulanā possessed wisdom;
his radiance encompassed heaven and earth. His influence permeated the five realms of existence; even the sun and moon personally paid him homage.
The twenty-fourth is the Honored One Siṃha, whose true Dharma-body is that of a lion.
It is ultimately without head or tail, yet it deceives those with blind eyes. They mistake the flower in the sky for something other than what it is.
The twenty-fifth, Venerable Vasishṭha:

Vasishṭha shouldered the wooden board and forged the adamantine eye through repeated smelting; the True Dharma remained unshaken by even a hair’s breadth, transcending his predecessors and surpassing his teachers without interval.
The twenty-sixth was the Venerable Ratnamati, whose virtue surpassed that of the Prince of King Devasena.
He was named Ratnamati; he pointed to the mountain and returned it to the Brahmin, leaving the host of Māras powerless.
The Dharma of the twenty-seventh patriarch, Prajñātāra:
it is neither broad nor narrow. Verdant bamboos and yellow chrysanthemums; tall pines and short cypresses.
The twenty-eighth, Venerable Bodhidharma:
the Great King of Physicians who fully upheld the True Dharma and crossed to the South; though his bones may be ground to powder and his body shattered, he has yet to fully repay [his debt];
to this day, he remains inseparable from this light of the mind.
The twenty-ninth, Chan Master Dazhu Huik'e, was direct and fiercely sharp.
He stood in the snow and severed his arm—an expression of a man’s spirit that endures for ten thousand ages. *Du!* (A shout of challenge).
The thirtieth, Chan Master Sengcan Jianzhi, was thoroughly proficient in the teaching of non-speaking.
In the fundamental ground, there is likewise no arising; flowers of non-arising fill the earth, and the original transmission is the lamp of inexhaustibility.
The thirty-first path: Chan Master Daxi of Daoxin rose from beneath Mount Poutou;
his pure waves flowed toward Huangmei, which could not contain them. Four times he was summoned by imperial decree, yet he remained unmoved;
his venerable majesty and wondrous depth drenched the Sahā world.
The thirty-second master, Chan Master Hongren Daman:
"A hundred birds carrying flowers is not enough to be considered marvelous; one must pass directly through it before one truly knows. Among the five hundred followers, who comprehends this?
At the head of the mortar, he privately granted his seal of approval to Old Lu."

It encompasses all things without excess or deficiency; atop the solitary peak where waves overflow the heavens, there is the adamantine flame within the great ocean.

Nanyue Huairang, the Great Wisdom Chan Master, was the "Horse's Hoof" that trampled all under heaven; yet what mutual connection or involvement could there be? Clouds form the branches and clouds form the flowers;
wondrous light enters perfect stillness, encompassing the kalpas of emptiness.
“Master Mazu Daoyi, the Chan Master Daji, ‘sucked up all the waters of the West River in one gulp. If you ponder this carefully, it is not yet remarkable. His body contains the infinite void;
this matter is fundamentally beyond deliberation. ‘Neither mind nor Buddha’ is still a step away; ‘this very mind is Buddha’ is likewise [a conceptualization].”

Within the Great Master Wuxiang (Emptiness) of Xuangjue from Yongjia in Wenzhou, the Buddhas of the ten directions enter;
the ten *pāramitās* are identical in their single radiance, and the ten ages of past and present are without interval.
Secluded. Ten bodies and a thousand billion dharma-bodies interpenetrate;

a hundred-jeweled radiance of blue, yellow, red, and white differs from the mundane world. Those who can understand this are as rare as finding someone like Hanshan. If Fenggan could not discern it, how could he claim superiority?
Tongue. It would be difficult to argue that the radiance does not pervade the path.

Each individual ray of light—whether from the sun, the moon, or a lamp—is not particularly wondrous; yet if encountered by those with physical eyes, it only increases their delusion and ignorance. Even for a retinue as vast as the sands of the Ganges, there is no such light.

The realm. Who would be willing to discern this work?

Great! Mount Sumeru is entirely contained within a single speck of dust;

My intention is this: one does not appreciate the plum blossoms before the Yellow Crane Tower.

When the assembly gazes upward, many perceive the manifold bodies as a single essence, yet few understand it. Failing to realize this, they remain empty and deluded in their own attachments. Unless one attains wondrous penetration of these three, [one cannot escape].
Obscure! Only Yuanwan was free from doubt here.
Fear and love are held together:
on South Mountain there is a striped "tortoise-nose" snake. Xuefeng used to boast of it constantly in the past; many have lost their bodies and lives knowing of it.
A little. Covering the ground, it is now called "vegetable flowers.

Seeking the Buddha’s compassionate protection, may mother and child meet again after tens of thousands of years. The dream ended with the setting sun—how can it be described? After such a long time apart, they are now [reunited].
I see it. Zhaozhou has thoroughly exposed the "old woman’s Chan.
With single-mindedness, listen to the Buddha;
when hearing ceases, doubt is severed. The floating clamor of the three realms is entirely unknown; the mud ox enters the sea, and all is dissolved.
The breath ceases; the wooden horse neighs crosswise, piercing the Purple Microcosm.

Beneath the Shadowless Tree, whose crown cannot be seen, who can recognize him? Within the Lapis Lazuli Palace, form and name are extinguished. Amidst a thousand crags, auspicious light manifests its color.
The pine winds from ten thousand ravines harmonize with those who have submerged themselves;

the Tathāgata Emitting Light and his retinue are layered upon one another, beyond compare in this world. This very day is that person of old. As for delusion and awakening—who is fit to speak of them?
Assembly! The Yao-huang and Wei-zǐ are but one springtime.

When proclaiming the divine mantra, the deluded person clings to colors and strikes at sounds; how could they understand that the perfect sound cannot be heard? From antiquity until now, it has never been proclaimed.
Severed. Only upon reaching home does one realize that those who truly understand are few.
Regarding the inscription on the bell tower:
A bell must contain resonance; it is only through the striking of the mysterious suspension that it is made manifest. Sound and form are entirely true; they are neither form nor sound.
Empty and vast, it simply uses all objective realms to point toward the mind; it seeks only to recognize the mind so as to achieve Buddhahood.

Belonging to the Longxi clan, he delighted in goodness and turned his heart [to the Dharma], seeking to repay the spiritual brilliance of his ancestors and ensure the long-term continuity of his descendants.

With seven-jeweled towers and terraces filling the entire dharma-realm, he desires that every buddha-field be endowed with the perfect sound [of the Dharma]. What calamities would not be dispelled? What grudges...

Revealing what was hidden without leaving anything unresolved, its principle encompasses all Buddhas and its wisdom embraces myriad conditions. Hearing it once and awakening to a thousand truths—how wondrous and inconceivable!
It penetrates stones and pierces through clouds in a thousand million ways.
Inscription for the Jewel Stūpa:
The stūpa is originally without seams; True Suchness is unmoving. At the place where this sūtra was preached, Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna emerged from the void.
Hearing and speaking are like a dream; east and west are non-dual. Yet, though they are one, their manifestations differ.
There is no land that does not embrace it; there is no form that does not merge with it. Layer upon layer, falling and unfolding, light and shadow multiply in successive strata.
Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all enter into its midst. All Buddhas of the three periods of time are one Dharma-body, impenetrable as if pierced by a needle;
their lifespan is infinite. The relics of Maudgalyāyana are eternally hidden within it.

The Image of King Aśoka: With a wondrous complexion and golden countenance, The eight classes of devas and nāgas— Ten billion possessing spiritual powers— Lift mountains and brandish maces, Pervading the entirety of empty space. They protect and venerate the stūpa, Crushing the traces of Māra;
This precious stūpa of the Manifest Truth Has eight facets, exquisite and translucent, Impervious to water and fire, And able to ward off the Vairambha wind.
Sentient beings who behold it shall forever escape the cage; those who believe and those who give, their merit shall not be in vain.
Unabiding generosity brings forth inexhaustible blessings; generosity that dwells on signs remains stranded midway.
O sons of the Buddhas, this is the merit-less merit: by completing such a stupa, one points toward the essential style of the school.
When the void kalpa ends and all is destroyed, this stupa shall not melt; though the fires of the kalpa blaze fiercely, its substance remains like empty space.
Ultimately entering nirvana, it manifests body and function according to the time, responding through transformation to suit the capacities of beings. There is no dharma that it does not encompass;
the imperial domain is eternally secure, like the rains of Shun and the winds of Yao. May the magistrates and officials of the prefectures and counties enjoy lofty rank and high status.
The myriad people are happy; the five grains are abundant and full. The smoke of war naturally subsides, and auspicious vapors blend in harmony.
Natures and characteristics are equal; the bodies of all sentient beings are one. In both the mundane and supramundane worlds, form is no different from emptiness.
I bow my head in prostration. The rites of worshiping the stupa are concluded. The fourth year of the Qian Dao era, the late winter of the Wuzi year.
The compassionate transformation of Nanquan preserves the legacy of the Venerable Su; may all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm hold this in deep reverence.
Regarding the inscription on the Scripture Tower:
I humbly submit that Prajñā penetrates the Avataṃsaka, and Nirvāṇa extends through the Ratnakūṭa. When deluded, they are the Dragon Palace and the Ocean Treasury; when awakened, they are...
Not recognizing a single character, he preached over three hundred assemblies of teachings and delivered countless hundreds of billions of people.

Now, with light radiating from his very eyes, the twelve divisions of the scriptures cannot fully describe him. Amidst the ancestral tombs of the Cui, Tian, and Peng clans, he stands alone like a solitary tower;
the great trichiliocosm of sand-grain worlds are contained within it. Without speech and without hearing, there is true benefit. My distant ancestor.

There is none among those who approach this school who does not transcend [the mundane]. Attaining the *manomayakāya* (mind-born body), they ride upon this power; even as they remain in this world, their family line’s merit flows on endlessly.
How could the merit of both the mundane and supramundane realms ever reach its limit?
Director Li left behind a poem of fourteen lines. Under one line, the Master added seven lines of verse:
"Monastics erecting large buildings Wastefully consume the gold and grain of others; Not being people of clear eyes, It is truly a great hell."
Yellow leaves stop a child’s crying; it is simply to avoid the weeping. Not a drop of wine is consumed, not a shred of meat is moved.
The eaves soar like pheasants; who in this world could know? It is not the wind or the banner that moves; it is the Suchness responding to the opportune moment.
Vivid green are these emerald bamboos; the solitary cloud has no nature to hasten. In every place where instruction is bestowed, one must clearly understand with meticulous care.
What is there within the halls? Dreams and illusions, neither firm nor enduring. From where do the bamboo and wood come? Each and every person is empty-handed.
The stone man unties his silken robes; the wooden woman adds oil to the lamp. Who can understand this matter? It is the true roar of the mud ox.
A clay Buddha is fashioned, its belly concealing profound mechanisms. Even gathering sand to build a stupa can still lead to the attainment of Bodhi.
The father saw that his sons were inferior, so he had them first taught to read books. Once they achieved renown in a single day, everyone in the world came to know them.

Morning after morning they went to pay their respects; who would have recognized Danxia among them? When the wooden Buddha was struck down and burned, the temple administrator instead incurred the blame.
To attain signs while being signless—whether one meets with or fails to meet the Way in traveling through various regions—the Tathāgata has no "great body. Old Lu quickly sets the pestle to grind;

he then says that auspicious signs follow him, and that rebirth in heaven is not yet late. Yet when strength is exhausted, the arrow falls back down; in a future life, things will not be as one wishes.

Even if one were to provisionally bestow a full seven treasures, it would not equal the true resolve to take refuge. To practice giving toward conditioned phenomena is to observe the coming [of truth] and yet remain deluded within oneself.
When asked why it is so, the sun is at its zenith; the nostrils are vast and reach the heavens. I say there are no gates or doors.
Only Buddhas and Buddhas know it; it is conditioned yet unconditioned action. If you ask how to speak of it, they stare with wide eyes and do not look at one another.
I wish to awaken those who are mired in delusion, yet the deluded see only greater folly. For nine years he sat facing the wall, not revealing so much as a hair’s breadth.
The Dharma is preached as being beyond speech; the capacity of the listener is revealed as non-dual. If you do not realize this within yourself, you must study Subhūti.
Your delusion has never been awakened; it merely exhausts my own clear-sighted eyes. Not a single thread or speck of dust is lost; the moon amidst the clouds remains ever fresh.
The man of realization who perceives the subtle signs constantly contemplates the Sutra of No Words; he beats the drum of Mount He and makes the spirit of Daowu dance.
Having long been deluded himself, he encounters delusion yet remains truly undeluded; he can cause the stone man to dance and knows how to make the wooden brother blow.
In the silence of a solitary cloud, I wander at ease; let no one know me. The Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of ten billion Ganges Rivers, are all of one identical nature and equal.
Yet this is not as good as covering one’s head with a thatch roof and wrapping a great withered skull within it—making one’s livelihood in a ghost cave, where Lord Yama will not yet grant respite.
The Buddha takes the Dharma as his body; he cannot be sought through physical marks. For one who is for a single thought-moment without mind, the entire dharma-realm is encompassed in an instant.
Sit quietly for but a brief moment, and you will know delusive thoughts within yourself. When the mind and mouth are at variance, one’s practice fails to penetrate the essential mechanism.
In the morning and in the days to come, one becomes a wild fox; cause and effect do not fall away at all, yet Baizhang’s single word causes confusion.
If someone comes to question me, how shall I answer them? At the place where one loses body and life, the people of the world fear death.
The three realms are but a single mind; the myriad dharmas are created by the mind alone. Those who do not awaken to birth and death will vainly summon retribution throughout kalpas.
This mountain monk knows nothing at all; whether he knows or does not know is truly wondrous. To know in vain without reaching the root is to fail to escape falling into the mechanism of dullness.
When the World-Honored One held up the flower, how could gods and humans have discerned it? Kāśyapa broke into a smile; this has been believed throughout antiquity and today without doubt.
The Master further said: "Pupan saw a single shrimp; he passes his days constantly swallowing turtles and nose-serpents.
Standing alone and towering, he is truly formidable; his body blends with clouds and moon, shining like stars and flowers. When Tai Gong saw him, he immediately reeled in his hook. Xie San—
The name "Xuansha" is well-deserved. How many solitary beasts are there who have no place to hide? An unceasing sound issues from a lone inquiry by the water’s edge.
A Verse on the Four Guests and Hosts (with Preface):
One day, two elders, Peng and Li, visited Puan in leisure. When the three of them met face-to-face, they were truly left with nothing to say.

This old monk again sighs, "How marvelous! overcome with profound grief. Thus, you should know that you have attained the principle beyond words;

"Adding frost on top of snow. Regarding your "Verses on the Profound Meaning," there is no need for the labor of a mind stuck in attachment;
it simply penetrates the function of the single gate. This is the "Sleeping Words" of Puan.
The guest among guests borrows money to buy wine and sets up a madman; constantly in debt and without reliance, he slanders the Teaching and vainly summons the causes for hell.
The six realms and four modes of birth share a single wheel; seeing the arising and ceasing of others is not yet the truth. One must directly shatter the monkey.
Mirror! Recognize the person playing with reflections within the light.

Listen for a moment to the speech of the Silent Child. If you have not yet penetrated through, it is like a second moon; the wondrous faculty universally seals that which is beyond thought—midsummer heat in the sky, yet a great snowfall is spread abroad.

Where no traces remain and there is no duality, there is not a single thing in heaven and earth that is not my own body.
