To realize the mind as it truly is and to witness non-duality, thereby being able to universally enter into all minds—this is called discerning the source.
If this is not yet the case, everything becomes mere deluded thought. Alas! The Buddha’s intent is profound and subtle; it is not something the mundane world can achieve.
It is simply the six supernormal powers, perfectly pervasive and divinely efficacious, never empty. Through the wisdom of non-action, the ten *pāramitās* manifest before one, without any hindrance.
I shall provide a footnote here: through immeasurable wisdom, hundreds of thousands of samādhis are fully manifested, allowing one to freely cite the ancients or address the present.
Having arrived at this point, a lion’s cub must let out a lion’s roar; a fox’s offspring will certainly only howl like a jackal. When the song of Ba is first raised, the whole world sings along;
when the high melody of the Snow Song is loftily played, no one joins in. Do not be surprised that the Buddha-dharma is not so very great.
It is difficult to regain life from within the midst of great death. It is not because of such things that one struggles with a hundred propositions;
though they flow like a vast expanse, they do not yet capture the truth. This was during the summer solstice in the fifth year of the Qiandao era.
To cite the Great Master Bodhidharma: Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty asked, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths?
The Master replied, "Vast emptiness; there is no sage. The Emperor asked, "Who is it that stands before me? The Master replied, "I do not know."
The Master holds up his staff and says: "When the Universal Monarch meets the Dharma King, it is like adding frost to snow;
when tortoise hair and rabbit horns are intermingled, who has personally witnessed this? Puan was not like this. He would have asked Emperor Wu of Liang: 'Your Majesty, what do you see?'"
After a long silence, he said: "It takes but one Bodhidharma not to recognize [him].

Surrounding all without remainder, there is no attachment to words. Before leaving the land of Chu, the light of his intent was perfect and round. Vast and empty, there is no sage—so who would indulge in such chatter?
Its brilliance shines forth through ten thousand ages, yet the world cannot transmit it."
To cite the Great Master Bodhidharma: Shenkang severed his arm and stood in the snow to inquire, "May I hear the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas?
The Master said, "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from another. Shenkang said, "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to bring it to rest for me.
The Master said, "Bring forth that mind, and I will bring it to rest for you. Shenkang said, "I have sought my mind, but it is utterly unobtainable. The Master—
He said, "I have finished settling your mind for you.
He then held up his staff and said, "Everyone says that Bodhidharma sat facing the wall for nine years. Puan said, 'Bodhidharma was momentarily ignorant.
Others say, 'Shenguang lost his money and suffered punishment. But I say, the Second Patriarch exerted himself for the sake of others. Now tell me—"
"Please let the Master settle my mind"—what kind of mind is this? "I have finished settling your mind"—what is this thing?
If you say it exists, the Second Patriarch could not find it; if you say it does not exist, Bodhidharma has already settled your mind. [O @ Ehi] The Great Sun shines directly upon all.
The frost melts and the ice dissolves;
who was it that first arose from delusion or awakening? This "old woman’s heart" forgets its body and risks its life; east and west, how could one ever leave the womb of Māyā?
North and south, the needle’s thread extends everywhere, yet it cannot bear the weight.

The Third Patriarch, Master Sengcan, spoke of the Fourth Patriarch, Daoxin. Daoxin paid obeisance to the Master and said, “I pray that you, Reverend, will out of compassion grant me the Dharma-gate of liberation.
The Master asked, “Who has bound you? Daoxin replied, “No one has bound me. The Master said, “Then why do you seek liberation?
At these words, Daoxin attained great enlightenment.
The Master held up the case and said: "If one were to examine this precedent, it was precisely because the Third Patriarch did not attain liberation.
Had I been there at that time and seen him ask such a question, I would have struck him across the back with a staff, reducing him to a hundred pieces and making him a man of immeasurable capacity.
Fortunately, he attained realization upon hearing my words. Had it not been so, I would have bound everyone here right where they stood. Furthermore—
Dazu asked, "What did the Fourth Patriarch see that he attained great enlightenment upon hearing the Third Patriarch’s words? After a long silence, [the Fourth Patriarch] said, "Do not hesitate;
speak quickly! Speak quickly!
In a single thought, the mind opened and the gate of liberation was reached: riding backward on an iron horse around Mount Kunlun, his backbone is made of pure gold.
Strike! Transmitted to the human world to provide shade for descendants.
Take up the case of the Great Master Mazu Daoyi of Jiangxi. There was a monk who, before the Master, drew four lines, the top one being long.
"Three short [breaths] at the end. He asked, "You cannot say 'one long and three short. Apart from these four characters, I ask the Master to answer.
The Master then drew a line on the ground and said, "Do not speak of long or short; my answer to you is complete. National Teacher Zhong gave a different version, saying:
"Why do you not ask the old monk?"
The Master [Zhaozhou] held up his staff and said: "At that time, Master Ma possessed only one eye; therefore, he exerted such effort.
He drew a line upon the ground, yet one still cannot say whether it is long or short. Reflect on this carefully:
Master Ma never departed from these four characters when answering this monk. If I were Puan, seeing such a clever spirit, I would draw a line both long and short."
He then struck right through the crown of the monk’s head with one direct blow, ensuring that for eternal kalpas this monk would not be able to move.
The National Teacher added a comment, saying: "Why did you not ask the old monk? This principle is not so. Even if you were to ask the National Teacher, I know you would be at a loss for what to do.

What can be done? What can be done? One long and three short—a great muddle. Had it not been for that old man of Jiangxi at the time, who would have swallowed the surging green waves with a single gulp?

Citing Zen Master Shanshan Zhijian: One day, while everyone was being pressed into communal labor to select bracken shoots, Nanquan picked up a single stalk and said, "This one is excellent for making an offering.
The Master [Zhijian] said, "It is not only this one; he would not even look at a hundred flavors of rare delicacies.
Nanquan said, "Even so, each and every one must taste it before they can truly know it. Xuangjue said, "Is this form? Is this..."
"Speech. It is not that the characteristic is speech; it is speech itself.
[The Master] picked up the subject and said: "When Shanshan went on a work detail and the assembly was picking ferns, they gained but a single awakening.
To truly see Huixuan, it is also most difficult, most difficult!"
To see through to the end and desire to deliver others from self-interest is like spreading a net to catch flying birds; out of ten million, not one is caught.
It is better to extend offerings with the compassionate heart of an old woman.

To cite Chan Master Baizhang Weizheng: There was an old monk who, seeing sunlight streaming through a window, asked the Master, "Is it that the window moves toward the sun, or the sun moves toward the window? The Master replied, "Venerable elder, there is a guest in your room; you had better go back.
The Master then asked Nanquan, "Among the spiritual friends of all quarters, is there any dharma that is not explained to people? Nanquan said, "There is."
The Master asked, "What is this dharma that cannot be described to others? Xuanquan said, "It is not mind, not Buddha, and not a thing.
The Master said, "If that is so, then you have already described it. Xuanquan said, "I only speak in this way. How would you, my venerable teacher, describe it?
The Master said, "I am no longer a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); how could I know what there is to say?"
He did not speak of the fundamental dharma. Quan said, "I do not understand; I beg you, Master, to explain it for me. The Master said, "I have already explained it thoroughly for you."
The Master [Zhaozhou] held up the case and said: "Baizhang knew there was a guest in the old monk’s room, yet the old monk did not know there was Baizhang in his room.
Try to judge this for me. Baizhang asked Nanquan: "What is the one phrase outside of the five thousand and four hundred and eighty volumes?"
Nanquan further said: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. To act according to the command and to reach a verdict based on the facts:
Baizhang is profoundly deep; Nanquan is greatly shallow. When the abyss is clear and still, there is no duality; there is nothing that does not manifest.
When emptiness is not yet understood, doubt is certain; teach them quickly to return home and do not let them linger. In all quarters, few can discern the wordless phrase;
from a lion, a lion cub is born.
Regarding Master Mazu of Jiangxi: A lecturer-monk came and asked, "Are you not a lion’s cub? The monk replied, "I dare not say so.
The Master made a sighing sound (*xū xū*). The monk said, "This is the Dharma. The Master asked, "What Dharma is this? The monk said—
Regarding the "Method of the Lion Emerging from its Cave": The Master remained silent. The monk said, "This too is a method. The Master asked, "What method is this?
The monk said, "The method of the lion being in its cave. The Master said, "Neither emerging nor entering—what method is this?
The monk had no reply. Baizhang spoke on his behalf, saying, "Do you see?"
The Master held up the staff and said: "This man transmits Mazu’s 'mind is Buddha. As for me, I see that Mazu was neither mind nor Buddha.
The disciples all watch Mazu playing with a lion; I alone say that Mazu was playing with a leopard cub.
Yet he could not avoid playing right into the point of 'neither coming out nor entering,' until this monk was left speechless and tongue-tied, along with the entire great earth."
People lose their very lives here. *Sigh.* How shameful! Everything is right here. It is also said: "Baizhang is still here;
the decrepit Chan monk points his toes toward heaven. Suspended by the profound mystery, one reaches the pinnacle of the summit. Following sounds and chasing forms is not the work of clear-eyed ones;
when faced directly, all is encompassed, and there is nothing more to say.
[The text] introduces Chan Master Shigong Huizang. The Master asked Xitang, "Can you still catch empty space?
Xitang replied, "I can catch it. The Master asked, "How do you catch it? Xitang reached out his hand and grasped at the air. The Master said, "How is it that you catch empty space like this?
Xitang then asked in return, "How does the elder brother catch it? The Master seized Xitang by the nose.
Kongyue pulled [on the nose-string]. Xitang made a sound of enduring pain and said, "He has pulled the person's nostrils so hard that they have come right off.
The Master said, "You must grasp empty space in this very way before you will succeed."
The Master picks up the case and says: "In the twelve hours of the day, Shigong was fortunately free from affairs;
yet he played with a dead corpse—what extraordinary thing is there in that? Nevertheless, how can one help it that Xitang did not believe he had nostrils?
I say that Shigong’s failure was no small matter."
The teaching instructs one to grasp empty space within a dream, seeking to reveal that blind inquiry transcends the common way. Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form;
form and emptiness are not different, for their essence is identical.
Citing Chan Master Datong of Ziyu Mountain: When Prime Minister Yu Di asked, "What is it like when black winds blow their ship and they are cast adrift into the realm of rākṣasa demons?
The Master said, "Yu Di, you hired laborer! Why do you ask such a thing? Prime Minister Yu turned pale with fear.
The Master pointed and said, "This very moment is being cast adrift into the realm of rākṣasa demons. Prime Minister Yu—
He asked again, "What is the Buddha? The Master called out, "Yu Ti! Yu Ti responded, "Yes.
The Master said, "Do not seek anything else. A monk reported this to Yaoshan. Yaoshan said, "This fellow will be tied up to death.
The monk asked, "How about you, Master? Yaoshan also called out, "I, [Name]! The monk responded, "Yes. Yaoshan said, "What is that?"
The Master held up his whisk and said: "When Purple Jade called out 'Yu Ti,' the pure wind swept across the earth. When Yu Ti responded with an assent, his true body revealed the golden waves.
Do not say that Yu Ti had not attained it; even the thousand sages could do nothing for him. Although Yaoshan spoke thus,"
Alas, this monk has not yet discerned good fortune from calamity;

he himself obscures his own numinous light and fears the black wind. To him, I speak directly, yet he turns deaf and blind. Within the sound, he reveals his true body, hoping for someone to understand it.
The meaning of Yaoshan’s purple jade is in harmony with this.
To cite Chan Master Baizhang Weizheng: While the Master was traveling to the capital, he encountered an official on the road who invited him to eat.

Suddenly, a donkey brayed. The official called out, "Head-tuo! The Master raised his head; the official then pointed at the donkey. The Master, in turn, pointed at the official. Fayen commented on this, saying:
"He should have simply made the sound of a donkey."
The Master picks up the subject, saying: "By opening one's mouth, one brings dust upon oneself. If you do not reach the inner core, how can you understand the donkey’s bray?
Now tell me: does the official’s pointing and Baizhang’s pointing coincide or differ? It is no hindrance for the Dharma-eye to encompass them both completely."
The donkey brays and the horse neighs, yet they do not turn their heads back. Within the radiance of the ancient Buddhas, they refuse to rest.
To understand that the probing of the spiritual mechanism involves no other thing, we meet and briefly point to the tip of the finger.
To cite Chan Master Hong'en of Zhongyi in Langzhou: Yangshan asked him, "How can one realize one's nature?
The Master said, "Suppose there is a house with six windows. Outside, there is a monkey; from the east it calls out, 'Shanshan! and 'Shanshan! responds."
Thus, at all six windows, they called out together and received answers together. Yangshan bowed in thanks and, rising, said:
"I have understood everything through the Master’s metaphors. Yet there is one further matter: when the inner monkey is fast asleep, how can the outer monkey wish to meet with it?
The Master descended from his rope-seat, took Yangshan by the hand, and performed a dance, saying: "Shan-shan yu (Mountain-Mountain Gives)."
You have seen it for yourself. It is like a gnat building a nest upon the eye-lashes of a mosquito, standing at a crossroads and crying out:
"The land is vast and the people are few; those who meet are scarce."

The Master picks up the whisk and says: "Two skulls; they have recognized the monkey. Calling out, 'Mountain! the mountain responds. They dance and shake their heads. The earth is vast and people are few;
the rain weeps and the wind grieves. Why is it so? Because they have closed off their throats."
Raising [the matter] brings clarity; harmonizing brings intimacy. To be pervasive in all directions, how could one wish to deceive others?
It simply requires that the reality itself be free from even a thread’s breadth of separation—like a thousand lamps illuminating a single room.
Citing Chan Master Baizhang Huaihai, who ascended the hall and said: "Close off your throats, lips, and mouths; speak quickly and bring it forth!
Guishan said, "I will not say it; I ask the Master to say it. The Master said, "I do not refuse to say it for you, but in the future it will cause the loss of my descendants.
Wufeng said, "The Master must close off [his own] as well. The Master said, "In a place where there is no one, I will rub my forehead [in anticipation]."
[The Master] looked toward him. Yunyan said, "I have a place where the Way resides. The Master raised his staff and said, "Along with your throat, lips, and mouth, speak it quickly!
Yunyan said, "Does the Master also have it? The Master said, "You will cause the loss of my descendants."
The Master picks up the case and says: “Haihai was pure and clean, yet he was simply not permitted to say he would bring it forth.
I would give him thirty blows with a staff made of rabbit horns—not to mow down the weeds, but to startle the snake. Wuyue and Miaoshan had their heels not touching the ground;
fortunately they met someone who could rescue them to the very marrow. Yunyan’s empty talk uses his own path; were there such a thing, it would destroy my descendants.”
In speech or silence, it is difficult to express the meaning; Bodhi is fundamentally perfect from the start. If you still do not understand, consider this:
once, while Mazu Daishi was admiring the moon, he asked, "At such a moment as this, what is it? Xitang Zang said, "It is precisely the time for making offerings.
Baizhang said, "It is precisely the time for practicing cultivation. Nanquan shook his sleeves and departed. The Master [Huangbo] said, "The sutras have entered..."
The Chan of the Tibetan [tradition] returns to the sea; only Puyuan alone transcends the mundane world.
He held up [the case] and said: "Master Mazu had nothing to do or fabricate; whenever he encountered a situation, he would improvise on the spot.
Old Xitang merely went along with the turn of events, while Baizhang intentionally acted with careless indifference. Only Nanquan was truly coarse and raw—he has never once been doused by others."
Dried up.

The sutras have entered the treasury and Chan has returned to the sea. I universally pray that the numinous constancy may remain forever. Only those who have transcended the mundane and possess the fullness of the moon can converse together and know that there is neither "this way" nor "that way," neither facing toward nor turning away.
The teaching is cited as follows: "The Buddha speaks, the lands speak, and sentient beings speak; they speak simultaneously throughout the three periods of time.
[The Master] picks up the theme and says: "When the pillar hears it, that is the Buddha speaking. When the lantern turns its entire body, that is the land speaking.

When an old woman in a village of three households calls out to her pig, that is sentient beings speaking. Question: "What is meant by 'speaking simultaneously throughout the three periods of time'? Answer: [The Master] remains silent.
When spring arrives, ten thousand flowers bloom together; when the clouds disperse, every household enjoys the wind and moon. If you still do not understand, then rest for a while.
A single sound is perfectly pervasive and never ceases; it is equally sustained by both suffering and joy, yet cannot be named.
I venture to borrow the resonance of the ocean tide from a thousand miles away to assist you in sounding the stringless lute.
To cite Chan Master Baizhang Huaihai: While the Master was performing manual labor with Guishan, he asked, "Is there a fire?
Guishan replied, "There is. The Master asked, "Where is it? Guishan took a piece of firewood, blew on it two or three times, and handed it to the Master.
The Master said, "It is like insects eating wood. The Master then said to the assembly, "There is one person who has never eaten since birth."
"Eat rice. [He] did not say "I am hungry. There was one person who ate all day long but did not say "I am full.
The assembly was speechless. [The Master] remarked: "Old man Baizhang twists the straight into the crooked; throughout the twelve periods of the day, he does nothing else but attend to this."
I fear only for my descendants: returning in secret at night, leaning on fences and groping along walls. Fortunately, they have Guishan;
with every thought in accord, this is why Baizhang opened his mouth and said, "When you close your mouth, you get it.

How much more so for the great assembly—how could they know that there are those who do not eat food yet are always full, while those who constantly eat food pass their days in hunger? Puan was not like this; he took up his staff and—
At that time, they were driven away. Fearing that there might be one who could not be driven off, I invited him to act as the host for the rice gruel and the meal;
I also wanted him to know that upon the tip of this old monk’s staff, there is a single eye.
The bottomless depths of the hundred-fathom pool; the towering peak of Wutai surges with great waves. Baizhang would surely not blow the whistle recklessly;
do not let hunger and satiety pass you by.
The Scripture says: "He closes the gates of all evil realms, yet manifests his body within the five paths of rebirth."
He held up his staff and said, "Tell me, how are the gates to the various evil realms closed?
He then struck once with the staff and set it back down in its original place, saying, "Fortunately, there is no connection here.
He then drew a line on the ground with his finger and said, "As for this one path, it does not even require [closing]."
Attained. What further body could he manifest?

Within one, he understands the immeasurable; within the immeasurable, he understands the one. Among the multitudes of the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system, not a single person recognizes him.
Weeping and laughing, they form the Brahma-sound; striking and clashing, they communicate the message. Amidst the clarity and darkness of form and emptiness lies the power of Mahāprajñā.
To cite Chan Master Baizhang Huaihai: when Mazu was ascending the hall, the great assembly had gathered like clouds; he remained upon the seat for a long while.
The Master then rolled up the sitting mat before him. The Patriarch immediately descended from the hall. The Master came for a second audience.
When Mazu saw the Master approaching, he took the whisk from the corner of his meditation seat and held it upright. The Master said, "Is this its function, or is it apart from its function?

Mazu hung the whisk back in its original place. After a long silence, the Master remained silent. Mazu said, "In the future, when you open your two flaps of skin [your mouth], what will you use as..."
The Master then took up the whisk and held it upright. Guishan said, "Use this very thing, yet remain detached from its use.
The Master hung the whisk back in its original place. Guishan then gave a shout, which left the Master deaf for three days straight.
The Master held up the staff and said: "The ancients were willing to say, 'For a thousand miles there is no one who can speak the Dharma. But what kind of equipment is required to ascend the hall?
Baizhang also had a liver and heart forged of raw iron; Mazu Daoshi, moreover, was cast from pure gold.
With a single great shout, one would be deaf for three days; even with his mouth shut, he could still say, 'De-de-de.'"
The matter of temporary unfolding and rolling up is subtle and profound; when humans and devas converge, who can know it?
In its application, there is no mind—neither identical nor separate—a single clap of thunder shakes Mount Sumeru.
A monk asked Mazu, “I beg the Master to depart from the four propositions and cut off the hundred negations, and point directly to the meaning of [Bodhidharma’s] coming from the West.
Mazu said, “I have no heart for this today; go ask Zhizang. The monk then went to ask Zhizang.
Zhizang said, “Why do you not ask the Master? The monk replied, “The Master told me to come ask the Venerable. Zhizang then—
Rubbing his head with his hand, Mazu said, "Today my head aches. Go ask your elder brother Hai.
The monk went to ask Hai, who replied, "When I arrived here, I did not understand it either. The monk then reported this to Mazu, who said, "Zangtou’s head is white;
Haitou’s head is black."
The Master [Xuedou] holds up the case and says: "How great was Master Mazu! When questioned by this monk, he was rendered speechless and could offer no reply.
Yet when it came to asking Zang, Zang could not help but show great compassion for this monk, placing his hand upon his head to bestow a prophecy that they would share the same ocean of wisdom.
Alas, this monk refused to accept it; he repeated what he had said before Mazu and failed to distinguish Zang."
The head is black and white;
if one does not transcend the four propositions, how can one cut off the hundred negations? To point directly at the meaning of the Western Coming: the meaning of the Western Coming is this:
when the provisional teachings involve Zang of Wisdom, black and white turn into doubt. When one wondrously attains that there is no thing that is "not," the Way of Suchness remains unknowable.
Take up the case of Chan Master Yunyan of Zhangjing. A monk came, circumambulated the master three times, shook his staff, and stood there. The master said, "Right, right.
That same monk later went to Nanquan and likewise circumambulated him three times, shook his staff, and stood there. Nanquan said:
"No, no. This is turned by the power of the wind; it is the beginning and end of formation and destruction. The monk said, "Zhangjing says it is so.
Why does the Master say it is not? Nanquan said, "Zhangjing is right, but you are wrong."
The Master held up his staff and said: "This monk’s application of the Way is no different [from others], yet because he relies on the principle to establish his realization, it becomes empty.

If one does not discern the treasure, how can one recognize the pearl of the black dragon? As for Changjing saying 'it is,' it is not; as for Nanquan saying 'it is not,' it is not. A true son of the Buddha remains free from doubt from beginning to end.
If someone can examine this monk and break through him, I shall present them with a single *maṇi* jewel. He then withdrew [the staff].
Penetrating the source and transcending all explanations, the soul flees and consciousness ceases; appearances are revealed as having no substance, like the moon in water.
A golden-maned lion speaks of non-speaking and speaking; if one does not understand this, their cleverness turns into clumsiness.
Regarding Chan Master Dayi of Geyu: Emperor Xianzong of the Tang dynasty issued an edict for him to enter the Linqide Hall to debate the principles of the Dharma.
A Dharma Master asked, "In the realm of desire there is no dhyāna; yet dhyāna resides within the realm of desire. Upon what basis does this land establish dhyāna? The Master replied:
The Dharma Master knew only that the realm of desire lacks dhyāna; he did not know that the realm of dhyāna lacks desire. The Dharma Master asked, "What is dhyāna?

The Master pointed to the empty space with his hand. The Dharma Master was speechless. The Emperor said, "The Dharma Master has lectured on countless sutras and śāstras, yet even this single point remains beyond his reach."

He held up his staff and said: "Always being without desire, one contemplates its subtlety; always having desire, one contemplates its periphery. Thus we know that Chan and Vinaya are different in name but identical in essence.
Subtle existence and subtle non-existence are the foremost in the Chan school; clinging to existence and clinging to non-existence, one cannot escape the bounds of Vinaya.
Pointing at space with his hand, his eyes went deaf and his ears were blocked. Again asking, 'How is it? after a long silence he said, 'Just look at the guest.'"
The ancient mirror in the hall shines without moving; it is simply that its true nature cannot be polished away. A single point of luminosity encompasses the entire assembly of dharmas;
the myriad phenomena of the universe cannot conceal it.
Citing Chan Master Qian’an of Yanguan: He called to his attendant, “Bring me the rhinoceros fan.
The attendant said, “The fan is broken. The Master said, “The fan is broken; give me back the rhinoceros. The attendant was speechless.

Touzi spoke on his behalf, saying, “I do not refuse to bring it forth, but I fear its horns and head are incomplete. Zifu spoke on his behalf by drawing a perfect circle (*maṇḍala*) with the characters written in its center.
Regarding the character for "ox" (牛), Shishuang said, "If it were up to you, Master, there would be none. Baofu said, "Master, you are advanced in years;
it would be better to invite someone else."
The Master picks up the case and says: "At that time, the attendant should have simply said to him: 'Where did you lose your ox, Master? Why must you seek it from me?
Even so, we are fortunate that the attendant did not see the ox; let us rejoice that there was no connection.
Touzi, Zifu, Shishuang, and Baofu—all these were cleared with one verdict. After a long silence, he says: "He has been thoroughly exposed."
It is round like the moon, difficult to complete in a painting; its horns are perfect and its nose is free of the tether. This is not some hidden object of the student;
though it may be recognized, one has not yet penetrated the truth.
The teaching is cited as follows: "You should know that empty space is born within your mind, like a fragment of cloud appearing within the vast clarity.
[The Master] picks it up and says: Pointing with his hand, he says: "This is merely a provisional name for 'vast clarity. Where is the cloud? He then gives a shout: "Tsk!"
Originally, one’s own body is luminous and vast; yet through delusion, one falsely identifies with empty space and creates strange distortions. To the wise, there is neither lack nor excess;
for the ignorant, kalpas are spent repaying debts.
Take for example Chan Master Dayi of Gehu: while preaching the Dharma in the Linqide Palace, he asked the eminent virtuous ones present, "In walking, standing..."
[The Master asked: "Whether sitting or lying down, what ultimately constitutes the Way? One replied: "Cognition is the Way. The Master said:
"It cannot be known by wisdom (*jñāna*), nor can it be cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*). How, then, can cognition be the Way? Another replied: "Non-discrimination is the Way. The Master said:
"If one is well able to discriminate the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) while remaining unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), how could there be non-discrimination?"

"Is discrimination the Way? Someone replied, "The four dhyānas and eight samādhis are the Way. The Master said, "The Buddha-body is unconditioned and does not fall within the realm of numerical categories.
How can the four dhyānas and eight samādhis be the Way? Thereupon, the assembly all remained speechless.
The Master held up the staff and said: "At Goose Lake, they both boasted of the Great Meaning, yet they did nothing but talk in their sleep for others.
It was so that even at the third watch, their eyes would not open; though the dawn broke with great clarity, they were still dozing.
Puan asked nothing else, but simply questioned the Elder: 'Right now, which meaning is this? I pray you will explain it clearly for me; I wish to hear it thus.'"
The Qilin De Hall brilliantly fills the six directions; where sovereign and subject meet in harmony, few can understand. The old woman speaks at length, raising the matter again and again;
though the mouth is closed and difficult to open, the underlying intent is profound.
To cite Chan Master Dayu of Mount Furong: One day, while serving food, he was with Layman Pang.
As the Layman received the food, the Master said, "Vimalakīrti long ago rebuked receiving alms with a conceptual mind. If you set aside this single instance, would you still find it acceptable?
The Layman replied, "At that time, was Subhūti not a master himself? The Master said, "That has nothing to do with him. The Layman—[remained silent].
[The Master] said: "When food reaches the edge of one's mouth, it is snatched away by another. The Master then set down his food. The Layman said:
"A single phrase does not suffice. [The Commentator] remarks: When the Elder Fuyong was serving food, he treated the noble as base. Fortunately, he encountered the Clear Dew of Master Pang.
Had it not been for Old Man Pang, one might have coveted a single grain of rice and ruined ten years' worth of provisions.

Vimalakīrti also loves to deal out blows; he delights in playing with the heart, liver, and five viscera. Unless one reaches within and sheds the stubborn mechanism, not even a single phrase can transcend the immeasurable.
Master Chan Master Qian’an of Yanguan was asked by a monk, “What is the Dharmakāya Vairocana? The Master said, “Bring me that pure water jar.
The monk immediately brought the pure water jar. The Master said, “Return it to its original place and set it down.
When the monk returned the jar to its original place and again questioned him on the previous words, the Master said, “The ancient Buddhas have long since passed away.”
The Master held up his staff and said: "If you look at it this way, Salt Official’s response is entirely without beginning or end. Furthermore, he has wounded this monk in his coming and going;
moreover, he does not recognize good from evil. So, how would you judge this? After a long silence, he said: 'The ancient Buddhas have been present for a long time.'"
[○@(貝-日+貝)]. His very body is Rūpaśobha; his radiant light pervades all.
Amidst emerald clouds, he has raised [his voice] for several thousand autumns. When questioned by others, he gives no partial answer:
the mountains are naturally green, and the waters flow of their own accord.
To cite Chan Master Zhichang of Guizong: he asked a newly arrived monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Fengxiang.
The Master said, "Have you brought that thing with you? The monk said, "I have brought it. The Master said, "Where is it?"

The monk took the object in his hand and held it up from the Master’s head to present it to him. The Master immediately raised his hand, making a gesture as if to receive it, and then tossed it behind his back.
The monk was speechless. The Master said, "This wild fox spirit!"

The Master holds up his staff and says: "When a man of knowledge examines and discriminates, not even a hair’s breadth is missed. Yet these blind fellows venture to inquire; it is like frost entering a flame.
Guizong asked a newly arrived monk, 'Where have you come from? This monk’s answer was no different from the babbling of one in a dream;
he displayed his wiles in vain, a wild fox that has lost its tracks."
Clad in clouds and wearing rain, the phoenix flies forth; dwelling in form and relying on sound, the eyes remain closed. Who has not once passed through the seam?
In vain they hasten to Nanyue and Tiantai.
The Master Nanyuan Puyuan addressed the assembly, saying: "To utter the word 'suchness' is already a transformation.

The teachers and monks of the present day must act within the midst of the heterodox species before they can succeed. Guizong said: "Though one performs the deeds of a beast, one does not receive the retribution of a beast.
The Master said: "Meng Babang has gone off in that manner once again."
The Master held up his whisk and said: "Nanquan spoke of 'suchness,' yet he was already wearing fur and horns.

Dailei and Guizong also went about in this same way. As for the teachers and monks of today, how do they practice? Is it acceptable to act as a donkey for the eastern neighbor and a horse for the western neighbor?"

Though there are hundreds of billions of transformation bodies, one cannot find a single person with whom to recognize them. How lamentable are those of the past and present! Who among you possesses the power to know gratitude?
The Master Chan Yan-guan Qi-an once said to the assembly: "Take empty space as the drum and Mount Sumeru as the mallet."
"What do you strike? The assembly had no reply. A monk reported this to Nanquan, who said, "Master Wang does not beat this broken drum.
Fayen offered a different version, saying, "Master Wang does not beat [it]."
The Master picks up the topic, saying: "Do not say that no one can do anything about it; even Yanguan himself could not bring his hand down upon it.
Now tell me: what kind of hide is used to skin this drum? How wide is it? How long is the drumstick? Old Teacher Wang of East Village knows the news well;
this man refuses to beat this broken drum. If one were to examine the matter thoroughly, Old Teacher Wang ought to..."
"Chewing on the staff. This drum of universal penetration resounds everywhere; its golden sound is unceasing. It is fundamentally perfected from the beginning—when has it ever been broken or missing?
Only Heyshan knows how to beat it, Deshan excels at singing it, and Daowu knows how to dance it.
Although this is so, one must still let it pass by one move.
A single strike makes the universe within hearing vast and wide; who is it that drums upon east, west, south, and north? The seamless mallet of Mount Sumeru accords with the reality;
in every atom and land, there is no emptiness, only the solid bone-drum.
To cite Chan Master Zhichang of Guizong: A monk asked, "How can a beginner find a point of entry?
The Master struck the lid of the cauldron three times and asked, "Do you hear it? The monk said, "I hear it. The Master said, "Why do I not hear it?
He struck it three times again and asked, "Do you hear it? The monk said, "I hear it. The Master said, "Why do I hear it? The monk was speechless. The Master said, "Observe..."
"The power of wisdom regarding the subtle nature of sound can rescue the world from suffering.
Nanquan said: "Guiyang exhausted his cleverness and Zongmi brought forth his clumsiness. If you ask about the original mind, why must you seek it in its final manifestation? Strike upon the head!"
Therefore, when the assembly heard the end [of the verse], they said, "The Master has no self;
that is why we did not hear it. Entering the gate with the initial mind is not difficult; yet losing the source and chasing after objects creates ten thousand layers of mountains.

Through the power of Avalokiteśvara’s wondrous wisdom and compassion, he struck three times in succession, and the essence was naturally at ease. Where has he gone now? He has wandered off into the distance, leaving only white clouds locked in the void.
Section on Guān.
It is said that one day, while Master Dèng Yìnféng of Mount Wǔtái was weeding grass with Shítóu Huáshān, the Master stood to the left with his hands folded in reverence.
Shítóu tossed the weeding tool toward the Master and, before him, cleared away a blade of grass. The Master—
Xuefeng said, "The Master has only cleared away this; he has not cleared away that. Shitou raised his hoe.
The Master took the hoe and made a gesture of hoeing. Shitou said, "You have only cleared away that;
you have not cleared away this. The Master was speechless. Dongshan spoke on his behalf, saying, "Is there still a mound?"
The Master picks up the case and says: "What did Deng Yinfeng see at that time? What is 'this one' and 'that one'?
What is it to hold it up and to receive it? If Deng Yinfeng had been truly and authentically present, he would have been able to respond to Master Shitou.
Dongshan is piling up earth mounds on level ground; who knows this is an illusion? He strikes the meditation seat.
Polishing the beginner’s mind is not a matter of total penetration; it results entirely in differentiation. The more one looks up, the higher it becomes;
the more one drills into it, the harder it grows. When gazed upon from behind, it suddenly appears in front. Thus, Shitou raises the point once again.
Yinpeṅ remained silent. If you do not understand this further, consider the case of Chan Master Zhichang of Guizong.
When the Regional Inspector Li Bo asked him, "In the scriptures it says that Mount Sumeru can contain a mustard seed;
I have no doubt regarding that. But as for a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru—is that not merely empty talk? The Master replied, "People say..."
"Governor, have you read the ten thousand scrolls of books? Li replied, "Yes. The Master said, "From the crown of your head to the soles of your feet, you are no larger than a coconut tree.
Where, then, would you place those ten thousand scrolls? Li bowed his head and remained silent. The Master asked again, "As for the Great Canon of the Teachings..."
"What kind of trivial matter have you understood? The Master raised his fist and showed it to him, saying, "Do you understand? Li said, "I do not understand.
The Master said, "This scholar does not even recognize a fist!"
The Master held up [the whisk] and said: "Sumeru contains a mustard seed; the mud ox swallows snow. How do you explain 'a mustard seed containing Sumeru'?
It can only be said to him: 'Bring forth that mustard seed! If you understand this, you will experience its total utilization.
If not, the Prefect has no other remark but to say: 'This fellow cannot even manage a single mustard seed—what more can he ask?'"
What is the matter of the limits of the treasury of teachings? One must simply reach the point where one does not understand.

Ten thousand scrolls of poetry and books are difficult to reject, yet easy; a single robe and mouthful of food are easy to reject, yet difficult. What need is there to speak of Mount Sumeru and a mustard seed?
The majestic body is bare and manifest; it points directly to the wind and the banner.
To cite Chan Master Nanquan Puyuan: Once, the monks of the East and West Halls were disputing over a cat.
The Master held up the cat and said, "If you can speak, I shall save this cat; if you cannot speak, I shall kill it. The assembly was speechless. The Master killed it.
When Zhaozhou returned from outside, the Master recounted the previous conversation. Zhaozhou then took off his straw sandals, placed them on his head, and [departed].

[The cat] went out. The Master said, "If you had been here, you would have saved the cat. [The commentator] remarks: When Nanquan gave this interpretation, he was nearly shot into hell by an arrow. Let alone saying the cat ate the sword; both the East and West Halls lost their lives at once, yet they remained unaware. Fortunately, they encountered Zhaozhou, who— [The text continues: ...toward [the cat]. The Master said, "If you had been here, you would have saved the cat. This is a case where the Buddha-Dharma is like a sharp sword. If one does not see it clearly, one will surely fall into the pit of birth and death. It is not that the cat was killed; rather, it is that the two halls were about to lose their lives. If one can discern the meaning of this, one will know that the cat was not killed.
