Presented face-to-face, how truly marvelous! There is no further discrimination or hesitation. Since the non-separation and non-union were attained, how could one let this luminous clarity pass by?
Only through a hundred refinements does fine gold become precious; the spirit of total liberation is beyond seeing and knowing.
Citing Zen Master Shitou Xiqian: He asked a newly arrived monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Jiangxi.
The Master said, "Have you seen Great Master Ma? The monk replied, "Yes. The Master then pointed to a piece of firewood and said, "How does Great Master Ma compare to this?
The monk was speechless. He returned and related this to Great Master Ma. Ma said, "You saw the piece of firewood."
The monk said, "Do not overestimate yourself. Mazu said, "You have great strength. The monk asked, "Why?
Mazu said, "You carried a bundle of firewood from Mount Nanyue; is that not being strong?"
The Master [Zhaozhou] held up his staff and said: "That monk liked to eat stones and sticks. Why was it so? His point of origin was not clear.
Thus, when he met Master Mazu, they became like kindred spirits. Fortunately, Master Mazu, out of compassion, emitted a ray of light that poured into the skull-mouth;
the skull also emitted a divine light that struck Master Mazu’s body, startling him."
Pupan did not dare to come out. At the site of Shitou’s stupa, the ground would not rise; he could only entrust the bamboo leaves to strike against one another like the snapping of fingers, sighing:
"How lamentable! Among people of the past and present, how few truly know the power of gratitude!"
A master who idly handles the firewood with skillful fingers loses the horse of the mind by a thousand li and wastes his effort; the Buddha-dharma is not this kind of principle.
To clumsily employ the golden-haired lion as a wild fox—how lamentable!
To cite Chan Master Tianran of Danxia: When he met National Teacher Zhong, he immediately spread out his sitting mat.

The National Teacher said, "No need, no need. The Master stepped back. The National Teacher said, "So it is, so it is. The Master then stepped forward again. The National Teacher said, "It is not so, it is not so.
The Master circumambulated the National Teacher once and departed. The National Teacher said, "The time since the Sage has passed; thirty... [years have elapsed].
After several years, this fellow was nowhere to be seen; indeed, he would have been difficult to find again.
[The Master] picked up the case and said: "Danxia chisels Guishan; two dragons play at leisure, surging forth vast waves.
If it were not for the Great Deity who presides over the ocean, others would surely be at a loss."

The words spoken are inexhaustible, yet the intent is universally pervasive; rare in this world, its meaning is harmonious and unified. In the third month of spring, the myriad flowers all seem to smile;
it is but a single wind that adorns the profusion of blossoms.
Citing Zen Master Yaoshan Weiyan: A monk asked, "What should I do when I intend to return to my hometown?
The Master said, "Your parents are lying in a thicket of thorns, their entire bodies raw and festering;
where will you go upon returning? The monk said, "If that is so, then I shall not return. The Master said, "You must indeed return. If you return to your hometown, I will show you something."
The "Recipe for Ceasing Grain. A monk said, "I request it at once. The Master said, "At the two formal assemblies, you need not chew so much as a single grain of rice.
*Commentary:* This monk was already leaning on a fence and groping along a wall; he was then pushed by Yaoshan into a deep pit.
This monk stubbornly refused to let go, yet he could not avoid being dragged through the mud and water all at once. In the end, his "ceasing grain" turned cleverness into clumsiness.
Pupan held up a tuft of cloth and said: "Hūṃ hūṃ!

When spinning a wheel, one knows the depth by letting out the thread; when grasping fire to burn a mountain, one must first discern what is appropriate. Do not say that meeting the occasion is merely playing a casual game;
one must directly prescribe a skilled physician for the ailment."
To cite the story of Master Huating Chuanzi: while Master Shanhui was paying his respects, the Master asked, "Seat-Master, in what monastery do you reside?
Shanhui replied, "I do not reside in any monastery. The Master asked, "If you do not reside in one, then what is it that you resemble neither? Shanhui replied: [He remained silent.]
“Currently there is nothing similar to this. Where did you learn it? Huì replied, “It is not something that reaches the ears or eyes.
The Master laughed and said, “A single phrase that fits the head is a tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas. A line lowered a thousand feet—the intent lies in the deep pool.
Three inches away from the hook—speak quickly, speak quickly! As Huì was about to open his mouth, the Master struck him into the water with his oar.
The Master held up his whisk and said: "The wind blows and the rain follows; the lion leaps into its mate. Without stirring the dust, they naturally accord.
If there were no Boatman to ferry them across, even those of fine understanding would not pass. Yet, if one does not attain such fine understanding, one fails to do justice to Huating."
A solitary boat, unmoored, plays upon Huating; its boundless splendor and spirit are pure. True understanding does not depend on the ears or eyes;
how could sound and form be entrusted to the primal spirit?
Citing Zen Master Yashan Yan: During a night assembly, he did not light the lamps. The Master gave this discourse: "I have a phrase;
I will tell it to you when a horned ox gives birth to a calf. At that time, a monk said, "A horned ox has given birth to a calf;
why do you not speak? The Master said, "Attendant, bring a lamp here! The monk withdrew and joined the assembly. Later, Yunyan recounted this story.
Dongshan said, "That monk understood it, yet he simply refused to prostrate. [The Master] comments: "Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down;
whether sun, moon, or the light of a lamp; whether mundane or supramundane—for one who has awakened, these things do not interfere with one another.
Puan, however, was not like this. He said, "I have a single phrase that enables even a stone woman to give birth to a child," and then he turned toward...
"You speak! Teach this monk and all people of the great earth. They cannot open their mouths to speak. It is a pity that Yaoshan let this monk go;
Yunyan lets out a long sigh, and Dongshan produces white mist. His words respond to samādhi; Xiyu, fellow practitioner, tell me:
whom do you take as your teacher? ○. The lands and their atoms—none can escape."
Those without eyes need not speak of seeing; they may avoid using light and darkness to warn the blind.

It is still easy for a wild ox to give birth to its young, but how could the child of a stone woman be anything but extraordinary? Solitary and radiant, its brilliance is peerless; one only fears the foolish monkey will stir the azure depths.
After the novice Gao was installed in his hermitage, he went to visit Yaoshan while it was raining. Yaoshan said, "You have come. The master replied, "I have.
Yaoshan said, "It is quite soaked. The master said, "This is not beating the drum and blowing the flute. Yunyan remarked, "There isn't even any hide."
"What drum are you beating? Daowu said, "There is no drum; what hide would you beat? Shanshan said, "Today there is truly a magnificent melody.
[The Master] commented: "A small stream returns to the sea; though the sea receives it, how could there be two sources? A disciple who seeks his teacher is granted permission by the teacher."

There is no other principle to consider. If one were to enter within, it would simply be all the Buddhas of the ten directions; why then would they further release the patriarchs of successive generations?
They chew up parents and six relations until they are a pulp; where could there be any conscious beings remaining? Therefore, the ancients said:
Without destroying conventional designations, one speaks of the true reality (*dharmatā*). Xuansha said: "In the place of function, the pivot does not change;
outside the mind, there is no separate dharma. Even so, it does not hinder beating the drum and playing the lute; it returns to that single assembly. Everyone, tell me:
where are the High Monk Yaoshan, the novice Yunyan, and Daowu right now? They are proclaiming the *prajñā*.

In the stage of faith, there is no place of idleness; know that the functioning of the mind is not erroneous. Within the Buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust, the wondrous essence lies in a single hair’s breadth.
You should perceive it in this way; what is spoken is merely according to suitability. The ancient masters were free from artifice; they needlessly blew upon a piece of cloth.
[The text] cites Master Shandao of the Stone Chamber. One night, while gazing at the moon with Yangshan, Yangshan asked:
"When this moon is crescent, where has its full aspect gone? When it is full, where has its crescent aspect gone? The Master said: "When it is crescent, the full aspect is hidden;
when it is full, the crescent aspect remains. Yunyan said: "When it is crescent, the full aspect remains; when it is full, [the crescent aspect] is absent."
The "Pointed" Form. Daowu said: "When it is pointed, it is not pointed; when it is round, it is not round. [The Commentator] says:
One night at Shishan, while sleeping and talking with Yangshan, he startled Yunyan and Daowu.
Without cause, at dawn he acted like a thief and refused to acknowledge his guilt. If this were not so, it would truly be difficult to expose him here at Puan.
On the thirtieth night, while Puan Hao was together with the Old Śākyamuni and all the Buddhas of the three periods of time enjoying the moon, he ventured to ask:
"Mountains, rivers, the great earth, form, emptiness, light, and darkness—where is this moon right now?"
If there were anyone who dared to step forward and could respond to this old monk with even a single word or phrase, I would cause their entire body to fester and rot,
causing them to fall into pits and ravines, leaving not even a hair’s breadth of them remaining.
The blue sky and white sun are ever in accord; only with clear eyes can one discern the monkey mirror. Since beginningless kalpas, it has not been polished;
those who know the sound in truth raise it in vain as a command for non-arising.
To cite Chan Master Deshan Xuanjian: When the Master arrived at Mount Gui, he walked from the west side of the Dharma Hall to the east, then turned to look back at the abbot’s quarters.
Mount Gui remained silent. The Master said, "Nothing! Nothing! He then went out to the front of the Sangha hall and said:

Nevertheless, he did not act with haste. He then prepared his formal demeanor and went up to visit. As soon as he stepped across the threshold, he held up his sitting cloth (zuoju) and called out, "Preceptor!
As Guishan was about to take up his whisk (boshi), the Master shouted at him and, shaking the hem of his robe, walked out.
The Master held up the whisk and said: "When the lion emerges from its den, the beasts of prey are struck with panic; when the great tiger crouches on the cliff, the wild jackals cannot pass.
Suddenly encountering one who subdues dragons and tames tigers—Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra—they must shed their fur and horns and return to the periphery.
With a single eye and no head, they sit sealing the void. At this very moment, Huishan and Deshan share a single nostril. Therefore, all..."
Just as he was traveling on foot, those without eyes were unwilling to believe him. Yet they were willing to believe Puan, who said of himself:
"This fellow who dandles his own shadow—difficult to believe, difficult to believe!"
Difficult to believe, difficult to hear—this One-Eyed Dragon. He spreads clouds and pours rain, yet leaves no trace to be found. Yet he was caught by Samantabhadra and pierced through the nose.
Now, the faith of the multitude shall never cease.

Citing Chan Master Dongshan Jia, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Brothers, at the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, whether heading east or west, you must go to a place where there are ten thousand miles of land without a single blade of grass;
only then will you succeed. He further said: "As for that very place of ten thousand miles without a single blade of grass—"
Furthermore, how does one proceed? Looking around at the assembly, he said: "If you wish to know this matter, it must be like flowers blooming upon a withered tree;
only then will you be in accord with it. Hearing this, Shishuang said: "Stepping out the door is already walking through weeds. Later, Ming'an said:
"Even if you do not step out the door, it is still a vast expanse of weeds."
The Master held up the staff and said: "Dongshan’s breath is clear and vigorous; he exerts his full strength for the sake of others, yet he still cannot avoid casting molten iron into the plow-mouth.
Shishuang is born in the great cold; following him, one adds frost upon ice, and can only attain Ming’an’s nobility."
Comparing these two, they were both as dull as straw mats. Puan examined them closely and could not find a single one who was sharp and quick-witted.
He then picked up his staff and said, "If you did not have this, you would never become sharp and quick-witted.
He threw down the staff, remained silent for a long while, and then asked, "Do you understand?"
Ten thousand *li* of land where no grass grows; this samādhi is named "Non-contention. Dreaming of traveling through the jade realm—after all, who is it that acts?
Wherever one is, the ground is vast and expansive; know that there are simply not two kinds. This Dharma-gate is neither entering nor exiting; let those who study it not be negligent.
To cite Chan Master Jianyuan Zhongxing: One day, he accompanied Daowu to attend a funeral. The Master reached out his hand and touched the coffin, asking, "Is it life?
Is it death? Daowu said, "I will not say it is life; I will not say it is death. The Master asked, "Why do you not say?
Daowu replied, "I will not say, I will not say. As they were returning together after the funeral, the Master said, "Today, the Master must..."
He said to Zhongxing, "If you do not speak further, I shall strike you. I replied, "Strike me as you please;
I will not speak when alive, nor will I speak when dead. The Master then struck me several times with his fist, after which I went to Shishuang and raised the previous question.
Shishuang said, "Did you not hear Daowu say, 'I will not speak when alive, nor will I speak when dead'? At that, I attained great enlightenment.
The Master held up the staff and said: "Jianyuan asked about life and death in his dreams; Daowu was beaten by ghosts during the day. Fortunately, he encountered Shishuang, who hurriedly woke him up.
Carrying consciousness, one handles a skull; handling a corpse—within this, I grant that it is truly difficult to do. Let him break my bones and dissolve my marrow."
[The Master] dispersed [the assembly]. In the end, he certainly did not deceive the son of Śākyamuni.
He cited the case of Chan Master Daodong of Qingping. The Master asked Cuibei, "What is the very meaning of the coming from the West?
Cuibei said, "Wait until there is no one, and I will tell you. After a long while, the Master said, "There is no one; please, Preceptor, speak. Cuibei—
Fayan descended from his meditation seat and led him into the Bamboo Grove. The Master said, "There is no one here; please, Venerable Sir, speak.
Fayan pointed to the bamboo and said, "This stalk is so long; that stalk is so short."
The Master holds up the staff and says: "Qingping was originally in a state of constant bliss, yet he refused to let his mind rest.

Because of his questioning, he became lost and entered the bamboo grove, whereupon distinctions of long and short were made. He then pronounces: "Cuiwei pointed to the bamboo to show Qingping; let us ask: has the elixir of immortality been perfected or not?
If one relies on sounds and forms to follow a master, even if one studies the profound for eons, one will not reach the ford. Puan, however, is not like this. Suppose there were...
A person asked about the direct meaning of the coming from the West. [The Master] held up a finger. After a long while, he said, "Do you understand?
If you do understand, it is just like this. If you do not understand, I shall spare you further instruction on climbing mountains and entering waters."
He leads the practitioners of dhyāna toward the Azure Peak; the path through its iron walls and bronze ramparts is no ordinary one. He points afar to the Twin Śāla Trees as the place of return;
even to this day, the spectral echoes still resound.
To cite Chan Master Datong of Touzi: While traveling, he encountered Zhaozhou on the road, who asked, "Are you not the Master of Mount Touzi?
The Master replied, "I beg for some money for tea and salt. Zhaozhou then went ahead and sat in the hermitage first.
When the Master later returned to the hermitage carrying a jar of oil, Zhaozhou said, "I have long admired Touzi; yet upon arriving, I find you are merely an oil-seller."
"Old man," the Master said, "you see only the oil-selling old man; you do not yet know Touzi. The monk asked, "What is Touzi?
The Master lifted up the jar and said, "Oil, oil."
The Master held up the staff and said: "Touzi was not right to let Zhaozhou off so easily, thereby allowing Zhaozhou to sit squarely upon the hearts of all saints and ordinary people alike.
Now that Touzi has returned, he has no place to hide his body or plant his feet;
what more can he say about 'oil'? Had Puan encountered him on the road at that time, the resulting defeat would have been no small matter."
"I now venture to ask you all: do you see Touzi? After a long silence, he looked around at those present and said, "This very Flower Eighteen is difficult to rival."
The ancients of Touzi continued the lineage; meeting a true adept, they immediately displayed their skill. Hanguang knew there was a master within the hermitage;
when the oil pitcher was raised, he responded without hesitation.

The story of Chan Master Qingzhu of Shishuang is recounted. While the Master was serving as the rice steward at Mount Gui, one day while he was sifting rice in his quarters, Mount Gui said, "Do not scatter the offerings of the donors. The Master replied, "I do not scatter them.
Mount Gui picked up a single grain from the ground and asked, "You say you do not scatter them; where did this one come from? The Master...
"No counterpart. Guishan further said, "Do not underestimate this single grain; hundreds of thousands of grains are born from this one grain.
The Master asked, "Hundreds of thousands of grains are born from this one grain; I wonder, from where is this one grain born?"
Guishan laughed "he-he" and returned to his quarters. That evening, he ascended the hall and said, "The assembly, there are worms in the rice!
[The Commentator] says: "Shishuang’s rice, together with the husks, is white as the heavens. When questioned, it turns out one cannot respond.
Do not let it be scattered, for it would be difficult to gather back; lest you be terrified by demons and heterodox paths. Now tell me: Does Shishuang have understanding, or does he not?"

"If there is seeing and understanding, why is there no response? If there is no seeing and understanding, why did Muzhou say, 'I cannot explain it,' and then laugh heartily before returning to his quarters?
Try to judge this for me. Muzhou said, "There are worms in the rice. Puan said, "There is rice in the worms.
For those who do not understand, their mouths are stuffed; for those who have awakened through understanding, they may freely interject. *Pfft!*
Wherever a man of the Way arrives, he fully manifests True Suchness (*tathatā*). If one seeks it through words and phrases, one cannot avoid being caught up in trivialities.
Take the Zen Master Xing of Jianyuan as an example: one day, while holding a spade, he walked from east to west and from west to east across the Dharma Hall.
Shishuang asked, "What are you doing? The Master replied, "I am seeking the sacred remains of the former master. Shishuang said, "The great waves are surging."
"Vast! White waves overflowing the heavens. What are you looking for—the spiritual bones of the former master? The Master said, "This is exactly when one must exert effort.
Fangshuang said, "In this place, not even a needle can pierce it. What effort could there be? The Master took a spade upon his shoulder and walked away.
Tayuan Fu said, "The spiritual bones of the former master still remain."
The Master held up the whisk and said: "Jianyuan seeking the sacred remains of his former master could not avoid wandering east and west;

Shishuang’s very foundation was crumbling like melting ice. Amidst the surging waves and white billows, tell me: are these all merely the views of those who travel to study? They seem to differentiate between distinctions.
If it were the Venerable Fu of Taiyuan, he would not have added these four characters; then the former master’s spirit would have been even less manifest, and his bones even more difficult to find."
The Old Man Pupan held up a clod of earth and said, "Spirit-bone, spirit-bone! Vague and indistinct. Brother Fu, brother Fu!
Deep and obscure. He then threw the earth onto the ground, looked around at those present, and asked, "Do you know where it has fallen?"
To investigate the source and examine the essentials, one must encounter the person directly; amidst the flames of the kalpa-ending fire, they pluck out the eyes.
Jianyuan suddenly entered the surging waves, yet even until this very day, his form remains unseen.
Citing Chan Master Dongshan Jia: He asked Elder Tai, "There is a thing that reaches up to heaven and down to earth, and is always present within movement and activity;
it is as black as lacquer. Where does its fault lie? Elder Tai said, "The fault lies in movement and activity.
The Master then snapped his fingers and said, "Get out!"
The Master held up the whisk and said: "Dongshan only managed to deceive the Elder.
If I were asked by Old Man Puan, 'There is a thing that reaches up to heaven and down to earth, is always present within activity, and is as black as lacquer—where does its fault lie?
I would have given him thirty blows of the staff immediately. Then I would ask Master Jia: 'Before heaven and earth existed, what did this thing rest upon?'"
What is it? Speak quickly, speak quickly! If you act like this, you will avoid being shouted out by him.

Dongshan’s livelihood has not yet been fully encompassed; he is too old, boring into the tortoise shell, rarely discerning the hexagram lines. There is a thing prior to heaven that possesses no form or appearance;
how could it be concerned with the interaction of movement and function or the crossing of colors?
Regarding Chan Master Hwangshan Wol-hyon: One day, Jak-san called out to him with a loud voice, asking, "Where are you from?
The Master replied, "I am a man from Min. Jak-san said, "Do you recognize this old monk? The Master asked, "Does the Monk recognize this student?
Jak-san said, "Not so. First, you must pay me the price for my straw sandals; only then will I [recognize you]."
[The monk] said, "I am returning to Jiangling; what is the price of rice there? The Master said, "If that is so, you do not recognize me.
[The monk] asked, "May I inquire, what is the price of rice in Jiangling? Jiashan said, "You are well able to roar."
The Master picks up the case and says: "The moon-disc of Mount Huang illuminates all things without exception; the straw sandals of Jia Shan are worth a price too difficult to repay.
If it is thus, then neither of the two recognizes the other, and not even one of them knows the other. The rice in Jiangling is used to pay for the straw sandals;
he is truly skilled at letting out a roar to communicate the news. *Du!* (A shout)

Not recognizing this as the true consciousness that possesses mind, one seeks no person throughout the reaches of the conscious mind. The rice fills the granaries of Jiangling and is originally priceless;
the full majesty of the lion cannot be captured in a painting.
A monk asked Luopu, "What is it like when a student intends to return home? The Master said, "The house is ruined and the people are gone; where would you go, my son?
The monk said, "If that is so, then I shall not return. The Master said, "The remaining snow in the courtyard is melted by the sun;
who will sweep away the drifting dust inside the room?"

The Master held up his whisk and said: "This monk heard that his house had been destroyed and saw it said that his family members were dead; thus he did not dare return home. Puan has nothing left to do.
Now, for the sake of Luopu, I shall offer a single moment of mourning: 'Alas! Heaven! Alas! Heaven!'"
The household is not broken and the people do not perish. Setting up a trap, it fails to respond and turns clumsy. The whisk made of tortoise hair laughs "he-he";
in the midsummer heat, there is a great frost.
Citing Chan Master Yungju Daoying: A monk asked, "What is it like when a wild goat hangs from its horns? The Master said, "Six times six is thirty-six.
He asked again, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Have you not heard it said that there are no tracks?
Another monk recounted this to Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou said, "Master Yungju is still around. The monk then asked, "When a wild goat hangs from its horns..."
"How is it at that time? Zhaozhou said, "Six times six is thirty-six.
[The Master] comments: Yunju’s response lacks a core; thus he says, "Six times six is thirty-six. This monk’s question is devoid of human sentiment;
he cannot avoid the "wild sheep hanging from a branch" (the tracks having vanished). Setting aside for a moment whether one understands or not, suppose this monk...
Questioning Puan: "What is it like when the wild goat hangs its horns? "Ninety-nine plus one equals eighty-one. "The eyes of the patch-robed monk are as black as lacquer;
leaning on the fence and groping along the wall, he does not know his own stench. Even the wild goat hanging from the horn does not recognize him. *O*—Bite!
Qianfeng raised his staff and addressed the assembly, saying: "If you raise one, you must not raise two. To let pass one move is to fall into the second.
Yunmen stepped forward from the assembly and said: "Yesterday someone came from Tiantai and is now heading for Nanyue.
Qianfeng sat down and said: "Tomorrow there will be no communal labor."
The Master picks up the case and says: "When Qiandeng opens his mouth, the moon is bright and the wind is clear. Yunmen’s response is wondrous and profound.
Unless one is a person who 'knows there is,' who can discern who it is that hears and probes amidst movement and stillness? Puan, however, was not like this: on the first mention he attained it;
on the second mention he did not let it pass; on the third mention he failed to pass the examination. But tell me, where does it ultimately land?"

Śakra, Brahmā, and the Heavenly Kings tread upon the ground with their jeweled crowns; yet if they do not recite the Avataṃsaka, the Buddha is neither rich nor noble. To transcend the four propositions is difficult;
to sever the hundred negations is easy. To sever the hundred negations is difficult; to transcend the four propositions is easy.
The Chan Master Wensui of Qishan is cited as an example. The Master entered the bathhouse and saw a monk treading a water wheel.
Upon seeing the Master, the monk stepped down from it and asked, "How is your health? The Master said, "Fortunately, you have been turning it along quite busily;
why must you act like this? The monk said, "If I did not do so, how else could it be? The Master said, "If it were like that, what would be the use of Qishan’s eyes? The monk said, "To act..."
"What is the Master’s eye? The Master then made a gesture with his hand as if brushing away his eyebrows.
The monk said, "The Master has attained such a state again. The Master said, "Yes, yes. Because I am thus, you may not be thus. The monk was speechless.

The Master said, "Seeking battle but failing to achieve merit—what a frustrating disappointment! After a long silence, he asked the monk, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master...
Qingyuan said, "Qinshan will carry a load for you.
He picked it up and said, "Qinshan recognizes his nature as he follows the current.
Although that monk was merely a mediocre fellow, at such a moment, he did not see Qinshan. How then could one avoid this old monk saying, "I will carry a load for you"?
Carrying a load. For those with eyes, it is no hindrance to add a footnote:
A single flick of the eyebrows reveals the eyes; yet, alas, this slight injury leaves no pupils. The lantern opens its mouth and laughs "he-he";
the patch-robed monk steps upon the wheel even in his dreams.
Let us cite Chan Master Xuansha Shibei. He offered this instruction, saying: "The venerable elders of all quarters all say they 'receive things and benefit living beings.
But let me ask you: suppose there are three types of patients—a blind person, a deaf person, and a mute person.

How would you receive them? If you raise your mallet or brandish your whisk, their eyes cannot see it; if you speak with them, they cannot hear you, and their mouths are mute. If you were to receive them..."
"No, the Buddha-dharma has no spiritual efficacy. At that time, a monk came forward and said, "Regarding the three types of sick people, does the Master permit us to deliberate upon them?
The Master said, "I do. "How would you deliberate on them? the monk asked. The monk then bowed respectfully and departed. The Master said:
"Not so, not so," said Luohan. "Guichen currently possesses eyes and ears; how do you, Master, receive him?
Zhongta said, "The three types of sick people—where are they right now?"
The Master holds up [the case] and says: "Although Great Master Xuansha possessed the eloquence to cut off the flow of all streams, what can he do?
He could only treat the illness of one who lacks eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind. This person is fundamentally without illness;

even if one were to cure them for their peace and happiness, it would not make one a masterful hand. Luohan (Arhat) has grown horns on his head and there is no way to bring him down; Zhongta cannot bear it."
What is the winter melon? It is a broken gourd. Puan shouted loudly into the nostrils of everyone, "Xuansha!
Xuansha! But first, take care of yourself; the wind has already arisen.
Throughout antiquity and today, those who study the Way and practice Zen have not yet mastered the subtle verbal expressions of the eyes and ears. A single grain of Xuan Sha has no abiding root;
from time to time he sets sail on a merchant ship to Hainan. *Kaido* (Swiftly Crossing).
Shaoxiu, the Mountain Master of Longji Mountain, addressed the assembly, saying: "The ordinary person possesses the dharmas of an ordinary person, yet the ordinary person does not know them.
The sage possesses the dharmas of a sage, yet the sage does not understand them. If the sage were to understand them, he would be an ordinary person;
if the ordinary person were to know them, he would be a sage. These two statements have one principle and two meanings. If anyone can discern them, they will not fail to be a Buddha."
Within the Dharma, there is a point of entry. If you cannot discern it, do not say that you have no doubts.
[The Master] remarked: "Old Master Xiu, though advanced in years, does not even hold a staff; he simply drills through the weeds like this."
"Running through the water—what cause for this? Puan picked up his staff and said, 'This has swallowed up both the holy and the ordinary;
now it is stable and convenient everywhere. He threw down the staff, his eyes circled about, and after a long while, he said:"
Do not say there is no doubt.

Longji raises clouds and rain, bestowing them everywhere; when neither sage nor ordinary person falls into extremes, with whom can he be compared? If one can uphold the Earth Store Seal of Emptiness, possessing both the round and the square, only then will there be no doubt.
Xuefeng addressed the assembly, saying: "The world is one zhang wide; the ancient mirror is one zhang wide.
The world is one chi wide; the ancient mirror is one chi wide. Xuansha pointed to the brazier before him and asked, "How wide is this brazier?
Xuefeng replied, "It is as wide as the ancient mirror. Xuansha said, "Old man, your feet have not yet touched the ground."
The Master picks up the case and says: "Xuefeng addressed the assembly: 'To have a mouth but no mind. Xuan Sha corresponds to this: 'To have a mind but no mouth. Now tell me:
Is Xuefeng’s world within the ancient mirror? Or is the ancient mirror within the world?
If you have not yet attained life, then go toward Xuan Sha’s brazier to smelt and refine the world, to polish the original radiance, until you lose sight of the moon in the water and the empty sky."
Flowers: only when every particle of dust is unobscured can one truly attain it.
A mirror contains worlds for thousands of springs; neither mark nor form, yet names are provisionally established. Though submerged in the world, they never depart from the substance of the mirror.
Who among those who pity living beings could truly join the company of Kāśyapa?

To cite Dongshan’s question to Yunju Deng: "In the case of a great icchantika who kills his father, harms his mother, sheds the blood of a Buddha, and breaks the harmony of the Sangha—amidst such various acts as these, where is filial piety? Yunju replied, "Only then does one attain true filial piety.
From that time on, Dongshan recognized him as the leader within the meditation hall.
The Master picks up the whisk and says: "Within the single Dharma-realm, there is only Dongshan who perceives that one who commits the five great rebellious acts is a filial son;
one who practices filial piety is a perpetrator of the five great rebellious acts. Now, Puan, with what do you provide for your parents?"
He stared with wide-open eyes and looked about in all directions. After a long while, he said, "In every place and at every turn, people do not recognize the Buddha's parents.
He asked again, "How does one commit the five heinous crimes? He replied, "Mutton broth and fine wine; vegetarian cakes and steamed buns.

Those who ride horses ride their horses; those who lead oxen lead their oxen. Some play the solitary flute horizontally; others clap their hands and sing aloud. Only one thing is absolutely forbidden."

It is said: "The man of snow within the fire at Zhao Yangzhou—neither a large scale can weigh it up, nor a small peck can measure it out. From immeasurable kalpas until this very moment, there is nothing that is not the Mind-Seal."
When Jia Shan was serving as a ferryman, an old woman carrying an infant boarded the boat and said, "I present my oars and dance with my paddles;
you do not even ask. She then asked, "Tell me, from where did the child in the old woman's arms come?
Jia Shan struck her with his oar. The old woman said, "This old woman has six children; five have not met a true teacher."
"Consciousness! This very thing is of no use either," he said, and threw it into the river. Jia Shan then stuck out his tongue. [The Master] commented:
"The teachers of all quarters say that at such a time, Jia Shan struck this old woman.
When Puan saw this woman, he shared one foot, one eye, and one mouth with Jia Shan; yet he could not speak it, nor could he go."
It cannot be attained. Even seeing it again, it cannot be attained. As for the child, that is not the question. How do you distinguish the place where Jia Shan stuck out his tongue?
The boatman’s vessel sails in vast stillness, never empty; time and again he clears the bright moon with the pure wind. Brandishing the oar and dancing with the paddle, there is nothing else.
The matter is simply intended to teach people how to understand the six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Xuefeng said: "Sitting by the rice fence, a starving dead man; standing by the river, a man dying of thirst. Xuansha said:
"Sitting inside the rice fence, a starving dead man; submerged head-first in the water, a man dying of thirst. Yunmen said: "The whole body is [the six powers]."
The rice. His whole body is water.
He picks it up and says: "Great indeed is Xuefeng! Even when one arrives here, one cannot avoid breaking one into two.
Puan recites a mantra: *Varoṭaṅga*. He removes the dead man from the edge of the rice basket. *Vaha*. This single grain is profound.
Xuedou said, "Sha is groundless. He was led by Xuefeng into the rice and the water. Now, all living beings throughout the great earth drink this water and eat this rice;
be careful to look after them closely. Though it was Xuan Sha, he could both kill people and bring them to life;
yet only the old fellow Yunmen swallowed his voice and endured his breath, unable to manage it. Therefore, he mixed mud with water."
Where there are no clouds, there is nowhere that is not the gate. When the blade is sheathed and not revealed, the principle is difficult to discuss. Xuefeng did not exhaust the meaning of Xuansha;
he merely provoked the villagers, village after village.
The scripture states: "An old woman to the east of the city was born at the same time as the Buddha. They lived together for a lifetime, yet she did not wish to see him.
Every time she saw the Buddha approaching, she would immediately turn away to avoid him; she retreated upward and downward in every direction, but could not escape him anywhere.
She then covered her face with her hands, yet within the palms of all ten fingers, she saw the Buddha everywhere."
The Master held up the whisk and said: "Tsk! This old woman has truly no sense of measure. She was contemporaneous with the Buddha; she is non-dual and unborn.
Since she could neither grasp nor reject, she should have simply sat steadily in the hall, opening her mouth when food arrived and reaching out her hand when chopsticks were presented.
Yet, for no reason, she has performed all this feigned strangeness, corrupting the sons and daughters of the family. Had she been instructed by Puhua at that time..."
As soon as Zen Master An saw the old woman, he buried both her and the Buddha at once, leaving behind only this "man who plays with shadows.
At all times, he provides skillful means for others; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, is this not a source of joy? It is further said: "Even now, nothing is lacking."
Like water for brewing tea, I wait for an old friend; when the one who knows the music tastes it, they smile with joy. Yet the tea and water originally have nothing to say;
to raise an eyebrow is already to deceive one's own mind.
Citing Master Yongjia, he said: "Neither form nor emptiness, yet nothing is not empty; this is the Tathāgata’s true mark.
[The Master] remarked: "Consider this carefully. When Master Yongjia speaks thus, he has no head or tail at all.

Now, if in a single thought you cast aside worldly entanglements and travel everywhere to seek out spiritual friends, with your staff slung over your shoulder, it is entirely for the sake of studying the Buddha."
Knowledge and vision. To thoroughly investigate this great matter of birth and death—how is it? There is no form; there is no emptiness; there is not even non-emptiness.
Yet you teach people: where are they to search? *Ei!* Within that which is unspeakable and beyond description, it is again unspeakable. In the end, it is thus.
I have not yet attained the ability to cite the ancients and discuss the present; even "wood-slave" and "grass-woman" must exert their skillful effort.
Grasses and trees know well that they are not external objects, yet sentient beings fail to believe they are themselves Vairocana.
Xuefeng led the community in a communal labor of weeding a field. Seeing a snake, he prodded it up with his staff and called to the assembly, saying, "Look!
Look! He then used a knife to cut it in two. Xuansha, however, tossed the staff behind him and did not look back.
The assembly was stunned. Xuefeng said, "How magnificent!"

The Master held up his whisk and said: "Xuefeng was a great practitioner, yet he did not act appropriately in slaying the snake. According to the law, this fellow shall never again return to this world or take human form.
Although Xuansha had no hand in the matter, it was improper for him to move the corpse right before one's face;
he too receives thirty blows with the 'hare-horn staff' and must return once more to the distant lands of rebirth. Truly a great ordeal, truly a great ordeal—for the sake of the assembly."
Exert yourself! What is the reason for such persistence? Suddenly raising his staff, he said, "There is yet another. He spoke again: "To let one move pass is to let go of a single point.

Flying through the air or touching the ground—sentiment relies on consciousness; the mountains and rivers of the great earth are worn away by sentiment and consciousness. Form and emptiness, light and darkness, are without marks."
It is like this. When you pick up the snake, do you understand?
When Jiufeng was serving as the attendant to Shishuang, Shishuang passed away. The assembly wished to invite the first seat in the hall to succeed him as abbot.
Jiufeng said, "Wait until I have questioned him; if he understands the late master’s meaning, we shall proceed exactly according to that."
The former master served him and was asked: "Rest! Cease! A single thought for ten thousand years!
Cold ashes and withered wood! A waterfall still within the mouth! A single length of white silk! A censer in an ancient temple, silent and cold—how do you understand this?
The monk said, "This is a matter of the realm of uniformity. Feng said, "If that is so, then you have not yet understood it before you even begin."

The Master’s intention was in the seat. [Fengxue] said, "Do you not agree with me? Bring some incense. If I do not understand the late master’s intention, I shall not be able to cast off my body when the smoke rises.
Having finished speaking, he cast off his body. Fengxue patted his back and said, "To sit and die or stand and die is certainly possible;
however, the late master’s intention has not yet been realized."
The Master picks up the case and says: "Jiupeng carries his board like this; the First Seat has an iron heart. Examining it closely, Jiupeng is at fault.
But tell me, where does the fault lie? When the incense smoke rises, Puan, if he were to grant permission, would say:
'Heaven! Heaven! He drives people to their deaths.'"
Standing to die or sitting to pass away is no marvel; few people know of Shishuang’s final transformation.
The Lion of Jiufeng roars across the heavens, startling the wild foxes to death in an instant.
The teaching is cited as follows: "Before leaving Tuṣita, he already descended into the royal palace; before emerging from his mother's womb, his work of saving beings was already complete.
[The Master] picks up the theme and says: "Sentient beings and all Buddhas are the empty nature of all phenomena; apart from descending, emerging, and saving, they are neither born nor extinguished."
Snow buries a cesspool; it is neither defiled nor pure. Carrying water and throwing it into a river; it neither increases nor decreases.
Opening up Tuṣita to reveal the royal palace, Queen Māyā vanishes into old age, and King Śuddhodana gives birth to a prince.
Every word and every phrase speaks of empty delusions. *Hūṃ*. *Uḥ*.
The record relates that while Xuansha and Xuefeng were out walking in the mountains, Xuansha said, "I am now going to employ my great function;
how will you respond, Preceptor? Xuefeng then took three wooden balls and threw them all at once. Xuansha made a gesture as if striking a shield, whereupon Xuefeng said:
Only by personally reaching Mount Ling could you attain such a state. Xuansha said, "It is simply one's own. [The Master] comments:
Xuefeng and Xuansha were father and son traveling together; their journey through the mountains was not two separate things.
Xuansha suddenly spoke in his sleep, while Xuefeng casually feigned strangeness. Their household goods were neither lacking nor deficient; there was simply nothing to buy.
There is no selling it off. Had he encountered Puan at the outset, he would have inevitably suffered a total defeat.
Xuansha’s great function and Xuefeng’s three performances caused the mountains and rivers of the great earth to tremble six times over.

Citing the teaching: When the World-Honored One was first born, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward earth, walked seven steps around, and looked in the four directions, saying, "In the heavens above and on the earth below, I alone am the Honored One. Yunmen said, "If you had asked me to see him at that time..."
"Strike him dead with a single blow! Give him to the dogs to eat, so that the world may enjoy peace. [The Master] then remarked:
"If it were the World-Honored One, he would not have had to take his first birth, nor would he have further extended his hands and feet or gazed about in the four directions."
They struggle for others and snatch from me, yet they claim supremacy where there is a Buddha. Do not say that Yunmen did not let them pass;
he suddenly took up his staff, stared with wide eyes, and after a long while said, "I am ashamed.

Then, having made the ten directions perpetually pure, he cast down the staff and asked the assembly, "Do you know where it has landed? If you have not yet understood, you are merely talking in your sleep."
By day one must not speak of people; by night one must not speak of ghosts. Since the accomplishment of the Way through immeasurable kalpas, everything has been present here all at once.
To cite the case of Danxia visiting National Teacher Zhong: He encountered the National Teacher’s attendant. Danxia asked, "Is the National Teacher here?
The attendant replied, "He is indeed here, yet even the Buddha-eye cannot see him. Danxia said, "The dragon begets dragon offspring; the phoenix begets phoenix chicks.
When the attendant reported this to the National Teacher, the National Teacher struck the attendant with twenty blows of the staff.
The Master holds up the case and says: "Danxia did not know how to act as a guest; therefore, he troubled the host.

The attendant had learned the words of the National Teacher but did not understand the National Teacher’s conduct. Consequently, he was doused with 'evil water' by Danxia and further received twenty blows of the National Teacher’s staff.
Now tell me, everyone: what was the National Teacher’s intention in striking the attendant? [The Master] provides the verse: "A thousand..."
The Great Compassionate One reaches out his hand, yet gropes and finds nothing.
A three-legged donkey trots on its hooves, merely seeking to press upon the young practitioners along the way. A single fragment of Danxia remains unstained by dust;
it encompasses all existence—how could it be called "able"?
Xuan Sha ascended the hall. Once the assembly had gathered and settled, he suddenly took up his staff and drove them all away.
Later, he said, "Today I offered an interpretation that nearly sent me shooting into hell like an arrow. An attendant remarked, "Fortunately, the Master has returned to human form once again."
The Master held up the case and said: "People say that Xuansha was beyond saving; I say that Xuansha was exactly like a wildcat roaming the fields.
If he could have been saved, he would have escaped hell and become a person of liberation; if he could not be saved, he followed others into hell."
A fish on the shore will not live long; a person falling into a deep abyss perishes instantly.
Who knows that river and land share the same nature? It is just like hell and heaven.
When Xuefeng passed away, Xuansha served as the presiding mourner. He assembled the great assembly to prepare tea, lifted up his cup, and said:
"If you can speak, the late master was without fault; if you cannot speak, the fault lies with the late master.
He asked this three times, yet none could respond. Xuansha smashed the cup to pieces and returned to his quarters.
The Master picked up the case and said: "I say that Xuansha did not know how to act as the chief mourner. This is why it is said:
'Whether the former master had faults or not—if you understand how to act as the chief mourner, you should naturally bury him all at once, skin and bone together.
This was merely to avoid a scene of domestic turmoil that would have startled the skull. Now that Puan has reached this point, how could he remain silent?"
Pointing to his nostrils, he said: "Alas! How lamentable! We humbly pray that you will graciously accept this offering.

Within the light of formlessness, one plays with shadows; though the form resembles those of other species, the nature is that of true heaven. Clad in fur and bearing horns, water and ice are blended;
shaving the head and donning robes, ice merges with water."
There was once a monk traveling to Mount Wutai who asked an old woman, "Which way does the road to Mount Wutai go?
The old woman said, "Go straight ahead. The monk then departed. The old woman called out after him, "Are you going that way again? The monk reported this to Zhaozhou.
Zhaozhou said, "I shall go and test this old woman. The next day, Zhaozhou went there and asked for the road to Mount Wutai.
"Where is the road leading? The old woman said, "Go straight ahead. Zhaozhou went on his way. The old woman said, "He has gone off in that manner again.
Upon returning, Zhaozhou said to the monks, "I have thoroughly exposed this old woman for you all."
The Master held up the staff and said: "No one knows that Zhaozhou reached Mount Tai without moving a step;
he passed through without opening his mouth and yet exposed the old woman. If you all believe the old woman’s words, go straight ahead;
if you do not believe them, then go in this way."
The ancients left behind their intent but did not leave words; the old woman at Mount Tai stands on one side.
Once you have recognized the old woman of Mount Tai, the news of Zhaozhou will never cease.
To cite Chan Master Zhaozhou Congshen: while he was serving as the fire-attendant under Nanquan, one day he bolted the door and shouted, "Help with the fire!
Help with the fire! When the assembly all arrived, the Master said, "If you can speak, I will open the door.
The assembly had no reply. Nanquan took the key and passed it through the window to the Master; the Master then opened the door.
The Master picks up the case and says: "It is clear that this old fellow Zhaozhou was right in the midst of a fire raging within the water.
To call forth a troop who were half-deaf and half-blind, making them lean on fences and grope along walls—what benefit was there in that? Fortunately, Nanquan’s heels did not touch the ground;
he used water to extinguish the water, and we can deeply rejoice that all is well."
Zhaozhou was in urgent need of someone to complete the task; the assembly lacked even a half-eye of intimacy. Riding upon a golden-haired lion, he roams beyond the mundane world;
Nanquan’s every drop of meaning is profoundly deep.
The Universal Hut’s Family Treasure, the Universal Hut’s Family Treasure— Do not seek it out. When deluded, it is not seen; Everywhere there is affliction.
When awakened, it is formless, Like the bright, shining sun. Neither grasping nor rejecting, It is naturally and perfectly so.
Who gives birth? Who falls ill? Who dies? Who grows old? The person of great realization has no proof; the ordinary person is inverted. When the sun sets, the path is late;
when the sun rises, the path is early. Having pupils but no eyes, they strike their heads and bump their foreheads, leaning on fences and groping along walls.
They cast away gold to embrace grass; they are wooden figures with mechanical joints, prying their mouths open to cry out "excellent!"
If pulled by a thread, it moves; if the rope is severed, it falls. Let it loose in a place of leisure.

Like a tattered scrap of paper, it is originally formless; yet it is manipulated by others, adorned with five colors, and names and titles are established merely to deceive them—when has it ever protected itself? One passes the days in clamor and bustle, utterly without reliance.
When asked about their noble surname, they immediately say: "Cao, Mu, Li, or Zhang. "Just now I have arrived;
what urgent matter is there? "I have come specifically to trouble you. "Insufficient food and clothing. "Do not be offended by my coarse speech; my mouth is uneasy.
"Drought and flood in the fields and gardens. "To entice the ancestors to be buried, I am moving graves for construction."

The practitioner of sorcery calculates that the years and months are unfavorable; yet, though they have traveled to sacred mountains and prostrated before the peaks, there is nowhere they have not been, and they have never once received a response.

To this day they remain clamorous and noisy. Furthermore, they encounter a diviner who speaks in gibberish and nonsense, urging them to quickly move their ancestors' graves, relocate the door and hearth, and claiming that silkworms and mulberry trees will flourish and official rank and emolument will soon arrive.
They merely believe in the Eight Trigrams and take pleasure in the transformations of Yin and Yang. Ministers and high officials are all those who have been stirred up by me;
their conduct is light and frivolous, shaking their heads and wagging their brains. They bestow bountiful gifts upon others while repeatedly exclaiming "excellent!
Because of this, they fall into poverty, suffering distress day and night. It is like adding frost to snow; in this bitter cold, they can hardly survive.
Suddenly, within my ears, I heard that Puan had attained the Way; He took earth in his hand and made it into incense.
One must go there in person to experience it for oneself. The sound of the bells rolled on and on; My own heart grew frantic. No one came to inform me;
the novice attendants paid no heed, And the *vinaya-dhara* was haughty and disdainful. I stilled my mind and settled my intent, Whispering these bitter words in a low voice.
Before long, I indeed saw an old man; Carrying a single staff and wearing a coarse cloth robe, he raised a finger.
He told me to speak quickly. His nostrils reach the heavens; his eyes are weary and spent.
He says no more of money, nor does he crave jewels. Do not harbor delusive thoughts; do not fabricate anything at all.
Simply by recognizing the mind, there is no dharma that cannot be reached. You are originally the Buddha; there is no need to seek elsewhere.
Free from all names and forms, the Dharma-body is naturally preserved. Birth and extinction are fundamentally non-existent.
The various Buddhas are merely provisional designations for worldly and trans-worldly phenomena; there is absolutely nothing that can be spoken of. This true single mind is the non-empty *lingbao*.
The Buddhas of the ten directions are all within this; all illusory conditions arise from this mind. Since there is no master to this mind, illusory transformations must be exhausted.
When the mind is equal to the great void, one recognizes this mind as being like a lapis lazuli bead that reflects colors according to its surroundings.
Without attachment and without departure, having attained the meaning, one forgets the words; once fully realized, there is nothing more to say.
There is nothing to be discarded, nor is there anything to be grasped. One does not burn scriptures, nor does one transform paper into offerings.
To hold a vegetarian feast for those without eyes is to offer sustenance to snakes and rats; such giving lacks clarity and leads instead to further sinking and falling.
Though these may be considered virtuous causes, they can give rise to evil consequences. Even the sons of nobles and princes, while cultivating merit and wisdom, [may fall into this error].
Observing the fast with diligence, giving alms of food and clothing—yet as soon as they lift their heads, everything is already prepared.
Why must one bury the corpse and seek out an auspicious site through divination? If the mind is not good, nothing will be beneficial;
every action performed and every place where ghosts are worshipped only serves to wear away the dry bones while the consciousness sinks into the depths.
If one does not contemplate the good while alive, the hells will appear at death. Wherever one dwells, one should practice compassion;
yet those who do not believe in the Buddha-dharma through skillful means will be reborn poor and lowly—less than one in ten thousand.
The forms of officials appear, filling the mountains and ridges; with long heads and sharp beaks, they catch fish and snare birds, tormenting one another through myriad kalpas.
Not a single hair’s breadth of goodness; all is but the binding of enmity. Failing to recognize one's parents, their cries and shouts fill the heavens.
Greed, lust, killing, and stealing—their sins are beyond description. Before the years of their lifespan are complete, they are ensnared by the king’s law.
The mind knows no satisfaction; afflictions reach the very heavens. For what reason do you not cease? Purify the field of the mind.
If one does not drink alcohol, the light of wisdom will be bright; by associating with the virtuous, the mind will naturally become refined and beautiful.
If one does not eat meat, parents-in-law will not weep; day and night the spirit will be tranquil, and benevolent deities will assist with blessings.
If one refrains from killing and stealing, one’s own person will be free from affliction; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, the mind will be without distress.
If one refrains from sexual misconduct, one’s pure conduct will be profound; the spirit shall not be impaired, and the body will be at peace.
If one refrains from false speech, one will always associate with noble companions; guarding the mouth like a sealed jar, one is undisturbed by cold or heat.
If one refrains from covetousness, one meets all things as they appear; seeing them as if not seeing, turning away as if not turning away.
If one is free from anger and delusion, The eyes and ears are like mud; Though heaven overturns and earth turns upside down, I myself remain unaware.
If one refrains from harsh speech, The body is like a clay dog; When people come, it does not bark, And when struck with a stick, it does not flee.
If one refrains from divisive speech, One rests in leisure without affairs; Who is right and who is wrong? It is but the clear breeze and the bright moon.
If one refrains from frivolous speech, with body and mind as one, one will be honored wherever one goes.
This is the tenth of the ten unwholesome paths; lost in delusion, people do not see it, but the Buddha has distinguished it for them. Through awakening, one sees for oneself;
by practicing according to this, one beholds one's original face. Among the sentient beings contained within the great earth, who would dare to treat such a person with contempt?
The mind is one with the One Mind; it transforms according to karma. If I am not as [I should be], I shall simply consume what is manifest before me.
I cause initial awakening to arise, responding to the Buddha’s skillful means. I turn the ten unwholesome deeds into the ten wholesome deeds, never again deceiving you.
Heaven also constantly wishes that you transcend the three realms and perceive the Buddha’s vision and knowledge.
The fleshly eyes of ordinary beings do not see because they lack clarity; there are no sun, moon, or lamps.
It is like opening one's eyes to look at colors against a surface of black lacquer: the colors immediately return to emptiness, and within that emptiness nothing can be grasped.
It is exactly as if one were blind and, though opening the eyes, sees nothing—just as if one had no eyes at all. Whether seeing or not seeing, there is absolutely nothing that can be called good.
The eye is not the eye; seeing is not seeing. Empty form has no reality.

If one does not understand the skillful means to reach the source and realize the mind, this is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. If the mind is not yet realized, the karma of consciousness turns black.
Today’s peace and joy are merely following light as it appears. When the light of the eyes falls to the ground, darkness pervades everywhere.
The karma of the mind manifests like thunderclaps and lightning flashes; it strikes terror into heaven and earth. Who can one turn to for refuge?
Amidst hundreds of thousands of sword-wheels and chariots of fire with flashing bolts, in a single kṣaṇa, the soul and consciousness are scattered and dispersed.
This may last for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, yet karma knows no interruption. How can this be compared to the worldly affairs of public entanglements and private fetters?
Alas for sentient beings! They still greedily crave their food; yet if they were to contemplate death, it would be urgent and difficult to discern the five thousand scriptures.
The secret words are infinite, yet it is only because of the ignorant mind that habitual tendencies have become so deeply ingrained.
Once one has been transformed by hearing the sutras, one’s own person will face no difficulty. When a single person attains full realization, they shall eliminate the afflictions for the multitude.
If one does not refrain from unwholesome deeds, evil will not dissipate. If one hears their cries, how can one bear to eat?
Upon seeing sentient beings, one should weep for them when they die. Even if one’s body is clothed and mouth is fed, it is difficult for the mind to find contentment.
Until the very moment of death, the consciousness clings and pursues; according to its thoughts, it takes rebirth, certain to enter among the fur-bearing beasts.
If the mind does not recollect the Buddha, one remains perpetually in prison; if the mind recollects what is good, then there are good fruits and good causes.
Though the whistling bamboos and shoots have never been planted, wild chrysanthemums cover the ground and grain is obtained from tilled fields;
from the plowed fallow land, millet is obtained. Delighting in goodness leads to heaven; committing evil leads to hell.
Good and evil are not different; they arise from the straightness or crookedness of the mind. Believing in the Buddha yet prostrating to clay [idols], one becomes increasingly deluded.
Believing in spirits and burning paper money, one merely wastes grain and bark. Believing in the sutras yet reading only the characters, one does not engage with their true meaning.
Believing in the Way yet practicing licentiousness, one only deceives one's own heart. Believing in goodness yet coveting wealth, one remains a fool until death.
Believing that killing and stealing bring no evil retribution before long, Believing that speaking of others' faults is right while one's own is wrong,
And believing in sin without repentance— Like a moth in its ignorance, scorched by fire and fried in oil, It departs only to return again, like a drifting vagrant.
With greed, anger, delusion, and craving, One thought-moment performs merit, While the next thought-moment undergoes punishment.
Failing to comprehend the principles of reality, people delusively cling to spirits and ghosts; failing to understand the nature of affairs, they add vinegar to the plums.
In times of urgency, they meet urgency with urgency; they refuse to do what ought to be done.

Seeing others' wealth and status, they single-mindedly attend upon them, using a single coin as a pretext to demand ten coins of profit; including wife and children, they become the servants of others.
Observe closely the spirit of the man: It is not that I am right and he is wrong; rather, it is that I am not.
The existence or non-existence of things is fixed; Causes and effects follow one another in succession. Laziness leads to poverty; Diligence brings wealth and honor.
By cultivating much Prajñā, One obtains the grace of compassion. In this life, one will be harmonious and gentle, And be respected wherever one goes.
Coming to be born in the Buddha-land, one awakens the faith of the multitude; habitual tendencies are purified, and whether walking or staying, one is always in meditative concentration.
Within this concentration there is wisdom, yet the essence of wisdom is like a mirror—a mirror that is not a mirror. To cling to "is" or "is not" creates illness;
one must lose both "is" and "is not. This is the Great Perfect Wisdom Mirror. If a person fully realizes this, what is defilement and what is purity?
Fundamentally there is no front or back; it is the radiance of one's vital nature. This nature is precisely Buddha-nature;
this life-force is precisely the life of wisdom. Neither born nor aging, who could die and who could fall ill? It encompasses both existence and non-existence, lacking nothing and having no surplus.
When the wind moves and dust arises, there is nothing that does not respond accordingly. Whether water or land, form or emptiness, the veins and blood are interconnected.
Not even a mote of dust can penetrate; the True Path is not realized.

Influences and echoes lack consciousness, like a corpse with a pin stuck in its head that makes the eyes blink, or a needle in its foot that causes it to groan and cry out in pain when questioned about its ailment—resembling a mere wriggling creature. Taking the false for a body, it is produced by the power of karma.

That which is formed must inevitably decay; that which decays takes shape once more. Formation is fundamentally empty—who can understand that the principle of both "following" and "not following" is the foundation?
Taking "non-abiding" as the principle, there is neither emptiness nor abiding;
it is no different from space. One must quickly realize this and cast off the cage! Through this, the Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the present attain great penetration.
Śākyamuni’s personal seal is like empty space; it is like the moon in water. It manifests its principle according to objects, just as water is its substance.
The moon in the water and space are identical; the appearances of existence and non-existence—both aspects are the same.
Where there is sameness, there is no obstruction; where there is obstruction, it is not the Middle Way. That which is not the Middle Way is not the Buddha; yet even the Buddha is without limit.
Shining through the present and illuminating the past, it cannot be deceived or obscured. It is the mother of the myriad dharmas, the public patriarch of all Buddhas and patriarchs.
If a person thoroughly understands this, they are identical to the Buddha. If a person does not understand, they are blind and deaf to the myriad dharmas;
it would be like idle chatter, a mere waste of one's daily labor. Such a family treasure shall never be empty.
Ultimate non-explanation; the Dharma is fundamentally not empty. Master Puan reveals his family treasure to the assembly. Imperial Composition:

A Praise for the Great Virtuous Bodhisattva Puan Zhi-shan Hong-ren Yuan-tong Zhi-hui Ji-gan Miao-ying Ci-ji Zhen-jue Zhao-xiang Hui-qing Huo-guo Xuan-jiao Ultimate non-explanation; the Dharma is fundamentally not empty. Master Puan reveals his family treasure to the assembly. Imperial Composition:
A Praise for the Great Virtuous Bodhisattva Puan Zhi-shan Hong-ren Yuan-tong Zhi-hui Ji-gan Miao-ying Ci-ji Zhen-jue Zhao-xiang Hui-qing Huo-guo Xuan-jiao.

I, the Emperor, reflect that the Way of the Buddha is vast and all-pervading; its myriad scriptures and ten thousand teachings are none other than exhortations toward goodness and transformations away from evil, intended to deliver and save all living beings.

The merit it encompasses is inexhaustible. To the Most Virtuous Bodhisattva Puan—whose supreme goodness and great benevolence are perfectly pervasive, whose wisdom is complete and penetrating, who responds wondrously to silent invocation, who provides compassionate salvation and true awakening, and who bestows auspicious blessings and sagely joy while protecting the state and propagating the teaching—I pay my respects.
He was truly a Buddha come again, manifesting his transformation at Cihua Temple in Yuanzhou, Jiangxi. His physical form was perfectly harmonious, and he was fully endowed with both merit and wisdom.
Internally, he harbored compassion and salvation; externally, he displayed supernatural powers. He subdued demons and spirits, and extinguished calamities and misfortunes.
He traveled extensively through all lands to rescue and deliver all beings; his spiritual responses were manifest and his wondrous power was unfathomable.
The precious instructions he bestowed consist of over one thousand six hundred words, which expound upon inexhaustible fundamental principles and reveal the most subtle and profound mysteries.
Vast, they encompass everything; precise, they leave nothing unprovided for. They serve as various skillful means for all sentient beings.

It is easy. Should there be those capable of donning this teaching with devotion and upholding it, they will be like those who travel through a treasury of jewels, each obtaining whatever they desire according to their wishes;
or like those who, hungry, partake of the food of Fragrant Accumulation, immediately attaining full satiety.

If one does not apply oneself to this, yet desires to seek the Unsurpassed, Right, and True [Enlightenment], it is like traveling a distant road in the darkness or sitting in a dark room—ultimately it will be of no benefit. I have recently gazed upon the True Truth.
Briefly investigating the ultimate purpose, one brings great benefit to the multitude of living beings in Jiaxing.

Those of virtuous faith who can guide themselves according to this shall enjoy blessings and attain auspiciousness; those who violate it and fail to observe it will inevitably tread upon calamity and summon misfortune.

As the Sutra says: "In families that accumulate goodness, there will surely be an abundance of blessings; in families that accumulate non-goodness, there will surely be an abundance of calamity. It further says:

"Performing good brings down a hundred blessings; performing evil brings down a hundred calamities. I have carefully recorded this general outline to instruct those who come after, and I append to it a eulogy, saying:
The Tathāgata’s manifested bodies fill every place; Their merit benefits all beings, pervading realms as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
The Great Awakened Teacher, suchness itself, Manifests inconceivable supernatural powers within the world.
The Buddha-body is non-dual; Its essence and form are profound, perfect, and luminous.
A mass of mani-jewels and purple gold, Exquisite, majestic, and sovereign;
Fully endowed with merit, wisdom, skillful means, and great compassion, With vows for vast salvation, Universally gathering all sentient beings;
The power of the Dharma reaches everywhere, Dispelling the heterodox and extinguishing demons and sprites, Stilling calamities and eliminating epidemics.
Washing away all transgressions, one attains auspiciousness as desired. The instructions bestow mantras that fully reveal the secrets of the Tathāgatas.
With earnest devotion, he guides the ignorant and deluded; With urgent sincerity, he transforms those of virtuous nature.
Like pearls and jewels compared to gold and jade, This supreme treasure has no equal— For those who hear it and those who see it.
There is none who does not give rise to joy, Universally exhorting all toward wholesome conditions. Reverently receive this treasure of the household;
If one does not value what is good, The arts and the Way will ultimately provide no salvation. It is like entering a mountain of jewels:
Only by obtaining the jewels can one’s purpose be fulfilled. If there are those who do not obtain the jewels, Returning empty-handed, what benefit is there in their intent?
Thus, these words of praise are composed to glorify [the Buddha] for all eternity, to assist and support our Imperial enterprise,
and to cause merit and virtue to pervade all beings. *Fubian Anlu*, Volume Three (End).
